Even if a complex-like type does provide ordering operators (for example, for use in containers), it is not misclassified as a real scalar: the field axis is read from numeric_field, whose default reports complex whenever the type exposes the real()/imag() API, so RealScalar, which requires a real field, is not satisfied regardless of ordering.

The different names reflect domain conventions: math::modulus is traditional complex analysis terminology, while math::magnitude follows physics and engineering conventions for vectors. Relationship to algebraic structures explains why the vector CPO is not named norm, and Customization Point Objects (CPOs) lists the norm-named fallbacks that let types from linear algebra libraries integrate without adaptation.

Arithmetic types like int and double satisfy requirements for multiple characters: real scalar (primary use), 1-dimensional vector, and scalar tensor measures like von Mises stress. Type safety comes from quantity_character matching in the quantity specification:

// All valid uses of double:
quantity mass = isq::mass(5.0 * kg);        // Scalar
quantity v = isq::velocity(10.0 * m/s);     // 1D vector
quantity sigma = isq::stress(100.0 * Pa);   // Degenerate (1×1) tensor

For the full second-order tensor, [mp-units] provides cartesian_tensor (a fixed 3×3 representation, not proposed in this paper), and third-party matrix types such as Eigen::Matrix3d work directly as well. In practice, though, most engineering extracts scalar measures from tensor fields rather than manipulating full 3×3 matrices (von Mises stress, principal stresses, shear components, hydrostatic stress), which is why arithmetic types remain useful as degenerate tensor representations for the tensor character.

12.2 Concept Hierarchy

Most of the concepts described below are exposition-only: they capture how the library classifies representation types internally and are not part of its public interface. The only public concept in this chapter is representation_of. The building-block and character concepts (Addable, ScalableWith, RealScalar, Vector, and the rest) exist to define it and to explain how a representation type is recognized. As in the Synopsis, their names are shown in italics.

These concepts are syntactic: they constrain which operations are available and that results have a common type with T (std::common_with). They do not (and a C++ concept cannot) enforce the algebraic laws (associativity, commutativity, distributivity, existence of identities, compatibility of an order with the arithmetic) that the corresponding mathematical structures require. This is the same limitation std::regular and std::totally_ordered already accept. For this reason the concepts are named for the role a type plays rather than for the structure it resembles; Relationship to algebraic structures below maps each one to the structure it approximates and lists the laws left unchecked.

The requirements summarized in the table above map directly to a hierarchy of C++ concepts. The lowest-level building blocks are:

template<typename T>
concept WeaklyRegular = copyable<T> && equality_comparable<T>;

template<typename T>
concept Addable = requires(const T a, const T b) {
  { -a } -> common_with<T>;
  { a + b } -> common_with<T>;
  { a - b } -> common_with<T>;
};

template<typename T, typename S>
concept ScalableWith = requires(const T v, const S s) {
  { v * s / s } -> common_with<T>;
  { s * v / s } -> common_with<T>;
  { v / s * s } -> common_with<T>;
};

WeaklyRegular is std::regular without default-initialization. Default construction is not required: some representation types cannot provide a meaningful default-constructed value (see, e.g., [P2993R0]) yet are otherwise well-behaved as quantity representations.

Addable requires unary negation (-a) alongside + and -, so it models an additive group. Inverses are required because the library forms differences (of deltas, and of points); types that support only accumulation are out of scope.

ScalableWith<T, S> constrains the round-trip v * s / s rather than the intermediate v * s. This lets types whose operator*/operator/ change the type (quantities being the canonical example) still satisfy the concept, as long as scaling by s and back lands on a type with a common type with T. The round-trip requirement also rejects irreversible type promotion, where operator* decays to a type that has no common type with T (e.g. a checked-integer wrapper without implicit conversions whose operator* returns a raw arithmetic type). The constraint is on the result type, not its value: over integer representations v * s / s need not equal v (integer division truncates). Because the round-trip divides by s, the scalar type S must itself be division-capable; scaling by ring-only scalars that lack division is not expressible through this concept.

The result types of +, -, and the scaling round-trip are guarded with std::common_with<T> rather than left unconstrained or pinned to a stronger concept, for these reasons:

  • A bare requirement ({ a + b };) is satisfied even by an operator+ returning void, so some return check is needed.
  • The natural ideal, requiring the result to be a scalar/vector again (true closure, { a + b } -> Scalar), is ill-formed: those character concepts are defined transitively through Addable/ScalableWith, so constraining their own results by them would make a concept depend on itself, which 6.4.2 Point of declaration [basic.scope.pdecl] forbids (and which would otherwise recurse without termination).
  • Requiring std::same_as<T> is well-formed but too strong: it forbids the type-changing arithmetic the round-trip is designed to permit (expression templates, quantities).

std::common_with<T> is not recursive, and it rejects void and unrelated return types while admitting any result that shares a common type with T. The standard’s cross-type comparison concepts (std::equality_comparable_with, std::three_way_comparable_with) constrain with a common reference relation, because they relate operands that may be lvalues or proxy references. Here the constrained expressions yield prvalues, so a common value type is the meaningful requirement, and std::common_with is the stronger relation anyway, entailing common_reference_with for the corresponding const lvalue references ([concept.common]).

std::common_with is also symmetric, so it never accepts a lossy conversion: a widening a + b (e.g. int16_t + int16_t -> int) is accepted because the result shares a common type with T, not because the wide result can be narrowed back into T. The internal scaling concepts (How Scaling Works) make the opposite choice, std::constructible_from rather than std::common_with, because there a narrowing back to the stored type is the intended operation; the note there explains the distinction.

These compose into the character-specific concepts:

template<typename T>
concept RegularAddable = Addable<T> && WeaklyRegular<T>;

// Scalars: self-scalable — T * T and T / T have a common type with T
template<typename T>
concept BaseScalar = RegularAddable<T> && ScalableWith<T, T>;

// The field axis, read from the numeric_field trait (the single source of truth)
template<typename T>
concept Real = (numeric_field<T> == quantity_field::real);

template<typename T>
concept Complex = (numeric_field<T> == quantity_field::complex);

// Real scalar: a real, totally-ordered scalar
template<typename T>
concept RealScalar = Real<T> && BaseScalar<T> && totally_ordered<T>;

// Complex scalar: constructible from real/imag parts; provides a modulus
template<typename T>
concept ComplexScalar = Complex<T> && BaseScalar<T> &&
  requires(const T v, const T& ref) {
    requires constructible_from<T, decltype(math::real(ref)), decltype(math::imag(ref))>;
    math::modulus(v);
    requires ScalableWith<T, decltype(math::modulus(v))>;
  };

// A scalar is an order-0 representation of either field
template<typename T>
concept Scalar = (RealScalar<T> || ComplexScalar<T>) && tensor_order<T> == 0;

// Exposes an L2 magnitude and is scalable by it — the container algebra a vector or tensor adds
template<typename T>
concept HasMagnitude =
  requires(const T& v) {
    math::magnitude(v);
    requires ScalableWith<T, decltype(math::magnitude(v))>;
  };

// The order axis, rank-ordered through the tensor_order trait: a scalar is a degenerate vector,
// a vector a degenerate tensor. An order-n representation fills a slot of order >= n.
template<typename T>
concept Vector = Scalar<T> || (tensor_order<T> == 1 && RegularAddable<T> && HasMagnitude<T>);

template<typename T>
concept Tensor = Vector<T> || (tensor_order<T> == 2 && RegularAddable<T> && HasMagnitude<T>);

The key structural difference between BaseScalar and Vector reflects the underlying mathematics. A scalar type must satisfy ScalableWith<T, T>. Multiplying two scalars yields another scalar of the same kind. A vector type is only required to satisfy ScalableWith<T, decltype(math::magnitude(v))>. It can be scaled by its magnitude (a scalar), but vector × vector is not required and is typically not defined at all.

The concept is named Vector to match the quantity_tensor_order::vector it identifies, not to assert that it models an arbitrary vector space. In the [ISO/IEC 80000] sense a vector quantity is characterized by a magnitude and a direction, so the math::magnitude(v) requirement is intrinsic to that character: the representation of a vector quantity is meant to be an element of a normed space.

The order axis is rank-ordered through the tensor_order trait, which reports 0, 1, or 2. Because a tensor of order zero is a scalar and a tensor of order one is a vector ([ISO/IEC 80000]), a lower-order representation may stand in for a higher-order quantity character: a real scalar satisfies the scalar, vector, and tensor characters, and a vector representation additionally satisfies the tensor character. The reverse never holds: a second-order tensor such as cartesian_tensor has tensor_order == 2, so it is not a vector.

ComplexScalar takes math::modulus(v) to be the Euclidean modulus |z|=re⁡(z)2+im⁡(z)2|z| = \sqrt{\operatorname{re}(z)^2 + \operatorname{im}(z)^2}, the same quantity math::magnitude computes for vectors, and not the algebraic field norm |z|2|z|^2 (see Relationship to algebraic structures).

Each character concept combines with RepresentationBaseline, the character-independent floor shared by every representation, to form the representation concepts the library checks internally. RepresentationBaseline requires that a type is not opted out (disable_representation) and that the library can scale it by a unit magnitude (UnitMagnitudeScalable, described in How Scaling Works):

template<typename T>
concept RepresentationBaseline = !disable_representation<T> && UnitMagnitudeScalable<T>;

template<typename T>
concept ScalarRepresentation = RepresentationBaseline<T> && Scalar<T>;

template<typename T>
concept VectorRepresentation = RepresentationBaseline<T> && Vector<T>;

template<typename T>
concept TensorRepresentation = RepresentationBaseline<T> && Tensor<T>;

// Rank-ordering makes every valid representation a (possibly degenerate) tensor representation
template<typename T>
concept SomeRepresentation = TensorRepresentation<T>;

RepresentationBaseline comes first in each conjunction. Its disable_representation opt-out defaults to rejecting any type that is, or whose elements are, a quantity or quantity-like type, so a bare quantity, a std::chrono::duration, and a container of either are all excluded (preventing inadvertent nesting of quantities), while a custom type bars itself with a one-line specialization. Leading with the guard also rejects a quantity before any character concept (and thus any of the quantity’s own operators) is examined, which avoids a constraint-satisfaction cycle.

The top-level public concept is representation_of<T, V>. The character is matched on each of its two axes separately: the order by rank, the field exactly. Both sides of each axis are described as a set of characters, and a match is a non-empty intersection: a representation contributes the slots it can fill, and V contributes the characters it admits.

// A character spelled directly: one axis, or both of them.
template<auto V>
concept CharacterValue =   // exposition only
  same_as<remove_cvref_t<decltype(V)>, quantity_tensor_order> ||
  same_as<remove_cvref_t<decltype(V)>, quantity_field> ||
  same_as<remove_cvref_t<decltype(V)>, quantity_character>;

// What a character constraint may be: a quantity specification or a character.
template<auto V>
concept CharacterConstraint =   // exposition only
  quantity_spec<decltype(V)> || CharacterValue<V>;

// What a quantity specification admits, as a set of values per axis (`.order` and `.field`): one
// value per axis for a concrete specification, and every value for a quantity kind.
template<quantity_spec QS>
consteval auto admitted-character(QS qs);   // exposition only

// Whether two sets of values of the same axis have a value in common.
template<typename Set>
consteval bool overlaps(Set lhs, Set rhs);   // exposition only

// The characters a representation can represent: on the order axis a scalar fills every slot, a
// vector fills vector and tensor, a tensor only tensor (a library rule generalizing clause 18 of
// ISO 80000-2:2019). The field has no such degeneracy, so a representation offers exactly its own.
template<typename T>
constexpr auto representable-character = see below;   // exposition only

// What `V` admits: a quantity specification contributes its own character, a bare axis constrains
// that axis and leaves the other free, and a quantity kind admits everything.
template<auto V>
consteval auto character-constraint();   // exposition only

template<typename T, auto V>
concept representation_of =
  SomeRepresentation<T> && CharacterConstraint<V> &&
  overlaps(representable-character<T>.order, character-constraint<V>().order) &&
  overlaps(representable-character<T>.field, character-constraint<V>().field);

What each type of V admits is listed under representation_of in Concepts. How a character set is represented is left to the implementation. The declarations above are expressed in terms of what a specification admits, which is the only observable behaviour; nothing in the interface exposes a set.

12.2.1 Relationship to algebraic structures

Each concept above approximates a classical algebraic structure but is named for the role it plays in the library rather than for that structure. We avoid the structural names (Field, OrderedField, VectorSpace, …):

  • A concept can only check that operations exist and that result types are stable; it cannot verify the defining laws. A concept named Field would promise associativity, distributivity, and inverses that the compiler never enforces.
  • The library admits types that are weaker than the named structure. int is not a field (it has no multiplicative inverses) yet must satisfy BaseScalar; int and double are accepted as one-dimensional vectors although they are not, in the usual sense, elements of a vector space. Role-oriented names (“scalar”, “vector”) communicate the intended use without making algebraic claims the type does not honor.
Concept
Structure approximated
Principal laws left unchecked
Addable additive group associativity & commutativity of +, existence of 0
WeaklyRegular a set with value semantics (copy + equality) —
RegularAddable a (regular) abelian group under addition the group axioms above
ScalableWith<T,S> a scalar action of S on T (module / vector-space multiplication) distributivity and associativity of the action; closure is approximated by round-trip type stability, not v*s/s == v
BaseScalar a field (commutative division ring) commutativity/associativity of ×, distributivity, existence of 0 and 1
RealScalar an ordered field compatibility of the order with + and × (std::totally_ordered is only a set order)
ComplexScalar the complex field ℂ (a 2-D real division algebra with modulus) field axioms; that math::real/math::imag genuinely coordinatize ℂ
Vector an element of a normed vector space the vector-space axioms and the norm axioms (homogeneity, triangle inequality)

The word “norm” is overloaded across mathematics:

  • the algebraic (field) norm N(z)=zz‾=|z|2N(z) = z\bar{z} = |z|^2, a multiplicative, quadratic form; and
  • the Euclidean (L2L^2) norm ‖z‖=N(z)=|z|\lVert z\rVert = \sqrt{N(z)} = |z|, the analytic norm satisfying the triangle inequality.

std::norm(std::complex) already exists and computes the field norm |z|2|z|^2, not |z||z|. A new customization point named norm returning ‖v‖\lVert v\rVert would therefore collide with std::norm, which already computes a different value. The library avoids the ambiguity by using:

  • math::modulus(z) for the complex absolute value |z||z| (the standard complex-analysis term), and
  • math::magnitude(v) for the vector Euclidean norm ‖v‖\lVert v\rVert,

and by exposing no customization point for the field norm.

A complex scalar is a degenerate vector and tensor by rank-ordering, and the field axis (numeric_field) keeps it classified as complex. The math::magnitude CPO routes it through math::modulus, yielding |z||z|, and never reaches for std::norm on a scalar (see Customization Point Objects (CPOs)).

12.3 Customization Points

The library provides several customization mechanisms for representation types. These fall into two categories: Character determination (what kind of representation type you have) and Behavior and values (how the library interacts with your type).

12.3.1 Character Determination

12.3.1.1 Customization Point Objects (CPOs)

The library uses several CPOs, declared in the nested namespace std::math (see Names that need a decision), to support different representation types. Providing these CPOs determines the character of the representation type. Each CPO checks for implementations in the following priority order:

math::real(c) - Returns the real part of a complex number:

  1. c.real() member function
  2. real(c) free function found via ADL

math::imag(c) - Returns the imaginary part of a complex number:

  1. c.imag() member function
  2. imag(c) free function found via ADL

math::modulus(c) - Returns the modulus |z| of a complex number:

  1. c.modulus() member function
  2. modulus(c) free function found via ADL
  3. c.abs() member function
  4. abs(c) free function found via ADL

math::real and math::imag return a real value of the argument’s tensor order (a real scalar for a complex scalar, a real vector for a complex vector), and math::modulus returns a real scalar. Only the first implementation found in the lists above counts: if it returns anything else, the CPO is not satisfied and the next one isn’t tried.

math::magnitude(v) - Returns the magnitude of a vector or tensor as a scalar:

  1. v.magnitude() member function
  2. magnitude(v) free function found via ADL
  3. v.norm() member function
  4. norm(v) free function found via ADL
  5. For arithmetic types: v for unsigned arithmetic types, std::abs(v) otherwise
  6. For complex scalar types: math::modulus(v) (a complex scalar is a degenerate 1-D complex vector, whose magnitude is its modulus |z|)
  7. For real scalar types: v.abs() member function
  8. For real scalar types: abs(v) free function found via ADL

Steps 3–4 are provided so that types from linear algebra libraries that follow the norm() naming convention work without adaptation. They are guarded to only apply when T is not a Scalar (i.e., neither a real nor a complex scalar): std::norm is overloaded both for arithmetic types and for std::complex, returning |x|² rather than |x| in either case, so scalar types are explicitly directed to the abs fallback below instead.

For math::modulus, abs() is accepted as a fallback for compatibility with std::complex and similar types that use that name. For math::magnitude, abs() enables arithmetic types to serve as 1-dimensional vectors and scalar tensor measures.

12.3.1.2 numeric_field<T>

numeric_field<T> reports the field axis (quantity_field::real or quantity_field::complex) and is the single source of truth for it. It reads the field off a scalar element of the representation rather than off the container’s surface: for an order ≥ 1 type it recurses into one element reached by indexing, and for a scalar it tests the real()/imag() API directly. The primary is left undefined; a specialization defines the field for a type whose order is known:

template<typename T>
  requires /* tensor_order<T> is defined, the type supports the indexing it implies, and a
              complex-element vector or tensor also exposes real()/imag() on its own surface */
constexpr quantity_field numeric_field<T> =
  /* complex if a scalar element of T exposes the real()/imag() API, real otherwise */;

Reading the element, rather than the container’s real()/imag(), is what lets the linear-algebra libraries be used with no field adapter at all: Eigen and Blaze expose real()/imag() on their real matrices and vectors too (a real value is a degenerate complex one), which would fool a check made on the container, but the element of a real matrix is a plain double, so it is classified as real. Because reaching the element needs the order, numeric_field is defined only where tensor_order is: an ambiguous type without a specialization (see below) has neither an order nor a field, so the two axes reject it together.

The element decides the field, with one consistency requirement in the other direction. A container whose element is complex must also expose real()/imag() on its own surface, because that is the API through which a complex representation is used (Eigen and Blaze complex matrices provide it, as does cartesian_vector<complex<double>>). A complex-element container that does not expose it cannot serve as a complex representation. numeric_field is left undefined for it, because classifying it as real would select a Euclidean instead of a Hermitian magnitude, exactly as tensor_order is left undefined for an ambiguous shape. The author then either exposes real()/imag() or specializes numeric_field explicitly.

12.3.1.3 tensor_order<T>

tensor_order<T> reports the order axis as 0 (scalar), 1 (vector), or 2 (tensor). Its primary is left undefined; a specialization detects the order structurally for a type that exposes exactly one indexing shape. Two-index access (t(i, j) or the C++23 t[i, j]) is order 2, single-index access (t[i]) is order 1, otherwise order 0:

template<typename T>
  requires /* T exposes exactly one indexing shape */
constexpr size_t tensor_order<T> = /* 2 for t(i, j)/t[i, j], 1 for t[i], else 0 */;

This trait replaces the disable_vector and disable_tensor opt-outs of earlier revisions. With the order known as a number, no type needs to opt out: cartesian_tensor has order 2, so it can’t fill a vector slot (see Concept Hierarchy). A type that exposes both indexing shapes is ambiguous. An Eigen column vector is an N × 1 matrix that offers both t[i] and t(i, j), and only its compile-time extents can decide its order, so it has no default and must be specialized, either by an integration adapter or by an ordinary full specialization:

template<typename T>
  requires /* T is an Eigen type */
constexpr std::size_t std::tensor_order<T> =
  (T::RowsAtCompileTime == 1 || T::ColsAtCompileTime == 1) ? 1 : 2;

Until specified, an ambiguous type is not a valid representation. The rejection is SFINAE-friendly, so forgetting the adapter gives a compile error instead of a misclassification (guessing would also disagree with an adapter across translation units, an ODR hazard).

12.3.1.4 disable_representation<T>

disable_representation<T> is the single, character-agnostic opt-out: when true, T is not accepted as a representation of any character. It replaces the former per-character disable_real / disable_vector / disable_tensor knobs. The default rejects any type that is, or whose elements are, a quantity or quantity-like type (so a bare quantity, a std::chrono::duration, and a container of either are excluded), and additionally opts out bool, which is totally ordered and arithmetic yet meaningless as a quantity representation. It also opts out char, wchar_t, char8_t, char16_t, and char32_t, which hold characters rather than numbers. signed char and unsigned char stay valid representation types, because programs use them for small numbers, and std::int8_t and std::uint8_t usually name them:

template<typename T>
constexpr bool disable_representation =
  /* true if T, or its element type, is a quantity or quantity-like type */;

template<>
inline constexpr bool disable_representation<bool> = true;
template<>
inline constexpr bool disable_representation<char> = true;
template<>
inline constexpr bool disable_representation<wchar_t> = true;
template<>
inline constexpr bool disable_representation<char8_t> = true;
template<>
inline constexpr bool disable_representation<char16_t> = true;
template<>
inline constexpr bool disable_representation<char32_t> = true;

A custom type that structurally satisfies a character but must never store a quantity bars itself in one line:

template<>
inline constexpr bool std::disable_representation<my_type> = true;

[ Note: There is no disable_complex or any per-axis opt-out. The field is determined by numeric_field and the order by tensor_order, so a type the structural detection would misclassify or leave ambiguous resolves the offending axis directly (the field follows the element, the order takes a tensor_order specialization) instead of being globally disabled. disable_representation only decides whether T is a representation at all. — end note ]

12.3.2 Behavior and Values

12.3.2.1 representation_underlying_type<T>

representation_underlying_type<T> is the extension point for exposing the underlying arithmetic or element type of a representation to the library. It drives the scaling factor type and the treat_as_floating_point check:

template<typename T>
struct representation_underlying_type;  // primary — empty

template<typename T>
using representation_underlying_type_t = representation_underlying_type<T>::type;

The library provides partial specializations that detect the underlying type in order:

  1. T::value_type or T::element_type member type (cv-qualification stripped)
  2. std::underlying_type_t<T> for scoped enumerations (unscoped enumerations are excluded, as they already implicitly convert to their underlying type). This case is there for libraries that implement their number types as scoped enumerations with overloaded operators. For example, the safe integers of [PSsimplesafeint] are enum class types, such as psssint::si32.
  3. T itself as a fallback

If both value_type and element_type are present with differing underlying types, the trait is empty and the library treats T as a leaf. Provide only value_type unless there is a specific reason to expose both (e.g., satisfying iterator concepts), in which case ensure they name the same underlying type.

A value_type member is the preferred form for types under the user’s control:

template<typename T>
class my_wrapper {
public:
  using value_type = T;
  // ...
};

When the source of a type cannot be modified, the trait may be specialized directly:

// MyFloat wraps long double internally
template<>
struct std::representation_underlying_type<MyFloat> {
  using type = long double;
};

[ Note: std::indirectly_readable_traits is not reused: that standard trait answers “what does *t yield?” and is the extension point for iterators and smart pointers, and specializing it for a non-iterator type is a semantic misuse. — end note ]

12.3.2.2 representation_canonical_type<T>

representation_canonical_type<T> maps a representation value type to the concrete type a quantity should store. The primary template maps a type to itself. A const-qualified type (mirroring representation_underlying_type) and a reference are forwarded to the unqualified type, so a specialization handles only the unqualified type, and it applies also when an arithmetic operator returns a const proxy or a reference to one:

template<typename T>
struct representation_canonical_type {
  using type = T;
};

template<typename T>
struct representation_canonical_type<const T> : representation_canonical_type<T> {};

template<typename T>
struct representation_canonical_type<T&> : representation_canonical_type<T> {};

template<typename T>
struct representation_canonical_type<T&&> : representation_canonical_type<T> {};

template<typename T>
using representation_canonical_type_t = representation_canonical_type<T>::type;

The trait exists for expression-template representations. Linear algebra libraries such as Eigen and Blaze evaluate lazily: their arithmetic operators return proxy types that hold references to their operands rather than a materialized vector or matrix. Such a proxy must be evaluated to a concrete type before being stored in a quantity; otherwise the quantity would retain dangling references once the operands (often temporaries) go out of scope. The quantity deduction guides, and the concepts that compute the representation type resulting from an arithmetic operation (e.g. the result of velocity * time), consult this trait, so an expression-template type for which the trait is specialized is stored as its materialized concrete type.

For a type whose operators already return a concrete value (arithmetic types, cartesian_vector, GLM), the default is correct and no specialization is needed. An expression-template type is taught its evaluated type by specializing the trait, for example, to Eigen’s PlainObject or Blaze’s ResultType:

template<typename T>
  requires /* T is an Eigen expression */
struct std::representation_canonical_type<T> {
  using type = std::remove_cvref_t<typename T::PlainObject>;
};

This is the mechanism that lets a third-party linear algebra type be used directly as a vector/tensor representation. This paper doesn’t propose an integration with any linear algebra library. [mp-units] provides opt-in headers (<mp-units/integrations/eigen.h>, <mp-units/integrations/glm.h>, and <mp-units/integrations/blaze.h>) that specialize the customization points for Eigen, GLM, and Blaze, so the vector and matrix types of those libraries work as representations once the header is included. Armadillo can’t be integrated this way: its operator== returns an element-wise mask rather than a bool, so its types are not std::equality_comparable and cannot satisfy the weakly-regular requirement.

12.3.2.3 Scaling operators

The library scales a representation value by calling value * factor and value / factor, where factor is of type representation_underlying_type_t<T> (or a wider integer type for the rational integer path, described in How Scaling Works). A type may additionally provide operator*(T, unit_magnitude) to receive the full compile-time unit magnitude; when present, this operator is called first and the factor-based operators serve as a fallback. The magnitude-aware operator may return a different type (see Magnitude-aware scaling for the full pattern).

These operators are found via ADL. Hidden friends are the preferred form for types under the user’s control; non-member operators placed in the type’s namespace serve the same role for third-party types:

template<typename T>
class my_wrapper {
  T value_;
public:
  using value_type = T;
  constexpr explicit my_wrapper(T v) : value_(v) {}

  friend constexpr my_wrapper operator*(my_wrapper v, T factor) { return my_wrapper{v.value_ * factor}; }
  friend constexpr my_wrapper operator/(my_wrapper v, T factor) { return my_wrapper{v.value_ / factor}; }

  // Optional: magnitude-aware scaling (return type may differ from my_wrapper)
  // template<std::unit_magnitude M>
  // friend constexpr auto operator*(const my_wrapper& v, M m) { /* ... */ }
};

12.3.2.4 treat_as_floating_point<Rep>

A specializable variable template that tells the library whether a type should be treated as floating-point for the purpose of allowing implicit conversions:

template<typename Rep>
constexpr bool treat_as_floating_point = see below;

By default, the value is determined by applying std::chrono::treat_as_floating_point_v (hosted) or std::is_floating_point_v (freestanding) to the recursively-unwrapped underlying type of Rep. When true, implicit conversions are enabled; otherwise an explicit value_cast is required (see Value conversions). A specialization is needed when automatic detection yields an incorrect result:

template<>
inline constexpr bool std::treat_as_floating_point<my_fixed_point_type> = true;

12.3.2.5 implicitly_scalable<FromUnit, FromRep, ToUnit, ToRep>

A specializable variable template that controls whether a conversion from quantity<FromUnit, FromRep> to quantity<ToUnit, ToRep> is implicit or requires an explicit cast via value_cast or a conversion with a rounding policy. It is the layer on top of treat_as_floating_point: the default formula derives the implicit-conversion decision from it, and a specialization overrides that decision for types where the derived rule is incorrect:

template<unit auto FromUnit, typename FromRep, unit auto ToUnit, typename ToRep>
constexpr bool implicitly_scalable =
  treat_as_floating_point<ToRep> ||
  (!treat_as_floating_point<FromRep> && is_integral_scaling(FromUnit, ToUnit));

is_integral_scaling(from, to) is a consteval predicate that can also be used in user specializations to distinguish the integral-factor case (e.g. m → mm (×1000)) from fractional ones (e.g. mm → m (÷1000), ft → m, deg → rad).

The default follows std::chrono::duration: a conversion to a floating-point representation is always implicit, a conversion between integer representations is implicit only when the unit ratio is an integer multiplier (exact, no truncation), and all other cases require an explicit cast. The integer types themselves are not compared, so quantity<m, std::int16_t> from 100'000 * m is implicit and wraps, as duration<std::int16_t> from duration<int>{100'000} does. [P4408R0] proposes making a conversion between integer representation types implicit only when the destination can represent every value of the source.

For example, a decimal fixed-point type that represents decimal ratios exactly can permit all unit conversions implicitly:

template<auto FromUnit, auto ToUnit>
constexpr bool std::implicitly_scalable<FromUnit, safe_decimal, ToUnit, safe_decimal> = true;

When precision is asymmetric between two types, the specialization can be directional:

template<auto FromUnit, auto ToUnit>
constexpr bool std::implicitly_scalable<FromUnit, double, ToUnit, my_decimal> = true;

template<auto FromUnit, auto ToUnit>
constexpr bool std::implicitly_scalable<FromUnit, my_decimal, ToUnit, double> = false;

is_integral_scaling may be reused in a specialization to distinguish integral from fractional unit ratios. See Value conversions for details.

12.3.2.6 representation_values<Rep>

A specializable class template that provides the special values used by quantity::zero(), quantity::min(), quantity::max(), mathematical rounding operations, and division-by-zero checks:

template<typename Rep>
struct representation_values {
  static constexpr Rep zero() noexcept;
  static constexpr Rep one() noexcept;
  static constexpr Rep min() noexcept;
  static constexpr Rep max() noexcept;
};

In hosted environments the primary specialization inherits zero(), min(), and max() from std::chrono::duration_values<Rep>; one() is always defined in the struct itself, constrained to std::constructible_from<Rep, int>. In freestanding environments all four methods are defined directly, each guarded by its own requires clause: zero() and one() require std::constructible_from<Rep, int>; min() requires std::numeric_limits<Rep>::is_specialized and that std::numeric_limits<Rep>::lowest() returns Rep; max() requires std::numeric_limits<Rep>::is_specialized and that std::numeric_limits<Rep>::max() returns Rep. An explicit specialization is required for types that cannot satisfy those constraints or that need non-standard special values:

template<typename T>
struct std::representation_values<my_custom_type<T>> {
  static constexpr my_custom_type<T> zero() noexcept
  { return my_custom_type<T>{T{0}}; }

  static constexpr my_custom_type<T> one() noexcept
  { return my_custom_type<T>{T{1}}; }

  static constexpr my_custom_type<T> min() noexcept
  { return my_custom_type<T>{std::numeric_limits<T>::lowest()}; }

  static constexpr my_custom_type<T> max() noexcept
  { return my_custom_type<T>{std::numeric_limits<T>::max()}; }
};

12.4 How Scaling Works

Every representation type must be unit-conversion scalable. The library must be able to apply a unit magnitude ratio to it internally. This is captured by the UnitMagnitudeScalable concept, which directly names the three built-in scaling paths:

template<typename T>
concept UnitMagnitudeScalable =
  WeaklyRegular<T> && (UsesUnitMagnitudeAwareScaling<T> || UsesFloatingPointScaling<T> || UsesIntegerScaling<T>);

UsesUnitMagnitudeAwareScaling is satisfied by any type that provides operator*(T, unit_magnitude), checked first by the scaling engine, before the two built-in numeric paths. The full pattern is described in Magnitude-aware scaling:

template<typename T>
concept UsesUnitMagnitudeAwareScaling = requires(const T& v) { v * mag<1>; };

UsesFloatingPointScaling matches any type (or container thereof) whose underlying type satisfies treat_as_floating_point, is constructible from long double (the precision at which magnitude constants are evaluated), and supports operator* and operator/ with that underlying type, returning a result that T can be constructed from:

template<typename T>
concept UsesFloatingPointScaling =
  (treat_as_floating_point<T> || treat_as_floating_point<representation_underlying_type_t<T>>) &&
  constructible_from<representation_underlying_type_t<T>, long double> &&
  requires(T value, representation_underlying_type_t<T> f) {
    requires constructible_from<T, decltype(value * f)>;
    requires constructible_from<T, decltype(value / f)>;
  };

UsesIntegerScaling matches any type whose underlying type satisfies detail::integral (the scaling engine uses get_value<wider_t>, wider_int_for<element_t>, and fixed_point<element_t> internally, all of which require an integer element type). Scaling is routed through the type’s own operator* and operator/, so wrappers can check for overflow and containers can scale element-wise. The factor type is wider_int_for<element_t>, a wider integer of matching sign (e.g. int64_t for int16_t, uint64_t for uint16_t), to prevent intermediate overflow in rational-magnitude conversions:

template<typename T>
concept UsesIntegerScaling =
  detail::integral<representation_underlying_type_t<T>> &&
  requires(T value, wider_int_for<representation_underlying_type_t<T>> wf) {
    requires constructible_from<T, decltype(value * wf)>;
    requires constructible_from<T, decltype(value / wf)>;
  };

[ Note: detail::integral is used rather than std::integral because on GCC in strict mode (-std=c++20) std::integral<__int128> is false, as the standard traits are not specialized for __int128 outside GNU extensions. When the platform lacks __SIZEOF_INT128__ entirely, int128_t and uint128_t are software-emulation types that also do not satisfy std::integral. detail::integral patches both gaps:

template<typename T>
concept detail::integral =
  std::integral<T> ||
  std::same_as<std::remove_cv_t<T>, int128_t> ||
  std::same_as<std::remove_cv_t<T>, uint128_t>;

The scaling engine internals (get_value, wider_int_for, fixed_point) are all specialized for int128_t / uint128_t, ensuring the full integer scaling pipeline works correctly for 128-bit element types on all supported compilers. — end note ]

[ Note: Both scaling concepts constrain the scaled result with std::constructible_from<T, R> (can T be built from the result R?), in contrast to Addable / ScalableWith, which use the symmetric std::common_with<T>. The asymmetry reflects two different operations:

  • The scaling engine materializes the result with static_cast<To> (direct-initialization), so constructible_from is exactly its precondition. This admits two important cases. First, expression-template results: Eigen::Vector3d * double yields a lazy proxy that is constructible into Eigen::Vector3d but is not itself weakly-regular, so a WeaklyRegular result check would reject it; the proxy is evaluated to its concrete type before storage (see representation_canonical_type). Second, the integer path widens to a transient and narrows back, e.g. safe_int<int> * std::int64_t yields safe_int<std::int64_t>, which is narrowed to safe_int<int> via static_cast. Here the narrowing is the intended operation.
  • Addable / ScalableWith describe the representation’s public arithmetic, where a narrowing must not be accepted implicitly, so they use the symmetric common_with (see Concept Hierarchy).
— end note ]

Most standard types satisfy UnitMagnitudeScalable automatically. See Scaling operators for how to provide operator* and operator/ for custom types.

12.4.1 Built-in scaling algorithm

When two quantities of convertible units are combined or converted, the library applies the unit magnitude M to the representation value via scale_by_magnitude<To>(M, value). The built-in decision tree is:

The magnitude-aware path (operator*(T, unit_magnitude)) is checked first, before any of the built-in paths. If a representation type provides this operator, it has full control over how scaling is performed and what type is returned. The built-in paths are only used as a fallback.

The integer path (UsesIntegerScaling) never promotes values to floating-point, even for the rational and irrational sub-paths. The user explicitly chose an integer representation type, opting out of floating-point arithmetic. The platform may lack FP hardware (embedded systems, DSPs), rely on software-emulated FP, or enforce a no-FP policy.

The design preference order is exact integer > exact rational > approximate irrational: integer multiplication keeps lossless conversions exact (42 * m → 42000 * mm without floating-point rounding); rational factors are applied as numerator × value ÷ denominator entirely in integer arithmetic; and irrational factors (π/180, √2, …) are approximated by a fixed-point constant computed at compile time and applied in integer arithmetic.

The rational path computes value * numerator / denominator entirely in integer arithmetic using widened types to prevent intermediate overflow. For example, converting feet to metres multiplies by 381 before dividing by 1250, which would overflow a 64-bit integer for values above ~2.4×10¹⁶ without extra width:

Source type
Widened to
Signed ≤ 32 bits (int8_t…int32_t) int64_t
Unsigned ≤ 32 bits uint64_t
int64_t __int128 or equivalent signed 128-bit
uint64_t unsigned __int128 or equivalent unsigned

Using long double instead would bring floating-point into the integer path and introduce rounding (0.3048 is not exactly representable in binary floating-point); on some platforms (MSVC, Apple Silicon) long double is the same as double anyway, giving no extra range.

Double-width arithmetic avoids most UB during intermediate scaling, but cannot prevent overflow in the final result when that result doesn’t fit in the target type. Runtime overflow detection requires a representation type that checks arithmetic operations. A checked-integer wrapper (e.g., safe_int<T> from mp-units) satisfies UsesIntegerScaling and will trap overflows in the final result.

Aggregate representation types that store multiple independently-scaled fields (e.g., uncertain<T> from mp-units, holding a central value and an error bound) implement operator* and operator/ to distribute scaling across all internal fields; the built-in integer and floating-point paths invoke those operators on the aggregate as a unit.

12.4.1.1 Floating-point precision

For floating-point representation types (UsesFloatingPointScaling), the unit magnitude is reduced to a single constexpr scalar (the ratio evaluated as a long double and then rounded to the element type of the representation) and applied as a single multiplication, value * factor, or as a single division when the inverse of the ratio is an integer (see Magnitude-aware scaling). This matches what equivalent hand-written code would do, except that the factor passes through long double first, so in rare cases it differs in the last bit from a literal written in the element type. The library makes no stronger precision guarantee than the underlying floating-point operations provide. In particular, it does not mandate any specific ULP bound. This is consistent with the rest of the C++ standard library, including std::chrono::duration, which likewise leaves floating-point conversion precision to the quality of the implementation.

A unit conversion never runs a chain of intermediate multiplications: the magnitude is always a single compile-time constant representing the full unit ratio. The order of operations can still differ from hand-written code where a value is multiplied by a constant. A physical constant is a unit, so speed_of_light_in_vacuum * t doesn’t multiply by the value of the constant where it is written. The value becomes part of the single conversion factor, applied when the user converts the result to another unit. Hand-written code multiplies at each step instead, so the two results can differ in the last bits, in either direction. A user who needs the hand-written order converts at that step (.in(m)). This proposal doesn’t provide a setting that selects the order of operations, because the explicit conversion already gives that control.

For integer types, widened arithmetic (as described above) prevents intermediate overflow. For floating-point types, implementations are encouraged to choose a representation of the conversion factor that minimises precision loss, but this is a quality-of-implementation concern, not a normative requirement.

12.4.2 Magnitude-aware scaling

A type satisfies UsesUnitMagnitudeAwareScaling (see How Scaling Works) by providing operator*(T, unit_magnitude). Unlike the built-in numeric paths, this operator receives the full compile-time unit magnitude and may return a different type. For example, a range-validated representation can adjust its bounds during conversion: constraining values to [-180, 180] in degrees should produce a type constrained to [-π, π] when converted to radians, otherwise the bounds would be meaningless in the target unit:

// Example custom type (not provided by the library)
template<typename T, auto Min, auto Max, typename Policy>
  requires std::treat_as_floating_point<T>
class bounded_value : /* ... */ {
public:
  template<std::unit_magnitude M>
  [[nodiscard]] friend constexpr auto operator*(const bounded_value& val, M m)
  {
    constexpr T new_lo = std::scale_by_magnitude<T>(M{}, T{Min});
    constexpr T new_hi = std::scale_by_magnitude<T>(M{}, T{Max});

    const T scaled = std::scale_by_magnitude<T>(m, val.value());

    if constexpr (new_lo <= new_hi)
      return bounded_value<T, new_lo, new_hi, Policy>(scaled);
    else
      return bounded_value<T, new_hi, new_lo, Policy>(scaled);
  }
};

When the inverse of the magnitude is an integer (e.g. millimetre to metre, whose inverse is 1000), scale_by_magnitude divides by the inverse instead of multiplying, which avoids the rounding error of the inexact factor 0.001.

The library calls value * M{} in scale_by_magnitude() before trying the built-in paths. Because the return type may differ from the input, quantity::in(unit) propagates the new representation type, and the resulting quantity, a delta or a point, uses the scaled-bounds representation.

12.5 Character-specific operations

This paper attaches a character to every quantity specification and checks that a representation type can fill it (see Quantity character). * and / are the operations of scalars. A vector or a tensor has no reciprocal, and the product of two of them is one of several products that clause 18 of [ISO/IEC 80000] part 2 defines. A complex quantity has a real part, an imaginary part, and a modulus, each a real quantity of its own. This paper proposes the restrictions that keep these apart, and magnitude(). The operations themselves are proposed in [P4487R0].

12.5.1 Arithmetic on vectors and tensors

operator* exists when at most one operand is declared a vector or a tensor, and operator/ when the divisor isn’t declared one. inverse(), pow<>(), sqrt(), and cbrt() exist for a scalar only, as the square of a vector is one of its products with itself (pow<1>(q), which is q, is the exception). The same holds for quantity specifications, for references, and for quantities. A quantity kind may be a scalar, so it is accepted, and its representation decides:

using vec = cartesian_vector<double>;

quantity force = isq::force(vec{1., 2., 3.} * N);
quantity displacement = isq::displacement(vec{3., 2., 1.} * m);

quantity momentum = isq::mass(2. * kg) * isq::velocity(vec{1., 0., 0.} * m / s);  // OK: a scalar times a vector
// auto q1 = force * displacement;                                                // Compile-time error
// auto q2 = isq::duration(1. * s) / displacement;                                // Compile-time error
// auto q3 = (vec{1., 2., 3.} * N) * (vec{3., 2., 1.} * m);                      // Compile-time error

q3 multiplies two quantities of a kind. The units say nothing about the character, so the quantity specifications allow the product, and it fails only because cartesian_vector has no operator* for two vectors.

Mechanical work and moment of force are both a force times a length, and only the first one is a scalar product. A plain force * displacement would give the two equations the same expression and make a moment of force convert implicitly to mechanical work. [P4487R0] spells them scalar_product(force, displacement) and vector_product(position_vector, force). Until then, two vector quantities with a typed specification have no product.

12.5.2 Conversions between characters

A quantity doesn’t convert to a quantity of another character, even with quantity_cast. This covers a vector or a tensor and a scalar, a vector and a tensor, and a complex and a real quantity, and two such quantities have no common quantity specification. A quantity kind has no character of its own (see Quantity character), so this rule doesn’t apply to it. The scalar that belongs to a vector is its magnitude:

quantity velocity = isq::velocity(vec{3., 4., 0.} * m / s);

// quantity<isq::speed[m / s]> q4 = velocity;               // Compile-time error
// quantity q5 = isq::speed(velocity);                      // Compile-time error
// quantity q6 = quantity_cast<isq::speed>(velocity);       // Compile-time error
quantity<isq::speed[m / s]> speed = velocity.magnitude();   // 5 m/s
// auto q7 = velocity + speed;                              // Compile-time error

magnitude() of a quantity of V is a quantity of the specification magnitude(V), a real scalar of the dimension of V. It converts implicitly to the nearest scalar quantity above V in its hierarchy, and that quantity converts to it only explicitly, as not every speed is the magnitude of a velocity. A system of quantities therefore defines a vector below the scalar that its magnitude is a special case of. The ISQ definitions used in this paper do so: velocity is below speed, displacement below distance, and position vector below radial distance:

inline constexpr struct displacement : named_quantity_spec<distance, quantity_tensor_order::vector> {} displacement;
inline constexpr struct position_vector : named_quantity_spec<radial_distance, quantity_tensor_order::vector> {} position_vector;

quantity<isq::distance[m]> distance = displacement.magnitude();

Two vectors that meet only in a scalar ancestor have no common quantity specification either. Displacement and position vector meet in distance, so they can’t be added or compared, and a position vector becomes a displacement with quantity_cast.

A quantity equation of a scalar quantity may take the magnitude of a vector it is made of, as in magnitude(force) / area. It converts to pressure only explicitly, as [P4487R0] defines pressure with the force normal to the surface. The magnitude of a quantity specification exists only for a specification that may be a vector or a tensor, and a point has none.

Angular velocity is declared a vector over angular_displacement / duration, a quotient of scalars. Such a declaration takes only the dimension and the kind from the equation, so the magnitude of an angular velocity converts to that quotient only explicitly.

A complex quantity converts to none of its real parts, such as active power or apparent power for a complex power, and none of them converts to it. The functions that take these parts belong to [P4487R0].

12.6 Logarithmic quantities and units

Logarithmic quantities and units, such as the decibel or the neper, are not part of this proposal. [mp-units logarithmic] describes a design for them and asks for feedback on it. A quantity specification log<QS> wraps the linear one, a level such as 10 dBm is a point whose origin is its reference level, and a gain such as 3 dB is a delta. The log domain needs no other abstraction. The conversions between a level and a linear quantity work with the absolute quantities of [P4185R3].

13 Hello units

This chapter traces a minimal example from user code down through the library’s layers, before the detailed specifications that follow.

13.1 The example

A smoot is a unit of length equal to the height of Oliver Smoot (five feet and seven inches), famously used to measure the Harvard Bridge in 1958. Adding it to the library takes exactly one line:

import std;

inline constexpr struct smoot : std::named_unit<"smoot", std::mag<67> * std::usc::inch> {} smoot;

int main()
{
  constexpr std::quantity dist = 364.4 * smoot;
  std::println("Harvard Bridge length = {::N[.1f]} ({::N[.1f]}, {::N[.2f]}) ± 1 εar",
               dist, dist.in(std::usc::foot), dist.in(std::si::metre));
}

Output:

Harvard Bridge length = 364.4 smoot (2034.6 ft, 620.14 m) ± 1 εar

The example defines a unit, creates a quantity, converts it, and formats the result. The sections below examine each step.

13.2 Units form a chain to a base unit

Every unit ultimately traces back to a base unit, a unit associated directly with a quantity kind rather than being defined relative to another unit. The named_unit<Symbol, kind_of<QS>> form is used for these coherent base units:

// base unit — anchored to the length quantity kind
struct metre : named_unit<"m", kind_of<isq::length>> {} metre;

From there, US customary units are defined as a chain of scaled aliases using the named_unit<Symbol, Scale> form, each expressed in terms of the one above:

struct yard : named_unit<"yd", mag_ratio<9144, 10000> * si::metre> {} yard;  // 0.9144 m
struct foot : named_unit<"ft", mag_ratio<1, 3>        * yard>      {} foot;  // 1/3 yd
struct inch : named_unit<"in", mag_ratio<1, 12>       * foot>      {} inch;  // 1/12 ft

Both forms assign a name and symbol to the unit and propagate the quantity kind down the chain. For example, inch is a unit of length with no extra annotation.

13.3 Exact compile-time magnitudes

The scaling factors mag_ratio<N, D> and mag<N> are exact compile-time rational numbers. [mp-units] stores them as products of prime powers (see Unit magnitudes). Combining them involves no floating-point arithmetic. When the library traverses the chain from inch to metre, it multiplies the accumulated factors:

1 inch = (1/12) × (1/3) × (9144/10000) m  =  127/5000 m  =  0.0254 m  (exact)

The conversion factor from smoot to metre is therefore:

1 smoot = 67 × (127/5000) m  =  8509/5000 m  (exact rational)

This ratio is available entirely at compile time and applied to the stored value only when the value is converted to another unit.

13.4 Named units

The expression mag<67> * usc::inch produces a scaled_unit<mag<67>, inch>. Wrapping it in named_unit:

struct smoot : named_unit<"smoot", mag<67> * usc::inch> {} smoot;

does three things:

  1. Records the symbol "smoot" for use in text output.
  2. Inherits the _base_type_ of the scaled unit, making smoot a unit of length.
  3. Records the scaling so that get-canonical-unit(smoot) can recover the exact magnitude relative to metre without any additional bookkeeping.

13.5 The quantity class template

The central type of the library is:

template<quantity_reference auto R, representation_of<get_quantity_spec(R)> Rep = double>
class quantity {
public:
  Rep numerical_value_is_an_implementation_detail_;  // the only runtime datum

  static constexpr quantity_reference auto reference    = R;
  static constexpr std::quantity_spec auto quantity_spec = get_quantity_spec(R);    // kind_of<isq::length>
  static constexpr std::dimension auto dimension         = get_dimension(quantity_spec); // dim_length
  static constexpr std::unit auto unit                   = get_unit(R);             // smoot
  using rep = Rep;
};

The unit, quantity specification, and dimension are part of the type. Only the numerical value is stored.

A bare unit with no point origin of its own, such as smoot, also satisfies the quantity_reference concept (since the quantity specification can be recovered from it via get_quantity_spec), so it can serve directly as the reference template argument.

13.6 Creating a quantity

The expression 364.4 * smoot invokes:

template<typename FwdRep, LinearReference R,
         representation_of<get_quantity_spec(R{})> Rep = remove_cvref_t<FwdRep>>
  requires(!OffsetUnit<decltype(get_unit(R{}))>)
constexpr quantity<R{}, Rep> operator*(FwdRep&& lhs, R) { return quantity{std::forward<FwdRep>(lhs), R{}}; }

The result is quantity<smoot{}, double>.

13.7 Unit conversion

.in(ToU) checks at compile time that ToU is a valid unit for the same quantity specification, then applies the conversion:

template<unit_of<quantity_spec> ToU>
  requires ImplicitScaling<unit, ToU{}, rep>
constexpr quantity_of<quantity_spec> auto in(ToU) const;

Internally, the conversion ratio is computed entirely at compile time:

constexpr unit_magnitude auto c_mag = get-canonical-unit(From::unit).mag / get-canonical-unit(To::unit).mag;

The exact rational 8509/5000 is then applied to the stored value at runtime. The fraction is evaluated as a long double at compile time and stored as a constant of the representation’s element type, so the actual runtime operation for a double representation is a single multiplication by a double:

364.4 × 1.7018 ≈ 620.14

Scaling behaviour for other representation types (integers, fixed-point, custom types) is discussed in How Scaling Works.

The return type is quantity<si::metre{}, double> holding 620.14. Attempting to convert to an incompatible unit, for example si::second, is a compile-time error because si::second does not satisfy unit_of<isq::length>.

13.8 Formatting

The library provides a std::formatter specialization for quantity. The format-specification grammar (described fully in Text output) gives independent control over the numerical part and the unit symbol. For dist.in(si::metre) formatted with {::N[.2f]}, the N[.2f] sub-spec is forwarded to the Rep formatter (producing "620.14"), after which the formatter appends the unit symbol "m", yielding "620.14 m".

This is a minimal example. Many library features (quantity convertibility, generic interfaces and concepts, the affine space, representation type constraints, mixed-unit arithmetic, value casts, and more) are not used here and therefore not described. They are covered in other chapters of this paper.

14 Usage examples

This chapter demonstrates key safety features through examples.

14.1 Basic quantity equations

Let’s start with a really simple example presenting basic operations that every physical quantities and units library should provide:

import std;

using namespace std::si::unit_symbols;

// simple numeric operations
static_assert(10 * km / 2 == 5 * km);

// conversions to common units
static_assert(1 * h == 3600 * s);
static_assert(1 * km + 1 * m == 1001 * m);

// derived quantities
static_assert(1 * km / (1 * s) == 1000 * m / s);
static_assert(2 * km / h * (2 * h) == 4 * km);
static_assert(2 * km / (2 * km / h) == 1 * h);

static_assert(2 * m * (3 * m) == 6 * m2);

static_assert(10 * km / (5 * km) == 2);

static_assert(1000 / (1 * s) == 1 * kHz);

Try it in the Compiler Explorer.

14.2 mp-units showcase

The next example serves as a showcase of various features available in the [mp-units] library.

import std;

constexpr std::quantity_of<std::isq::speed> auto avg_speed(std::quantity_of<std::isq::length> auto d,
                                                            std::quantity_of<std::isq::time> auto t)
{
  return d / t;
}

int main()
{
  using namespace std::si::unit_symbols;
  using namespace std::yard_pound::unit_symbols;

  constexpr std::quantity v1 = 110 * km / h;
  constexpr std::quantity v2 = 70 * mph;
  constexpr std::quantity v3 = avg_speed(220. * std::isq::distance[km], 2 * h);
  constexpr std::quantity v4 = avg_speed(std::isq::distance(140. * mi), 2 * h);
  constexpr std::quantity v5 = v3.in(m / s);
  constexpr std::quantity v6 = value_cast<m / s>(v4);
  constexpr std::quantity v7 = value_cast<int>(v6);

  std::cout << v1 << '\n';                                        // 110 km/h
  std::cout << std::setw(10) << std::setfill('*') << v2 << '\n';  // ***70 mi/h
  std::cout << std::format("{:*^10}\n", v3);                      // *110 km/h*
  std::println("{:%N in %U of %D}", v4);                          // 70 in mi/h of LT⁻¹
  std::println("{::N[.2f]}", v5);                                 // 30.56 m/s
  std::println("{::N[.2f]U[dn]}", v6);                            // 31.29 m⋅s⁻¹
  std::println("{:%N}", v7);                                      // 31
}

Try it in the Compiler Explorer.

14.3 Storage tank

This example estimates the process of filling a storage tank with some contents. It presents:

  • The importance of supporting more than one distinct quantity of the same kind,
  • faster-than-lightspeed constants,
  • how easy it is to add custom quantity types when needed, and
  • interoperability with std::chrono::duration.
import std;
#include <cassert>

namespace {

using namespace std::si::unit_symbols;

// add a custom quantity type of kind isq::length
inline constexpr struct horizontal_length : std::named_quantity_spec<std::isq::length> {} horizontal_length;

// add a custom derived quantity type of kind isq::area
// with a constrained quantity equation
inline constexpr struct horizontal_area : std::named_quantity_spec<horizontal_length * std::isq::width> {} horizontal_area;

inline constexpr auto g = 1 * std::codata::standard_gravity;
inline constexpr auto air_density = std::isq::mass_density(1.225 * kg / m3);

class StorageTank {
  std::quantity<horizontal_area[m2]> base_;
  std::quantity<std::isq::height[m]> height_;
  std::quantity<std::isq::mass_density[kg / m3]> density_ = air_density;
public:
  constexpr StorageTank(const std::quantity<horizontal_area[m2]>& base,
                        const std::quantity<std::isq::height[m]>& height) :
      base_(base), height_(height)
  {
  }

  constexpr void set_contents_density(const std::quantity<std::isq::mass_density[kg / m3]>& density)
  {
    assert(density > air_density);
    density_ = density;
  }

  [[nodiscard]] constexpr std::quantity_of<std::isq::weight> auto filled_weight() const
  {
    std::quantity volume = std::isq::volume(base_ * height_);
    const std::quantity_of<std::isq::mass> auto mass = density_ * volume;
    return std::isq::weight(mass * g);
  }

  [[nodiscard]] constexpr std::quantity<std::isq::height[m]> fill_level(const std::quantity<std::isq::mass[kg]>& measured_mass) const
  {
    return height_ * measured_mass * g / filled_weight().magnitude();
  }

  [[nodiscard]] constexpr std::quantity<std::isq::volume[m3]> spare_capacity(
    const std::quantity<std::isq::mass[kg]>& measured_mass) const
  {
    return (height_ - fill_level(measured_mass)) * base_;
  }
};


class CylindricalStorageTank : public StorageTank {
public:
  constexpr CylindricalStorageTank(const std::quantity<std::isq::radius[m]>& radius,
                                   const std::quantity<std::isq::height[m]>& height) :
      StorageTank(std::quantity_cast<horizontal_area>(std::numbers::pi * pow<2>(radius)), height)
  {
  }
};

class RectangularStorageTank : public StorageTank {
public:
  constexpr RectangularStorageTank(const std::quantity<horizontal_length[m]>& length,
                                   const std::quantity<std::isq::width[m]>& width,
                                   const std::quantity<std::isq::height[m]>& height) :
      StorageTank(length * width, height)
  {
  }
};

}  // namespace


int main()
{
  const std::quantity height = std::isq::height(200 * mm);
  auto tank = RectangularStorageTank(horizontal_length(1'000 * mm), std::isq::width(500 * mm), height);
  tank.set_contents_density(1'000 * kg / m3);

  const auto duration = std::chrono::seconds{200};
  const std::quantity fill_time = std::value_cast<int>(std::quantity{duration});  // time since starting fill
  const std::quantity measured_mass = 20. * kg;                                   // measured mass at fill_time

  const std::quantity fill_level = tank.fill_level(measured_mass);
  const std::quantity spare_capacity = tank.spare_capacity(measured_mass);
  const std::quantity filled_weight = tank.filled_weight();

  const std::quantity_of<std::isq::mass_change_rate> auto input_flow_rate = measured_mass / fill_time;
  const std::quantity_of<std::isq::speed> auto float_rise_rate = fill_level / fill_time;
  const std::quantity_of<std::isq::time> auto fill_time_left = (height / fill_level - 1 * one) * fill_time;

  const std::quantity fill_ratio = fill_level / height;

  std::println("fill height at {} = {} ({} full)", fill_time, fill_level, fill_ratio.in(percent));
  std::println("fill weight at {} = {} ({})", fill_time, filled_weight, filled_weight.in(N));
  std::println("spare capacity at {} = {}", fill_time, spare_capacity);
  std::println("input flow rate = {}", input_flow_rate);
  std::println("float rise rate = {}", float_rise_rate);
  std::println("tank full E.T.A. at current flow rate = {}", fill_time_left.in(s));
}

The above code outputs:

fill height at 200 s = 0.04 m (20 % full)
fill weight at 200 s = 100 g₀ kg (980.665 N)
spare capacity at 200 s = 0.08 m³
input flow rate = 0.1 kg/s
float rise rate = 2e-04 m/s
tank full E.T.A. at current flow rate = 800 s

Try it in the Compiler Explorer.

14.4 Bridge across the Rhine

The following example codifies the history of a famous issue during the construction of a bridge across the Rhine River between the German and Swiss parts of the town Laufenburg [Hochrheinbrücke]. It also nicely presents how the Affine Space is being modeled in the library.

import std;

using namespace std::si::unit_symbols;

inline constexpr struct amsterdam_sea_level : std::absolute_point_origin<std::isq::altitude> {
} amsterdam_sea_level;

inline constexpr struct mediterranean_sea_level : std::relative_point_origin<amsterdam_sea_level - 27 * cm> {
} mediterranean_sea_level;

using altitude_DE = std::quantity<std::point<std::isq::altitude, amsterdam_sea_level>[m]>;
using altitude_CH = std::quantity<std::point<std::isq::altitude, mediterranean_sea_level>[m]>;

template<auto R, typename Rep>
  requires(std::quantity<R, Rep>::point_origin == altitude_DE::point_origin)
std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const std::quantity<R, Rep>& alt)
{
  return os << alt.delta_from(altitude_DE::point_origin) << " AMSL(DE)";
}

template<auto R, typename Rep>
  requires(std::quantity<R, Rep>::point_origin == altitude_CH::point_origin)
std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const std::quantity<R, Rep>& alt)
{
  return os << alt.delta_from(altitude_CH::point_origin) << " AMSL(CH)";
}

template<auto R, typename Rep>
  requires(std::quantity<R, Rep>::point_origin == altitude_DE::point_origin)
struct std::formatter<std::quantity<R, Rep>> : std::formatter<typename std::quantity<R, Rep>::quantity_type> {
  template<typename FormatContext>
  auto format(const std::quantity<R, Rep>& alt, FormatContext& ctx) const
  {
    ctx.advance_to(std::formatter<typename std::quantity<R, Rep>::quantity_type>::format(
      alt.delta_from(altitude_DE::point_origin), ctx));
    return std::format_to(ctx.out(), " AMSL(DE)");
  }
};

template<auto R, typename Rep>
  requires(std::quantity<R, Rep>::point_origin == altitude_CH::point_origin)
struct std::formatter<std::quantity<R, Rep>> : std::formatter<typename std::quantity<R, Rep>::quantity_type> {
  template<typename FormatContext>
  auto format(const std::quantity<R, Rep>& alt, FormatContext& ctx) const
  {
    ctx.advance_to(std::formatter<typename std::quantity<R, Rep>::quantity_type>::format(
      alt.delta_from(altitude_CH::point_origin), ctx));
    return std::format_to(ctx.out(), " AMSL(CH)");
  }
};

int main()
{
  // expected bridge altitude in a specific reference system
  std::quantity expected_bridge_alt = amsterdam_sea_level + 330 * m;

  // some nearest landmark altitudes on both sides of the river
  // equal but not equal ;-)
  altitude_DE landmark_alt_DE = altitude_DE::point_origin + 300 * m;
  altitude_CH landmark_alt_CH = altitude_CH::point_origin + 300 * m;

  // artificial deltas from landmarks of the bridge base on both sides of the river
  std::quantity delta_DE = std::isq::altitude(3 * m);
  std::quantity delta_CH = std::isq::altitude(-2 * m);

  // artificial altitude of the bridge base on both sides of the river
  std::quantity bridge_base_alt_DE = landmark_alt_DE + delta_DE;
  std::quantity bridge_base_alt_CH = landmark_alt_CH + delta_CH;

  // artificial height of the required bridge pillar height on both sides of the river
  std::quantity bridge_pillar_height_DE = expected_bridge_alt - bridge_base_alt_DE;
  std::quantity bridge_pillar_height_CH = expected_bridge_alt - bridge_base_alt_CH;

  std::println("Bridge pillars height:");
  std::println("- Germany:     {}", bridge_pillar_height_DE);
  std::println("- Switzerland: {}", bridge_pillar_height_CH);

  // artificial bridge altitude on both sides of the river in both systems
  std::quantity bridge_road_alt_DE = bridge_base_alt_DE + bridge_pillar_height_DE;
  std::quantity bridge_road_alt_CH = bridge_base_alt_CH + bridge_pillar_height_CH;

  std::println("Bridge road altitude:");
  std::println("- Germany:     {}", bridge_road_alt_DE);
  std::println("- Switzerland: {}", bridge_road_alt_CH);

  std::println("Bridge road altitude relative to the Amsterdam Sea Level:");
  std::println("- Germany:     {}", bridge_road_alt_DE.delta_from(amsterdam_sea_level));
  std::println("- Switzerland: {}", bridge_road_alt_CH.delta_from(amsterdam_sea_level));
}

The above provides the following text output:

Bridge pillars height:
- Germany:     27 m
- Switzerland: 3227 cm
Bridge road altitude:
- Germany:     330 m AMSL(DE)
- Switzerland: 33027 cm AMSL(CH)
Bridge road altitude relative to the Amsterdam Sea Level:
- Germany:     330 m
- Switzerland: 33000 cm

Try it in the Compiler Explorer.

14.5 Hardware voltage measurement readout

Every measurement can (and probably should) be modeled as a point and this is a perfect example of such a use case.

This example implements a simplified scenario of measuring voltage read from hardware through a mapped 16-bits register. The actual voltage range of [-10 V, 10 V] is mapped to [0, 65534] on hardware and the value 65535 is used for error reporting. Translation of the value requires not only scaling of the value but also applying of an offset.

import std;

// real voltage range
inline constexpr int min_voltage = -10;
inline constexpr int max_voltage = 10;
inline constexpr int voltage_range = max_voltage - min_voltage;

// hardware encoding of voltage
using voltage_hw_t = std::uint16_t;
inline constexpr voltage_hw_t voltage_hw_error = std::numeric_limits<voltage_hw_t>::max();
inline constexpr voltage_hw_t voltage_hw_min = 0;
inline constexpr voltage_hw_t voltage_hw_max = voltage_hw_error - 1;
inline constexpr voltage_hw_t voltage_hw_range = voltage_hw_max - voltage_hw_min;
inline constexpr voltage_hw_t voltage_hw_zero = voltage_hw_range / 2;

inline constexpr struct hw_voltage_origin :
  std::relative_point_origin<std::point<std::si::volt>(min_voltage)> {} hw_voltage_origin;

inline constexpr struct hw_voltage_unit :
  std::named_unit<"hwV", std::mag_ratio<voltage_range, voltage_hw_range> * std::si::volt, hw_voltage_origin> {} hw_voltage_unit;

using hw_voltage_quantity_point = std::quantity<std::point<hw_voltage_unit, hw_voltage_origin>, voltage_hw_t>;

// mapped HW register
volatile voltage_hw_t hw_voltage_value;

std::optional<hw_voltage_quantity_point> read_hw_voltage()
{
  voltage_hw_t local_copy = hw_voltage_value;
  if (local_copy == voltage_hw_error) return std::nullopt;
  return std::point<hw_voltage_unit>(local_copy);
}

void print(std::point_quantity auto qp)
{
  std::println("{:10} ({:5})", qp,
               std::value_cast<double, std::si::volt>(qp)
                 .delta_from(std::natural_point_origin<std::isq::voltage>)
                 .in(std::si::volt));
}

int main()
{
  // simulate reading of 3 values from the hardware
  hw_voltage_value = voltage_hw_min;
  std::quantity qp1 = read_hw_voltage().value();
  hw_voltage_value = voltage_hw_zero;
  std::quantity qp2 = read_hw_voltage().value();
  hw_voltage_value = voltage_hw_max;
  std::quantity qp3 = read_hw_voltage().value();

  print(qp1);
  print(qp2);
  print(qp3);
}

The above prints:

     0 hwV (-10 V)
 32767 hwV (  0 V)
 65534 hwV ( 10 V)

Try it in the Compiler Explorer.

14.6 User defined quantities and units

Users can easily define new quantities and units for domain-specific use-cases. This example from digital signal processing domain will show how to define custom strongly typed dimensionless quantities, units for them, and how they can be converted to time measured in milliseconds:

import std;

namespace ni {

// quantities
inline constexpr struct SampleCount : std::named_quantity_spec<std::dimensionless, std::subkind> {} SampleCount;
inline constexpr struct SampleDuration : std::named_quantity_spec<std::isq::period_duration> {} SampleDuration;
inline constexpr struct SamplingRate :
  std::named_quantity_spec<std::isq::frequency, SampleCount / SampleDuration> {} SamplingRate;

inline constexpr struct UnitSampleAmount : std::named_quantity_spec<std::dimensionless, std::subkind> {} UnitSampleAmount;
inline constexpr auto Amplitude = UnitSampleAmount;
inline constexpr auto Level = UnitSampleAmount;
inline constexpr struct Power : std::named_quantity_spec<Level * Level> {} Power;

inline constexpr struct MIDIClock : std::named_quantity_spec<std::dimensionless, std::subkind> {} MIDIClock;

inline constexpr struct BeatCount : std::named_quantity_spec<std::dimensionless, std::subkind> {} BeatCount;
inline constexpr struct BeatDuration : std::named_quantity_spec<std::isq::period_duration> {} BeatDuration;
inline constexpr struct Tempo : std::named_quantity_spec<std::isq::frequency, BeatCount / BeatDuration> {} Tempo;

// units
inline constexpr struct Sample : std::named_unit<"Smpl", std::one, std::kind_of<SampleCount>> {} Sample;
inline constexpr struct SampleValue : std::named_unit<"PCM", std::one, std::kind_of<UnitSampleAmount>> {} SampleValue;
inline constexpr struct MIDIPulse : std::named_unit<"p", std::one, std::kind_of<MIDIClock>> {} MIDIPulse;

inline constexpr struct QuarterNote : std::named_unit<"q", std::one, std::kind_of<BeatCount>> {} QuarterNote;
inline constexpr struct HalfNote : std::named_unit<"h", std::mag<2> * QuarterNote> {} HalfNote;
inline constexpr struct DottedHalfNote : std::named_unit<"h.", std::mag<3> * QuarterNote> {} DottedHalfNote;
inline constexpr struct WholeNote : std::named_unit<"w", std::mag<4> * QuarterNote> {} WholeNote;
inline constexpr struct EighthNote : std::named_unit<"8th", std::mag_ratio<1, 2> * QuarterNote> {} EighthNote;
inline constexpr struct DottedQuarterNote : std::named_unit<"q.", std::mag<3> * EighthNote> {} DottedQuarterNote;
inline constexpr struct QuarterNoteTriplet : std::named_unit<"qt", std::mag_ratio<1, 3> * HalfNote> {} QuarterNoteTriplet;
inline constexpr struct SixteenthNote : std::named_unit<"16th", std::mag_ratio<1, 2> * EighthNote> {} SixteenthNote;
inline constexpr struct DottedEighthNote : std::named_unit<"q.", std::mag<3> * SixteenthNote> {} DottedEighthNote;

inline constexpr auto Beat = QuarterNote;

inline constexpr struct BeatsPerMinute : std::named_unit<"bpm", Beat / std::si::minute> {} BeatsPerMinute;
inline constexpr struct MIDIPulsePerQuarter : std::named_unit<"ppqn", MIDIPulse / QuarterNote> {} MIDIPulsePerQuarter;

namespace unit_symbols {

inline constexpr auto Smpl = Sample;
inline constexpr auto pcm = SampleValue;
inline constexpr auto p = MIDIPulse;

inline constexpr auto n_wd = std::mag<3> * HalfNote;
inline constexpr auto n_w = WholeNote;
inline constexpr auto n_hd = DottedHalfNote;
inline constexpr auto n_h = HalfNote;
inline constexpr auto n_qd = DottedQuarterNote;
inline constexpr auto n_q = QuarterNote;
inline constexpr auto n_qt = QuarterNoteTriplet;
inline constexpr auto n_8thd = DottedEighthNote;
inline constexpr auto n_8th = EighthNote;
inline constexpr auto n_16th = SixteenthNote;

}

std::quantity<BeatsPerMinute, float> GetTempo()
{
  return 110 * BeatsPerMinute;
}

std::quantity<MIDIPulsePerQuarter, unsigned> GetPPQN()
{
  return 960u * MIDIPulse / QuarterNote;
}

std::quantity<MIDIPulse, unsigned> GetTransportPos()
{
  return 15'836u * MIDIPulse;
}

std::quantity<SamplingRate[std::si::hertz], float> GetSampleRate()
{
  return 44'100.f * std::si::hertz;
}

}

int main()
{
  using namespace ni::unit_symbols;
  using namespace std::si::unit_symbols;

  const std::quantity sr1 = ni::GetSampleRate();
  const std::quantity sr2 = 48'000.f * Smpl / s;

  const std::quantity samples = 512 * Smpl;

  const std::quantity sampleTime1 = (samples.in<float>() / sr1).in(s);
  const std::quantity sampleTime2 = (samples.in<float>() / sr2).in(ms);

  const std::quantity sampleDuration1 = std::inverse<ms>(sr1);
  const std::quantity sampleDuration2 = std::inverse<ms>(sr2);

  const std::quantity rampTime = 35.f * ms;
  const std::quantity rampSamples1 = ni::SampleCount((rampTime * sr1).in(std::one)).in<int>(Smpl, std::rounded);
  const std::quantity rampSamples2 = (rampTime * sr2).in<int>(Smpl, std::rounded);

  std::println("Sample rate 1 is: {}", sr1);
  std::println("Sample rate 2 is: {}", sr2);

  std::println("{} @ {} is {::N[.5f]}", samples, sr1, sampleTime1);
  std::println("{} @ {} is {::N[.5f]}", samples, sr2, sampleTime2);

  std::println("One sample @ {} is {::N[.5f]}", sr1, sampleDuration1);
  std::println("One sample @ {} is {::N[.5f]}", sr2, sampleDuration2);

  std::println("{} is {} @ {}", rampTime, rampSamples1, sr1);
  std::println("{} is {} @ {}", rampTime, rampSamples2, sr2);

  const std::quantity sampleValue = -0.4f * pcm;
  const std::quantity power1 = sampleValue * sampleValue;
  const std::quantity power2 = -0.2 * pow<2>(pcm);

  const std::quantity tempo = ni::GetTempo();
  const std::quantity reverbBeats = 1 * n_qd;
  const std::quantity reverbTime = reverbBeats / tempo;

  const std::quantity pulsePerQuarter = std::value_cast<float>(ni::GetPPQN());
  const std::quantity transportPosition = ni::GetTransportPos();
  const std::quantity transportBeats = (transportPosition / pulsePerQuarter).in(n_q);
