They provide long-awaited strong-type support not only for physical quantities and units but also for anything that resembles a measurable number (e.g., longitude and latitude, pixel coordinates, prices). The affine space abstraction has similarly broad applicability.

We propose placing all framework entities directly in namespace std. The primary motivation is error message quality: when a type mismatch occurs, the compiler reports the full qualified name of every type involved. Nesting framework types inside std::units or a similar intermediate namespace adds that prefix to every diagnostic line, making already-complex template error messages significantly harder to read. Since the library’s chief value proposition is catching unit errors at compile time, readable diagnostics are a first-class concern.

Some entities would need to be renamed to avoid ambiguity with existing std identifiers (see Names that need a decision).

During Croydon 2026, SG18 raised three concerns about this placement. The first was coherence with the rest of the standard library. Short names aid error messages within the library but may feel inconsistent alongside the rest of std::. Our answer is that longer qualified names would harm the user experience that motivates the library’s existence, and implementations also have scope to improve diagnostics beyond what the library alone can do. The second was the volume of names in std::. The framework itself contributes a bounded number of names, and system definitions (SI units, ISQ quantities) live in their own subnamespaces and do not pollute std:: directly.

The third concern was naming conflicts with existing identifiers, and pi was the most concrete example. std::numbers::pi is an existing floating-point constant, while this library defines pi as a unit (an exact dimensionless scaling factor). Both stand for π, but they have different types, so the compiler never uses one for the other. However, where both using namespace std; and using namespace std::numbers; are in effect, an unqualified pi is ambiguous. This is an open question (see Dimensionless and framework-level entities below).

20.3.2 System definitions in subnamespaces

Quantity types and units from concrete systems (SI, ISQ, US customary, …) are placed in their own subnamespaces under std:

using namespace std::si::unit_symbols;

std::quantity<std::si::metre> q = 42 * m;

20.3.3 Dimensionless and framework-level entities

Beyond the framework types and the named systems, several entities belong to no concrete system namespace yet are more than library machinery.

20.3.3.1 Algebraic identities

dimension_one, dimensionless, and one are the algebraic identity elements of the framework’s type system: the dimension, quantity specification, and unit of dimensionless quantities respectively. They are mandatory infrastructure: any quantity equation that produces a dimensionless result relies on them implicitly. As such they are arguably framework entities and could live in std:: alongside quantity and named_unit. However, placing one directly in std:: raises a naming concern: to be consistent with the existing dimension_one and dimensionless names in the same group, and to avoid potential conflicts with user-defined one identifiers, it may need to be renamed to unit_one.

20.3.3.2 pi, a system-required constant

pi occupies a special position: it is a mandatory magnitude factor for defining units accepted for use with the SI. The degree (plane angle), a non-SI unit accepted for use with the SI, is defined as mag_ratio<1, 180> * pi * si::radian, making pi a dependency of the SI system definitions. This suggests placing it in std::si::, but users working with angles in non-SI contexts (custom unit systems, pure mathematics, signal processing) need pi independently of the SI system, so requiring std::si::pi would impose an unwanted SI dependency.

Placing it in std:: alongside the framework types is the most accessible option. The name is close to std::numbers::pi. Both represent π but are different kinds of entity: std::numbers::pi is a floating-point approximation, while std::pi would be a compile-time exact symbolic constant, evaluated to floating-point only when applied to a concrete value. However, this paper argues throughout that quantity is not merely a physics type but a safer numeric wrapper for any arithmetic value. Under that framing, pi can be seen as a safer version of std::numbers::pi: it carries the same mathematical meaning but defers floating-point evaluation and composes exactly with unit magnitudes. The naming proximity in std:: would then reflect their relationship, especially since the library uses std::numbers::pi under the hood when materialising the floating-point value of pi. Its cost is that an unqualified pi becomes ambiguous where both namespaces are used (see above). We ask LEWG to decide whether this reasoning justifies std::pi.

20.3.3.3 Useful dimensionless units with no system home

percent (%), per_mille (‰), and parts_per_million (ppm) are widely used in production code but, to our knowledge, are not defined by any standard system of units (neither SI nor any other system included in this proposal). They are convenient extensions of one that belong to no particular domain. Whether they should share a namespace with the algebraic identities or be grouped separately is unclear.

20.3.3.4 Short helpers and factory functions

delta<U> and point<U> (the references and construction helpers of the affine space) are terse to keep quantity equations and construction syntax readable. Their brevity could be problematic in the flat std:: namespace. However, unlike the units and quantity specs above, these are helpers that form part of the core API and are arguably framework entities in the same sense as quantity itself.

20.3.3.5 Summary

The placement of all of the above is an open question for LEWG. The four categories above may warrant different namespaces, or a single shared subnamespace (e.g., std::units:: or std::qty::). The tradeoff is consistent with the broader framework discussion: a subnamespace reduces name-conflict risk but requires using namespace to keep equations readable.

20.3.4 Names that need a decision

Some names of the proposed interface collide with existing names in std or may mislead there. Below are the alternatives we considered. Each of them is an open question for LEWG.

20.3.4.1 real, imag, and modulus

[mp-units] provides the customization point objects real, imag, modulus, and magnitude. They let generic code take the parts and the magnitude of a representation type, whether it provides a member function, a free function found by argument-dependent lookup, or, for the modulus, abs as std::complex does. They are general-purpose customization points that work with any representation type, not only with the representation of a quantity. Three of these names cannot denote objects in namespace std. std::real and std::imag are function templates in <complex> that would have to be respecified, and std::modulus is a class template in <functional>. If std::real and std::imag became objects, an unqualified real(z) would no longer find them by argument-dependent lookup, which considers only functions. magnitude does not collide with anything in std, although it shares a word with unit magnitudes (unit_magnitude).

We considered three options:

  1. Move all four objects to a nested namespace, the way std::ranges::begin lives next to std::begin. The names stay, but generic code has to spell the namespace: math::real(v).
  2. Rename three of them, e.g., to real_part, imag_part, and complex_modulus, and keep magnitude. No new namespace is needed, but the names move away from the vocabulary of std::complex.
  3. Add no new public objects and specify the library’s own uses with exposition-only helpers that try a member function and then a free function found by argument-dependent lookup. Generic user code gets no such helper: the using std::real; real(v); two-step finds only free functions, so a representation type that provides only member functions needs an adapter, and the abs fallback for the modulus is lost. magnitude has no std counterpart (std::norm returns |z|²), so it would still need an object of its own.

We propose option 1 with the namespace std::math. std::real, std::imag, and std::modulus keep their meaning, and generic code calls std::math::real(v), std::math::modulus(v), and std::math::magnitude(v). The name of the namespace is an open question for LEWG.

20.3.4.2 treat_as_floating_point

The library uses treat_as_floating_point<Rep> to decide which conversions may be implicit, as std::chrono::duration does with std::chrono::treat_as_floating_point. We can’t reuse the chrono trait directly:

  • It lives in std::chrono, and quantities are not only about time. A user of a custom representation type should not have to specialize a chrono trait to make it work with quantity.
  • It is a class template with a _v variable template. The boolean customization points of this library (e.g., disable_representation) are variable templates, like std::ranges::enable_borrowed_range.
  • It is asked about the representation type itself. This library asks about the element type underneath it: double for std::complex<double> or for a vector of double.

The default of our trait is std::chrono::treat_as_floating_point_v (hosted) or std::is_floating_point_v (freestanding) of that element type. On a hosted implementation, a type that exposes no underlying element type and already specializes the chrono trait needs nothing more. This leaves two traits named treat_as_floating_point in two namespaces. LEWG may prefer a distinct name for the new one.

20.4 Concepts

This chapter enumerates all the user-facing concepts in the library.

20.4.1 dimension<T> concept

dimension concept matches a dimension of either a base or derived quantity:

  • Base dimensions are explicitly defined by the user by inheriting from the instantiation of a base_dimension class template. It should be instantiated with a unique symbol identifier describing this dimension in a specific system of quantities.
  • Derived dimensions are implicitly created by the library’s framework based on the quantity equation provided in the quantity specification.

20.4.2 quantity_spec<T> concept

quantity_spec concept matches all the quantity specifications including:

  • Base quantities defined by a user by inheriting from the named_quantity_spec class template instantiated with a base dimension argument.
  • Derived named quantities defined by a user by inheriting from the named_quantity_spec class template instantiated with a result of a quantity equation passed as an argument.
  • Other named quantities forming a hierarchy of quantities of the same kind defined by a user by inheriting from the named_quantity_spec class template instantiated with another “parent” quantity specification passed as an argument.
  • Quantity kinds describing a family of mutually comparable quantities.
  • Intermediate derived quantity specifications being a result of a quantity equations on other specifications.
  • Point quantity specifications, point<QS> and point<QS, PO>, describing a point on the scale of any of the above, measured from the natural origin of QS or from the origin PO. QS may be a kind, but a point is never a kind: kind_of<point<QS>> is ill-formed. A point can’t be multiplied, divided, or raised to a power.

20.4.2.1 quantity_spec_of<T, V> concept

quantity_spec_of concept is satisfied by all the quantity specifications T satisfying a quantity_spec concept that match the following value V:

V
Condition
quantity_spec T is implicitly convertible to V.
Quantity character T admits that character, as described in representation_of<T, V>.

A quantity character is a quantity_tensor_order, a quantity_field, or a quantity_character value. A concrete specification admits one character per axis, while a quantity kind admits every character (see Quantity character).

Two points convert as the specifications of their scales do, along one branch of the tree and from compatible origins (see Checks that come first), and a point never converts to or from a delta, so quantity_spec_of<decltype(point<isq::height>), point<isq::length>> is true while quantity_spec_of<decltype(point<isq::height>), isq::length> is false.

20.4.3 unit_magnitude<T>

unit_magnitude concept is satisfied by all types defining a unit magnitude.

Note: Unit magnitude implementation is a private implementation detail of the library.

20.4.4 unit<T> concept

unit concept matches all the units in the library including:

  • Base units defined by a user by inheriting from the named_unit class template instantiated with a unique symbol identifier describing this unit in a specific system of units.
  • Named scaled units defined by a user by inheriting from the named_unit class template instantiated with a unique symbol identifier and a product of multiplying another unit with some magnitude.
  • Prefixed units defined by a user by inheriting from the prefixed_unit class template instantiated with a prefix symbol, a magnitude, and a unit to be prefixed.
  • Derived named units defined by a user by inheriting from the named_unit class template instantiated with a unique symbol identifier and a result of unit equation passed as an argument.
  • Derived unnamed units being a result of a unit equations on other units.
  • Physical constants defined by a user by inheriting from the named_constant class template instantiated with a unique symbol identifier and a product of multiplying another unit with some magnitude.

20.4.4.1 prefixable_unit<T>

prefixable_unit concept is satisfied by all units derived from a named_unit class template. Such units can be passed as an argument to a prefixed_unit class template.

20.4.4.2 unit_of<T, V> concept

unit_of concept is satisfied for all units T for which an associated quantity spec is implicitly convertible to the provided quantity_spec value. A unit of a point, point<QS> or point<QS, PO>, is a unit of its scale QS.

20.4.5 quantity_reference<T> concept

quantity_reference concept is satisfied by all quantity reference types. Such types provide all the meta-information required to create a delta_quantity or a point_quantity.

A quantity_reference can either be:

  • A unit U other than an offset one.
  • A delta reference, the type of delta<QS>[U] or delta<U>, for any unit U and a plain quantity_spec QS, or of QS[U] for a unit U other than an offset one, which is the same as delta<QS>[U]. Its quantity specification is QS.
  • A point reference, the type of point<QS>[U], point<QS, PO>[U], point<U>, or point<U, PO>, for any unit U, a quantity_spec QS that isn’t a point, and a point origin PO. Its quantity specification is the point specification, origin included, so get_quantity_spec(point<isq::altitude, mean_sea_level>[m]) is point<isq::altitude, mean_sea_level>.

delta<QS[U]>, point<QS[U]>, and point<QS[U], PO> are ill-formed: delta<> and point<> take a plain quantity specification or a unit, and nothing else.

20.4.5.1 quantity_reference_of<T, V> concept

quantity_reference_of concept is satisfied by references T which have a quantity specification that satisfies quantity_spec_of<V> concept. As a point reference has a point quantity specification, quantity_reference_of<decltype(point<m>), point<isq::length>> is true while quantity_reference_of<decltype(point<m>), isq::length> is false.

As quantity_spec_of does, it also takes a quantity character as V, and then it is satisfied when the reference’s quantity specification admits that character. A reference has no representation type, so this asks only the specification half. To ask about a quantity, use quantity_of<V>, which also weighs the representation.

20.4.6 representation_of<T, V>

representation_of concept constrains a type T of a number that stores the numerical value of a quantity.

Every representation type must satisfy a common baseline:

  • Weakly regular: copyable and equality comparable (default-constructibility is not required).
  • UnitMagnitudeScalable: the library must be able to apply a unit magnitude ratio to it internally. Most standard types satisfy this automatically; see Representation Types for details.
  • Character-specific operations: additional arithmetic operations required by the quantity character (e.g. total ordering for real scalars, math::real()/math::imag()/ math::modulus() CPOs for complex scalars, math::magnitude() CPO for vectors and tensors).

The second template argument V says which characters are acceptable, and matching is one intersection per axis: the slots T can fill have to meet the characters V admits.

On the order axis T fills a slot of equal or higher order, and on the field axis the match is exact (see Concept Hierarchy).

What V admits depends on its type:

  • if the type of V satisfies quantity_spec, the characters that specification admits (one per axis for a concrete specification, and every character for a quantity kind, which therefore accepts every representation type),
  • if V is a quantity_tensor_order, that order on the order axis and every field,
  • if V is a quantity_field, that field on the field axis and every order,
  • if V is a quantity_character, its order and its field.

20.4.7 delta_quantity<T> concept

delta_quantity concept matches every delta in the library and is satisfied by every possibly cv-qualified specialization of the quantity class template whose reference is not a point reference (a point reference makes it a point_quantity instead). A reference type, such as quantity<si::metre>&, doesn’t satisfy it.

20.4.7.1 quantity_of<T, V> concept

quantity_of concept is satisfied by all the quantities T, deltas and points alike, that match the following value V:

V
Condition
quantity_spec The quantity reference satisfies quantity_reference_of<V> concept.
A point origin The quantity is a point and it has the same absolute point origin as V.
Quantity character The quantity specification satisfies quantity_spec_of<V> and the representation type satisfies representation_of<V>.

A delta quantity specification matches a delta (quantity_of<quantity<m>, isq::length>), and point<QS> matches a point (quantity_of<quantity<point<m>>, point<isq::length>>). Neither matches the other form.

The origin is part of a point quantity specification, so it takes part in the match. quantity_of<Q, point<QS>> matches the points of QS measured from an origin compatible with the natural origin of QS, and quantity_of<Q, point<QS, PO>> the points of QS measured from an origin compatible with PO. Two origins are compatible when they share their absolute point origin, and two natural origins are the same origin when the quantity of one converts implicitly to the other (see Checks that come first). quantity_of<Q, point<isq::thermodynamic_temperature>> matches point<deg_C>(20.), whose origin si::ice_point is defined from si::absolute_zero, while a point of altitude measured from an absolute_point_origin of its own, such as mean_sea_level, is matched only by quantity_of<Q, point<isq::altitude, mean_sea_level>>, or by quantity_of<Q, mean_sea_level>.

For a quantity of a kind stored in a double, every order is admitted, so overloads on different orders can be ambiguous for it (see Quantity character).

quantity_of is defined as a disjunction whose two branches start with delta_quantity<Q> and point_quantity<Q>. This makes it more constrained than a fallback overload constrained with delta_quantity<Q> || point_quantity<Q>. When both overloads take the argument through the same parameter type, the one constrained with quantity_of is chosen for every quantity it matches:

template<typename Q>
  requires delta_quantity<Q> || point_quantity<Q>
void print(const Q& q);                              // any delta or point

void print(const quantity_of<isq::length> auto& q);  // a length, preferred

20.4.8 point_origin_for<T, V> concept

point_origin_for concept is satisfied by all point origins, the types derived from an absolute_point_origin or a relative_point_origin class template, that are origins for the points of the quantity specification V. V names either the scale (isq::altitude, the specification of the deltas measured from the origin) or a point of it (point<isq::altitude>). An origin denotes a point, so its quantity specification is the point of its scale measured from its absolute point origin, and the scale of V must be implicitly convertible to the scale of the origin.

For example, si::ice_point can serve as a point origin for points of isq::thermodynamic_temperature, and of every quantity type that implicitly converts to it.

However, if we define mean_sea_level in the following way:

inline constexpr struct mean_sea_level : absolute_point_origin<isq::altitude> {} mean_sea_level;

then it can’t be used as a point origin for points of isq::length or isq::width as none of them is implicitly convertible to isq::altitude:

  • not every length is an altitude,
  • width is not compatible with altitude.

20.4.9 point_quantity<T> concept

point_quantity concept is satisfied by every possibly cv-qualified specialization of the quantity class template instantiated with a point reference (quantity<point<QS, PO>[U], Rep>). As for delta_quantity, a reference type doesn’t satisfy it.

A point is constrained with quantity_of: by the point of a quantity specification (quantity_of<Q, point<isq::altitude>> or quantity_of<Q, point<isq::altitude, mean_sea_level>>), by a point origin (quantity_of<Q, mean_sea_level>), or by a character. The character form is checked against the point’s own quantity specification and representation (see Quantity character).

20.5 Symbolic expressions

Modern C++ physical quantities and units libraries use opaque types to improve the user experience while analyzing compile-time errors or inspecting types in a debugger. This is a huge usability improvement over the older libraries that use aliases to refer to long instantiations of class templates.

20.5.1 Derived entities

Having such strong types for entities is not enough. While doing arithmetics on them, we get derived entities, and they also should be easy to understand and correlate with the code written by the user. This is where symbolic expressions come into play.

The library should use the same unified approach to represent the results of arithmetics on all kinds of entities. It is worth mentioning that a generic purpose symbolic expressions library is not a good solution for a physical quantities and units library.

Let’s assume that we want to represent the results of the following two unit equations:

  • metre / second * second
  • metre * metre / metre

Both of them should result in a type equivalent to metre. A general-purpose library will probably result with the types similar to the below:

  • mul<div<metre, second>, second>
  • div<mul<metre, metre>, metre>

Comparing such types for equivalence would not only be very expensive at compile-time but would also be really confusing to the users observing them in the compilation logs. This is why we need a dedicated solution here.

In a physical quantities and units library, we need symbolic expressions to express the results of

  • dimension equations,
  • quantity type equations,
  • unit equations, and
  • unit magnitude equations.

If the above equation results in a derived entity, we must create a type that clearly describes what we are dealing with. We need to pack a simplified expression template into some container for that. There are various possibilities here. The table below presents the types generated from unit expressions by two leading products on the market in this subject:

Unit
[mp-units]
[Au]
N⋅m derived_unit<metre, newton> UnitProduct<Meters, Newtons>
1/s derived_unit<one, per<second>> Pow<Seconds, -1>
km/h derived_unit<kilo_<metre>, per<hour>> UnitProduct<Kilo<Meters>, Pow<Hours, -1>>
kg⋅m²/(s³⋅K) derived_unit<kilo_<gram>, power<metre, 2>, per<kelvin, power<second, 3>>> UnitProduct<Pow<Meters, 2>, Kilo<Grams>, Pow<Seconds, -3>, Pow<Kelvins, -1>>
m²/m metre Meters
km/m derived_unit<kilo_<metre>, per<metre>> UnitProduct<Pow<Meters, -1>, Kilo<Meters>>
m/m one UnitProduct<>

It is a matter of taste which solution is better. While discussing the pros and cons here, we should remember that our users often do not have a scientific background. This is why we recommend to use syntax that is as similar to the correct English language as possible. It consistently uses the derived_ prefix for types representing derived units, dimensions, and quantity specifications. Those are instantiated first with the contents of the numerator followed by the entities of the denominator (if present) enclosed in the per<...> symbolic expression.

20.5.2 Identities

The arithmetics on units, dimensions, and quantity types require a special identity value. Such value can be returned as a result of the division of the same entities, or using it should not modify the symbolic expression on multiplication.

We chose the following names here:

  • one in the domain of units,
  • dimension_one in the domain of dimensions,
  • dimensionless in the domain of quantity types.

The above names were selected based on the following quote from [ISO/IEC 80000]:

A quantity whose dimensional exponents are all equal to zero has the dimensional product denoted A0B0C0… = 1, where the symbol 1 denotes the corresponding dimension. There is no agreement on how to refer to such quantities. They have been called dimensionless quantities (although this term should now be avoided), quantities with dimension one, quantities with dimension number, or quantities with the unit one. Such quantities are dimensionally simply numbers. To avoid confusion, it is helpful to use explicit units with these quantities where possible, e.g., m/m, nmol/mol, rad, as specified in the SI Brochure.

20.5.3 Supported operations and their results

The table below presents all the operations that can be done on units, dimensions, and quantity types in a quantities and units library. The right column presents corresponding expression templates being their results:

Operation
Resulting template expression arguments
A * B A, B
B * A A, B
A * A power<A, 2>
{identity} * A A
A * {identity} A
A / B A, per<B>
A / A {identity}
A / {identity} A
{identity} / A {identity}, per<A>
pow<2>(A) power<A, 2>
pow<2>({identity}) {identity}
sqrt(A) or pow<1, 2>(A) power<A, 1, 2>
sqrt({identity}) or pow<1, 2>({identity}) {identity}

20.5.4 Simplifying the resulting symbolic expressions

To limit the length and improve the readability of generated types, there are many rules to simplify the resulting symbolic expression.

  1. Ordering

    The resulting comma-separated arguments of multiplication are always sorted according to a specific predicate. This is why:

    static_assert(A * B == B * A);
static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(A * B), decltype(B * A)>);

    This is probably the most important of all the steps, as it allows comparing types and enables the rest of the simplification rules.

    User-provided symbols (when available) are not guaranteed to be unique in the project. For example, someone may use "s" as a symbol for a count of samples, which, when used in a unit expression with seconds, would cause fatal consequences (e.g., sample * second would yield s², or sample / second would result in one).

    This is why the order uses the names of the entities instead of their symbols.

    The order is visible to users:

    • it decides the type of an expression, which shows in decltype, in diagnostics, and in mangled names: decltype(si::newton * si::metre) is derived_unit<si::metre, si::newton>,
    • it decides the order of factors in text output: std::format("{}", 1 * N * m) prints 1 m N, and get-common-reference(km, mi) prints as [(1/15625 km), (1/25146 mi)].

    The algorithms that combine symbolic expressions merge two sorted lists in one pass, so all of them have to use the same order.

    The type names produced by compilers can’t serve as this order. Compilers spell an unnamed namespace differently ({anonymous}, (anonymous namespace), and `anonymous-namespace'), and Clang leaves an inline namespace out of a type name unless that would make the name ambiguous, while GCC and MSVC keep it. For example, si::speed_of_light_in_vacuum is declared in the inline namespace si::si2019, so ordering by type names prints 1 c S for 1 * si::siemens * si::speed_of_light_in_vacuum with GCC and MSVC, and 1 S c with Clang.

    This is why we propose to specify the order:

    • entities are ordered by their fully qualified names, compared character by character by code unit value, in which an unnamed namespace has an empty name, so it sorts before its sibling namespaces, and inline namespaces don’t appear; the name of a class template specialization includes its template arguments, with types named by the same rule and integers written in decimal,
    • a scaled unit is ordered by its reference unit and then by increasing magnitude, as the members of a common_unit are (see Common units), so (mag<60> * s) * (mag<1000> * m) would print (10³ m) (60 s), and (mag<1000> * m) * (mag_ratio<1, 3> * m) would print (1/3 m) (10³ m),
    • the factors of a derived quantity specification are ordered by their hierarchy roots, then by their kind roots, then by their own names, and then a quantity before the kind of it.

    Entities without a qualified name of their own, such as classes declared in function bodies or unnamed classes, can still tie. They have no portable name to order by, so the proposal leaves them to std::type_order [P2830R10].

    std::type_order can’t replace the rules above. Its order is implementation-defined ([compare.type]). GCC 16, for example, compares mangled names (libstdc++ patch), so it orders a class ab (mangled 2ab) after a class b (1b).

    The rules need to know which namespaces of an entity are inline, which scope is a function, and what value a template argument has. A C++20 library can only approximate them by parsing the type names that compilers produce. A prototype of mp-units compares those names with whitespace and MSVC class-keys skipped and an unnamed namespace read as an empty name. It follows the order above except for inline namespaces, local classes, and scaled units. Parsing out the rest in a prototype made a translation unit that includes all the ISQ headers 7% slower to compile with GCC 16 (2150 ms instead of 2004 ms). An implementation in the standard library can use compiler intrinsics, or reflection (std::meta::identifier_of, std::meta::template_arguments_of, and std::meta::parent_of), instead.

    The order never chooses between two equivalent units. Of two equivalent units, a common unit keeps the preferred one or, when neither is preferred, both (see Common units), so the common unit of mag<1000> * W and km * N / s is (10³ W), which has fewer unit factors.

  2. Aggregation

    In case two of the same type identifiers are found next to each other on the argument list, they will be aggregated in one entry:

    Before
    After
    A, A power<A, 2>
    A, power<A, 2> power<A, 3>
    power<A, 1, 2>, power<A, 2> power<A, 5, 2>
    power<A, 1, 2>, power<A, 1, 2> A

  3. Simplification

    In case two of the same type identifiers are found in the numerator and denominator argument lists, they are being simplified into one entry:

    Before
    After
    A, per<A> {identity}
    power<A, 2>, per<A> A
    power<A, 3>, per<A> power<A, 2>
    A, per<power<A, 2>> {identity}, per<A>

    It is important to notice here that only the elements with exactly the same type are being simplified. This means that, for example, m/m results in one, but km/m will not be simplified. The resulting derived unit will preserve both symbols and their relative magnitude. This allows us to properly print symbols of some units or constants that require such behavior. For example, the Hubble constant is expressed in km⋅s⁻¹⋅Mpc⁻¹, where both km and Mpc are units of length.

    In [mp-units] library, we’ve tried to refine symbolic expressions simplification rules to preserve the information of the origin. However, we were not satisfied with the results. The generated types were much longer and harder to reason about, which decreased the compile-time errors user experience. We’ve also got issues with basic library operations (e.g., determining the best common unit). More details can be found in Refining symbolic expressions simplification rules discussion.

  4. Repacking

    In case an expression uses two results of some other operations, the components of its arguments are repacked into one resulting type and simplified there.

    For example, assuming:

    constexpr auto X = A / B;

    then:

    Operation
    Resulting template expression arguments
    X * B A
    X * A power<A, 2>, per<B>
    X * X power<A, 2>, per<power<B, 2>>
    X / X {identity}
    X / A {identity}, per<B>
    X / B A, per<power<B, 2>>

20.5.5 Symbolic expressions in action

Thanks to all of the steps described above, a user may write the code like this one:

using namespace si::unit_symbols;
quantity speed = isq::speed(60. * km / h);
quantity duration = 8 * s;
quantity acceleration1 = speed / duration;
quantity acceleration2 = isq::acceleration(acceleration1.in(m / s2));
std::cout << "acceleration: " << acceleration1 << " (" << acceleration2 << ")\n";

the text output provides:

acceleration: 7.5 km h⁻¹ s⁻¹ (2.08333 m/s²)

The above program will produce the following types for acceleration quantities:

  • acceleration1

    quantity<delta_<derived_quantity_spec<isq::speed, per<kind_of_<isq::duration>>>,
                derived_unit<si::kilo_<si::metre>, per<non_si::hour, si::second>>>{},
         double>

  • acceleration2

    quantity<delta_<isq::acceleration, derived_unit<si::metre, per<power<si::second, 2>>>>{}, double>

20.6 Operations on units, dimensions, quantity types, and references

Modern C++ physical quantities and units library should expose compile-time constants for units, dimensions, and quantity types. Each of such constants should be of a different type. Said otherwise, every unit, dimension, and quantity type has a unique type and a compile-time instance. This allows us to do regular algebra on such identifiers and get proper types as results of such operations.

The operations exposed by such a library should include at least:

  • multiplication (e.g., newton * metre),
  • division (e.g., metre / second),
  • power (e.g., pow<2>(metre) or pow<1, 2>(metre * metre)).

To improve the usability of the library, we also recommend adding:

  • square root (e.g., sqrt(metre * metre) as equivalent to pow<1, 2>(metre * metre)),
  • cubic root (e.g., cbrt(metre * metre * metre) as equivalent to pow<1, 3>(metre * metre * metre)),
  • inversion (e.g., inverse(second) as equivalent to one / second).

Additionally, for units only, to improve the readability of the code, it makes sense to expose the following:

  • square power (e.g., square(metre) is equivalent to pow<2>(metre)),
  • cubic power (e.g., cubic(metre) is equivalent to pow<3>(metre)).

The above two functions could also be considered for dimensions and quantity types. However, cubic(length) does not seem to make much sense, and probably pow<3>(length) should be preferred instead.

Please note that we want to keep most of the unit magnitude’s interface implementation-defined. This is why we provide only a minimal mandatory interface for them. For example, we have introduced a mag_power<Basis, Num, Den = 1> helper to get a power of a magnitude. With that, a user should probably never need to reach for an alternative pow<Num, Den>(mag<Base>) version. However, the latter could be considered more consistent with the same operation done on other abstractions. Let’s compare how a unit can be defined using both of those syntaxes:

  • with mag_power:
inline constexpr struct electronvolt :
  named_unit<"eV", mag_ratio<1'602'176'634, 1'000'000'000> * mag_power<10, -19> * si::joule> {} electronvolt;
  • with pow<>(mag<>):
 inline constexpr struct electronvolt :
   named_unit<"eV", mag_ratio<1'602'176'634, 1'000'000'000> * pow<-19>(mag<10>) * si::joule> {} electronvolt;

Even though it might be inconsistent with operations on other abstractions, we’ve decided to use the first one as it seems easier to read and better resembles what we write on paper. However, we are not married to it, and we can change it if the LEWG prefers consistency here. Please note, that in such a case, for consistency, we probably should also provide sqrt() and cbrt() operations. However, those are really rare operations for magnitudes (we have not found any use cases for those in [mp-units] so far).

20.6.1 Equality and equivalence

Units, their magnitudes, dimensions, quantity types, and references can be checked for equality with operator==. Equality for all the tag types is a simple check if both arguments are of the same type. For example, for dimensions, we do the following:

template<dimension Lhs, dimension Rhs>
consteval bool operator==(Lhs lhs, Rhs rhs)
{
  return is_same_v<Lhs, Rhs>;
}

Equality for references is a bit more complex: two delta references are equal when their quantity specifications and their units are equal, and a delta reference equals a unit when it has the quantity specification associated with that unit and the unit itself. The second rule allows us to mix associated units and delta references (both of them satisfy quantity_reference concept). Thanks to this, we can check the following:

static_assert(isq::time[second] != second);
static_assert(delta<second> == second);

Units may have many shades. This is why an equality check is not enough for them. In many cases, we don’t need to check against a concrete unit, but we want to ensure that the underlying numerical value will not change during a unit conversion. In such cases we check for equivalence. Watt (W) should be equivalent to J/s and kg m²/s³. Also, a litre (l) should be equivalent to a cubic decimetre (dm³).

The library checks unit equivalence in its own constraints, for example on numerical_value_ref_in(), so equivalent is exposition-only. [mp-units] provides it publicly as equivalent.

To check for unit equivalence, currently we convert each unit to its canonical representation (scaled unit with magnitude expressed relative to some “blessed” implementation-specific reference unit) and then, we compare if the reference units and the magnitudes are the same:

consteval bool equivalent(unit auto lhs, unit auto rhs)
{
  const auto lhs_canonical = get-canonical-unit(lhs);
  const auto rhs_canonical = get-canonical-unit(rhs);
  return lhs_canonical.mag == rhs_canonical.mag && lhs_canonical.reference_unit == rhs_canonical.reference_unit;
}

Note: get-canonical-unit and the canonical unit it returns are exposition-only.

For example:

static_assert(N != kg * m / s2);
static_assert(equivalent(N, kg * m / s2));

It is also worth noting that the above implementation makes the last line below pass, even though we can’t convert a quantity measured in Hz to the one in Bq:

quantity q1 = (42 * Hz).in(one / s);
quantity q2 = (42 * Bq).in(one / s);
quantity q3 = (42 * one / s).in(Hz);
quantity q4 = (42 * one / s).in(Bq);
// quantity q5 = (42 * Hz).in(Bq);  // does not compile

quantity q6 = 1 * Hz + 1 * one / s;
quantity q7 = 1 * Bq + 1 * one / s;
// quantity q8 = 1 * Hz + 1 * Bq;   // does not compile

static_assert(Hz != Bq);
static_assert(Hz != one / s);
static_assert(Bq != one / s);
static_assert(equivalent(Hz, one / s));
static_assert(equivalent(Bq, one / s));
static_assert(equivalent(Hz, Bq));

equivalent compares canonical units, so it is an equivalence relation: Hz and Bq are both equivalent to one / s, so they are equivalent to each other, even though their quantity kinds (frequency and activity) do not convert.

20.6.2 Ordering

Ordering for dimensions and quantity types has no physical sense.

We could entertain adding ordering for units, but this would work only for quantities having the same reference unit, which would be inconsistent with how equality works.

Let’s see the following example:

constexpr unit auto my_unit = si::second;
if constexpr (my_unit == si::metre) {
 // ...
}
if constexpr (my_unit > si::metre) {
 // ...
}
if constexpr (my_unit > si::nano<si::second>) {
 // ...
}

In the above code, the first check could be useful for some use cases. However, the second one is impossible to implement and should not compile. The third one could be considered useful, but the current version of [mp-units] does not expose such an interface to limit potential confusion. Also, it is really hard to mathematically prove that the unit magnitude representation that we use in the library is greater or smaller than the other one in some cases.

This is why we discourage providing ordering operations for any of those entities.

20.6.3 Arithmetics

For consistency, we could also define arithmetic operator+ and operator- for such entities to resemble the operations performed on quantities. For example:

quantity q1 = isq::radius(1 * m) + isq::distance(1 * cm);

returns quantity<isq::length[cm], int>.

Users may be interested to check what will be the result of performing such operations on ingredients of the quantity. As we say that “addition of a radius and a distance should yield a length” it would be good to model this arithmetics on our symbolic constants as well:

static_assert(isq::radius + isq::distance == isq::length);

A position vector is a position, so the difference of two of them could be a displacement, and their sum could be refused. That is the affine space within a quantity hierarchy that [P4185R1] explored. This paper keeps the rule of the library: the difference of two position vectors is a position vector, and their sum is well-formed.

A later revision of this paper plans to let a quantity specification declare that its quantities are points, so that position vector is the point of displacement. A delta of a position vector doesn’t make sense, because a change of position is a displacement. Once the specification says that its quantities are points, the library can refuse delta<isq::position_vector>[m] and give the difference of two position vectors the type of a displacement. We will propose such a specifier when we have more experience with it.

magnitude() has the same algebra on quantity specifications. The magnitude of a vector converts implicitly to the nearest scalar above it (see Conversions between characters):

static_assert(implicitly-convertible(magnitude(isq::velocity), isq::speed));
static_assert(!castable(isq::velocity, isq::speed));

The other operations of Character-specific operations are proposed in [P4487R0]. With them, the following hold:

static_assert(implicitly-convertible(scalar_product(isq::force, isq::displacement), isq::mechanical_work));
static_assert(implicitly-convertible(vector_product(isq::position_vector, isq::force), isq::moment_of_force));
static_assert(implicitly-convertible(real(isq::complex_power), isq::active_power));
static_assert(implicitly-convertible(imag(isq::complex_power), isq::reactive_power));
static_assert(implicitly-convertible(modulus(isq::complex_power), isq::apparent_power));

Addition and subtractions on units is also possible, but it is more controversial and less useful, so we do not propose them at this time:

static_assert(m + cm == cm);
static_assert(km + mi == get-common-reference(km, mi));

20.7 Units

ISO specifies a measurement unit as a real scalar quantity, defined and adopted by convention, with which any other quantity of the same kind can be compared to express the ratio of the two quantities as a number.

In other words, a unit is a specific amount of a quantity. Such a definition is impractical from the programming language point of view. Let’s see the following hypothetical example (the below API is not a part of this proposal):

namespace si {

constexpr auto metre = quantity<length>{1};
constexpr auto kilometre = 1000 * metre;

}

quantity<si::kilometre> distance = 42 * si::kilometre;

The above code would be consistent with the ISO definition however, it imposes several issues:

  • creates a circular dependency for a quantity class,
  • embeds a concrete representation type in the unit,
  • loses all the benefits associated with our prime-factorized unit magnitudes (i.e., being able to express any ratio without the overflow of the underlying representation type),
  • quantity<length>{1} may mean different things in namespaces of different systems which makes it much harder to provide interoperability between them,
  • does not provide an opportunity to specify the unit symbol.

This is why decided to base unit definitions on tag types.

20.7.1 space_before_unit_symbol alternatives

As described in the space_before_unit_symbol customization point chapter, some units should not be prepended with a space. We proposed the following customization point:

template<unit auto U>
constexpr bool space_before_unit_symbol = true;

It is important to note that the need for some customization is only for a small fraction of all units. It works but it has some disadvantages. First, it might be harder to reason about the units definitions because the spacialization of this variable template may be in a different location in the source code than the unit definition. Also, it breaks our assumption that we can define all the properties of the entity with a single line of a C++ code.

Maybe we should add an additional parameter (defaulted to true) to the named_unit class template to handle this?

20.7.2 Prefixing units with prefixes

Initially [mp-units] library had one additional customization point for units:

template<prefixable_unit auto U>
constexpr bool unit_can_be_prefixed = true;

The above was used to disallow prefixes for some units, such as hours or degrees Celsius. However, after some time, we got the issue on GitHub asking to allow prefixes for the latter.

It turns out that the certification organizations are not consistent here. ISO 80000-5 says:

Prefixes are not allowed in combination with the unit °C.

However, NIST states:

Prefix symbols may be used with the unit symbol ºC, and prefix names may be used with the unit name “degree Celsius.” For example, 12 mºC (12 millidegrees Celsius) is acceptable. However, to avoid confusion, prefix symbols (and prefix names) are not used with the time-related unit symbols (names) min (minute), h (hour), d (day); nor with the angle-related symbols (names) º (degree), ’ (minute), and ” (second).

As a result of this issue and associated discussion, we decided to remove unit_can_be_prefixed support from the library, and we do not propose it here either.

20.8 Unit magnitudes

[ Note: The word “magnitude” appears in this paper with three distinct meanings:

  • Quantity magnitude (ISO 80000): the “magnitude of a quantity” is how large the quantity is; a quantity value (a number and a reference together) expresses it.
  • Vector magnitude: the Euclidean norm of a vector, |v|, provided by the math::magnitude() CPO (norm-named member and free functions are accepted as fallbacks).
  • Unit magnitude (this section): a compile-time scaling factor relating a unit to other units of the same dimension.
— end note ]

A very common operation is to multiply an existing unit by a factor, creating a new, scaled unit. For example, the unit foot can be multiplied by 3, producing the unit yard.

The process also works in reverse; the ratio between any two units of the same dimension is a well-defined number. For example, the ratio between one foot and one inch is 12.

In principle, this scaling factor can be any positive real number. In [mp-units] and [Au], we have used the term “magnitude” to refer to this scaling factor. (This should not be confused with other uses of the term, such as the logarithmic “magnitude” unit commonly used in astronomy).

In the library implementation, each unit is associated with a magnitude. However, for most units, the magnitude is a fully encapsulated implementation detail, not a user-facing value.

This is because the notion of “the” magnitude of a unit is not generally meaningful: it has no physically observable consequence. What is meaningful is the ratio of magnitudes between two units of the same quantity kind. We could associate the foot, say, with any magnitude mfm_f that we like — but once we make that choice, we must assign 3mf3m_f to the yard, and mf/12m_f/12 to the inch. Separately and independently, we can assign any magnitude msm_s to the second, because it’s an independent dimension — but once we make that choice, it fixes the magnitude for derived units, and we must assign, say, (5280mf)/(3600ms)(5280 m_f) / (3600 m_s) to the mile per hour.

Even when sometimes magnitudes are observable by the user, we’ve decided to make most of their interfaces implementation-defined. We expose only minimal public interfaces for interoperability, and we leave freedom to implementers on how they want to solve this problem in their libraries.

Below, we describe how magnitudes were implemented by [mp-units] and [Au].

20.8.1 Requirements and representation

A magnitude is a positive real number. The best way to represent it depends on how we will use it.

To derive our requirements, note that magnitudes must support every operation which units do. Units are closed under products and rational powers. Therefore, our magnitude representation must support these operations natively and robustly; this is the most basic requirement. We must also support certain irrational “ratios”, such as the factor of π180\frac{\pi}{180} between degrees and radians.

The usual approach, std::ratio, fails to satisfy these requirements in multiple ways.

  • Its integral types are too small to represent eight of SI prefixes.
  • It is not closed under rational powers (rather infamously, in the case of 21/2).
  • It cannot represent irrational factors such as π\pi.
  • It is too vulnerable to overflow when raised to powers.

This motivates us to search for a better representation.

20.8.1.1 Vector spaces, dimensions, and prime numbers

The quickest way to find this better representation is via a quick detour.

Consider the dimensions of units, such as length, or speed. All of the above requirements apply to dimensions, too — but in this case, we already have a very good representation. We start by singling out a set of dimensions to act as “base” dimensions: for example, the SI uses length, mass, time, electric current, temperature, amount of substance, and luminous intensity. Other dimensions are formed by taking products and rational powers of these. Our choice of base dimensions must satisfy two properties: spanning (i.e., every dimension can be expressed as some product-of-powers of base dimensions), and independence (i.e., no dimension can be expressed by multiple products-of-powers of base dimensions).

We call this scheme the “vector space” representation, because it satisfies all of the axioms of a vector space. Choosing the base dimensions is equivalent to choosing a set of basis vectors. Multiplying dimensions is equivalent to vector addition. And raising dimensions to rational powers is equivalent to scalar multiplication.

Dimension concept
Corresponding vector space concept
Base dimensions Basis vectors
Multiplication Vector addition
Raising to rational power Scalar multiplication
Null dimension (“dimensionless”) Zero vector

This viewpoint lets us derive insights from our intuitions about vectors. For example, just as we’re free to make a change of basis, we could also choose a different set of base dimensions: an SI-like system could treat charge as fundamental rather than electrical current, and would still produce all the same results.

Returning to our magnitude representation problem, it should be clear that a vector space solution would meet all of our requirements — if we can find a suitable choice of basis.

To begin our search, note that each magnitude must have a unique representation. This means that every combination of our basis elements must produce a unique value. Prime numbers have this property! Take any arbitrarily large (but finite) collection of primes, raise each prime to some chosen exponent, and compute the product: the result can’t be expressed by any other collection of exponents.

Already, this lets us represent every positive real number which std::ratio can represent, by breaking the numerator and denominator into their prime factorizations. But we can go further, and handle irrational factors such as π\pi by introducing them as new basis vectors. π\pi cannot be represented by the product of powers of any finite collection of primes, which means that it is “linearly independent” in the sense of our vector space representation.

This completes our recipe for basis construction. First, any prime number is automatically a basis element. Next, any time we encounter a magnitude that can’t be expressed in terms of the existing basis elements, then it is necessarily independent, which means we can simply add it as a new basis element. It’s true that, for reasons of real analysis, this approach can’t rigorously represent every positive real number simultaneously. However, it does provide an approach that works in practice for the finite set of magnitudes that we can use in real computer programs.

On the C++ implementation side, we use variadic templates to define our magnitude. Each element is a basis number raised to some rational power (which may be omitted or abbreviated as appropriate).

20.8.2 Advantages and disadvantages

This representation has tradeoffs relative to other approaches, such as std::ratio and other related types.

The core advantage is, of course, its ability to satisfy the requirements. Several real-world operations that are impossible for std::ratio are effortless with vector space magnitudes. Here are some examples, using Astronomical Units (au), meters (m), degrees (deg), and radians (rad).

Unit ratio
std::ratio representation
vector space representation
(aum)\left(\frac{\text{au}}{\text{m}}\right) std::ratio<149'597'870'700> magnitude<power_v<2, 2>(), 3, power_v<5, 2>(), 73, 877, 7789>
(aum)2\left(\frac{\text{au}}{\text{m}}\right)^2 Unrepresentable (overflow) magnitude<power_v<2, 4>(), power_v<3, 2>(), power_v<5, 4>(), power_v<73, 2>(), power_v<877, 2>(), power_v<7789, 2>()>
aum\sqrt{\frac{\text{au}}{\text{m}}} Unrepresentable magnitude<2, power_v<3, 1, 2>(), 5, power_v<73, 1, 2>(), power_v<877, 1, 2>(), power_v<7789, 1, 2>()>
(raddeg)\left(\frac{\text{rad}}{\text{deg}}\right) Unrepresentable magnitude<power_v<2, 2>(), power_v<3, 2>(), power_v<pi_c{}, -1>(), 5>

One disadvantage of the vector space magnitudes is that the type names are more verbose. As seen in the table above, users would have to perform arithmetic to decode which number is being represented. We expect that we can mitigate this with the same strategy we used to clean up the unit type names: hide them via opaque types with more human-friendly names.

The other disadvantage is that it incurs a dependency on the ability to compute prime factorizations at compile time, as we explore in the next section.

20.8.3 Compile-time factorization

End users don’t construct magnitudes directly. If they want to implement, say, the “astronomical unit” referenced above, they would write something like mag<149'597'870'700>. The library would automatically expand this to magnitude<power_v<2, 2>(), 3, power_v<5, 2>(), 73, 877, 7789>. To do so requires the ability to factor the number 149'597'870'700 at compile time.

This turns out to be challenging in many practical cases. For example, the proton mass involves a factor of 1,672,621,923,6951,672,621,923,695, which has a large prime factor: 334,524,384,739334,524,384,739. The usual method of factorization, trial division, requires many iterations to discover that this factor is prime — so many, in fact, that every major compiler will hit its constant-evaluation limit and terminate the compilation!

One of us wrote the paper [P3133R0] to explore a possible solution to this problem: a new standard library function, std::first_factor(uint64_t). This function would be required to return a result at compile time for any 64-bit integer — possibly with the help of compiler built-ins, if it could not be done any other way. The feedback to this paper showed that this wasn’t actually a hard-blocker: it turns out that every practical case we have could be satisfied by a fast primality checker. Still, we plan to continue investigating this avenue, both because it would make the standard units library implementation much easier, and because this function would be widely useful in many other domains.

20.8.4 Common unit magnitude

In our vector space representation, we can easily compute the magnitude of the common unit by taking the smallest exponent, across all participating magnitudes, for each individual basis vector — as long as we remember to use the implicit “0” exponent for any basis vector that is omitted.

The following example may help make this clear. If we use COM[U1,⋯,Un]\text{COM}\left[U_1, \cdots, U_n\right] as notation to represent “the common unit of U1,⋯,UnU_1, \cdots, U_n”, and we show only the magnitudes for simplicity, here are the steps we would follow to find the magnitude of the common unit.

COM[18,803]=COM[(2⋅32),(24⋅3−1⋅5)]=COM[(21⋅32⋅50),(24⋅3−1⋅51)]=2min[1,4]⋅3min[2,−1]⋅5min[0,1]=21⋅3−1⋅50=23 \begin{align} \text{COM}\left[18, \frac{80}{3}\right] &= \text{COM}\left[(2 \cdot 3^2), (2^4 \cdot 3^{-1} \cdot 5)\right] \\ &= \text{COM}\left[(2^1 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5^0), (2^4 \cdot 3^{-1} \cdot 5^1)\right] \\ &= 2^{\text{min}[1, 4]} \cdot 3^{\text{min}[2, -1]} \cdot 5^{\text{min}[0, 1]} \\ &= 2^1 \cdot 3^{-1} \cdot 5^0 \\ &= \frac{2}{3} \end{align}

This procedure produces the unambiguous correct answer whenever it is well defined. It also produces an answer for irrational “ratios”, where there is no uniquely defined result. This provides the practical benefit of making it easy to compare, say, an angle in degrees to one in radians, as long as at least one of them is represented in a floating point type.

20.9 Physical constants

20.9.1 Constants as units

Physical constants are implemented as units rather than constexpr quantity values. Benefits:

  • Constants in both numerator and denominator simplify at compile-time, like regular units.
  • Expensive multiplication and division are delayed until the user selects an output unit.
  • Representation types can be simpler and faster (e.g., integral instead of floating-point).

Example definitions:

namespace si {

inline namespace si2019 {

inline constexpr struct speed_of_light_in_vacuum :
  named_constant<"c", mag<299'792'458> * metre / second> {} speed_of_light_in_vacuum;

}  // namespace si2019

}  // namespace si

namespace codata {

inline namespace codata2022 {

inline constexpr struct magnetic_constant :
  named_constant<{u8"μ₀", "u_0"}, mag_ratio<125'663'706'127, 100'000'000'000> * mag_power<10, -6> *
                                    si::newton / square(si::ampere)> {} magnetic_constant;

}  // namespace codata2022

}  // namespace codata

Usage example (vacuum permittivity):

constexpr auto permeability_of_vacuum = 1. * codata::magnetic_constant;
constexpr auto speed_of_light_in_vacuum = 1 * si::si2019::speed_of_light_in_vacuum;
quantity_of<isq::permittivity_of_vacuum> auto q = 1 / (permeability_of_vacuum * pow<2>(speed_of_light_in_vacuum));
std::cout << q << " = " << q.in(F / m) << "\n";  // prints: 1 μ₀⁻¹ c⁻² = 8.85419e-12 F/m

20.9.2 Negative constants

Named units may not be enough to model all of the constants out there. It turns out that there are many negative constants. Some of them can be found in CODATA. One such constant is helion g factor.

Trying to model this with named_unit fails to compile. The reason of the error is the fact that the conversion factors between units should be positive. This means that reusing named_unit to define constants may not be the best idea and we probably need to introduce a dedicated class.

This is why we need to introduce a new class template:

inline constexpr struct helion_g_factor :
  named_constant<symbol_text{u8"𝘨ₕ", "g_h"}, -mag_ratio<4'255'250'615, 1'000'000'000> * one> {} helion_g_factor;

Additionally, such a solution does not allow the constant to be prefixed or associated with a quantity_spec.

20.10 Quantity specifications

Quantity specification provides all the data about the quantity type (i.e., kind, character, recipe, relation to other quantities in the hierarchy). It does not specify a unit, though.

20.10.1 Bikeshedding quantity_spec

The “quantity specification” term is not provided in ISO or BIPM metrology dictionaries and was invented for the need of this library. This means that we should probably consider some other names for this abstraction:

  • quantity_specification,
  • q_spec,
  • q_specification,
  • quantity_definition,
  • quantity_def,
  • quantity_data,
  • q_data.

20.11 Quantity specification conversions

Quantity kind & type and Quantity specification explain that a dimension does not identify a quantity. Work and torque, frequency and activity, width and height are pairs of quantities of one dimension that are not interchangeable, and the library records what distinguishes them in a quantity specification. Three facilities convert a quantity of one specification to another: copy-initialization of a quantity from another, the call operator of a quantity specification (the explicit constructor of quantity accepts the same conversions and converts the unit as well), and quantity_cast. Each accepts a strictly larger set of conversions between quantity specifications than the one before, which gives the four user-visible outcomes shown on the length hierarchy in Converting between quantities of the same kind: implicit conversion, explicit conversion, explicit cast, and no conversion at all.

Hierarchies of derived quantities shows the same outcomes once quantity equations are involved, and Creating distinct quantity kinds with subkind and Nested quantity kinds show them for declared kinds. This chapter states the rule those sections illustrate and explains the alternatives that were rejected.

The specification describes the relation with four exposition-only predicates. interconvertible is implicitly-convertible in both directions:

consteval bool implicitly-convertible(quantity_spec auto from, quantity_spec auto to);  // exposition only
consteval bool explicitly-convertible(quantity_spec auto from, quantity_spec auto to);  // exposition only
consteval bool castable(quantity_spec auto from, quantity_spec auto to);                // exposition only
consteval bool interconvertible(quantity_spec auto qs1, quantity_spec auto qs2);        // exposition only

Generic code doesn’t ask these questions directly. It constrains a parameter with quantity_of, which checks implicit convertibility for the quantity at hand.

20.11.1 Vocabulary

A quantity specification comes in one of four shapes:

  • A named quantity is defined with named_quantity_spec. It has a dimension, an optional parent, an optional equation, and may be marked with subkind.
  • A derived quantity is a product of powers of named quantities, such as isq::mass * pow<2>(isq::length) / pow<2>(isq::time), where isq::time names isq::duration. The library keeps it normalized: equal names are merged, zero exponents disappear, and dimensionless is the identity, so isq::length / isq::length is dimensionless while isq::width / isq::length stays a derived quantity. The same normalization runs again after every expansion.
  • A kind, spelled kind_of<K>, where K is a kind root or a product of kind roots, stands for any quantity of the hierarchy below K. This is what a bare unit carries: 42 * m has the quantity specification kind_of<isq::length>.
  • A magnitude, spelled magnitude(V) for a vector or a tensor V, is a real scalar. It is one factor of an equation, like a named quantity. The magnitudes of the quantities of one tree form a tree of their own, so magnitude(isq::static_friction_force) converts implicitly to magnitude(isq::force), and the equation of magnitude(V) is the one of V with the magnitude taken of its vector factor. magnitude(V) converts implicitly to the nearest scalar quantity above V, and that quantity converts to it only explicitly.

The rules refer to a few facts about a named quantity:

  • Its tree is the chain of parents, and the root is the top of that chain. Two named quantities are in the same tree when they share a root.
  • Its kind root is the nearest quantity on the way up, itself included, that was declared with subkind. If there is none, the kind root is the root. A quantity declared with subkind is a declared kind. Angular measure and storage capacity are the usual examples.
  • Its equation is the one given in its definition or, if none was given, its parent’s, recursively. A base quantity has none. A quantity defines its equation when it has one that it did not take over from its parent: it is a root, its parent has no equation, or its equation differs from its parent’s. A child that restates its parent’s equation does not define it. The defining ancestor of a quantity is the nearest quantity on the way up, itself included, that defines the equation the quantity has. dimensionless is a root whose equation is the empty product, so rotation, a child of dimensionless without an equation of its own, has dimensionless as its defining ancestor.
  • Its depth says how many levels of equations lie below it. A quantity with no equation at all, such as a base quantity, has depth 0. A quantity with an equation has depth one more than the deepest factor of that equation, so speed (length / duration) has depth 1 and acceleration (velocity / duration) has depth 2. The empty product is an equation too, one without factors, so dimensionless and rotation, which takes it over, have depth 1. A derived quantity has the depth of its deepest factor.
  • Its carried kinds are the declared kinds it carries, each with a count that may be negative or fractional. The count comes from two places. First, the quantity itself and every quantity on its way up count once each if they are declared kinds, so phase angle carries phase angle once and angular measure once. Second, every factor of its equation adds its own carried kinds multiplied by the factor’s exponent, so a factor in a denominator subtracts. Angular velocity, defined over an angular displacement, carries angular measure once this way. Counts of one kind add up and a count of zero is dropped, so speed carries nothing. A derived quantity carries the sum over its factors: isq::angular_displacement / isq::duration * isq::radius / isq::angular_measure / isq::speed carries nothing, because its numerator angle and its denominator angle cancel.

For the ISQ definitions below, with the local addition special_speed used by the examples:

inline constexpr struct special_speed : named_quantity_spec<isq::speed> {} special_speed;

the facts are the following, with the names of isq except special_speed and dimensionless:

Quantity
Root
Kind root
Depth
width length length 0
speed speed speed 1
special_speed speed speed 1
velocity speed speed 1
acceleration acceleration acceleration 2
angular_acceleration angular_acceleration angular_acceleration 3
frequency frequency frequency 1
angular_measure dimensionless angular_measure 1
phase_angle dimensionless phase_angle 1
rotational_displacement dimensionless angular_measure 1
rotation dimensionless dimensionless 1
Quantity
Equation
Defining ancestor
Carried kinds
width none none none
speed length / duration speed none
special_speed length / duration speed none
velocity displacement / duration velocity none
acceleration velocity / duration acceleration none
angular_acceleration angular_velocity / duration angular_acceleration angular_measure
frequency inverse(period_duration) frequency none
angular_measure path_length / radius angular_measure angular_measure
phase_angle path_length / radius angular_measure phase_angle, angular_measure
rotational_displacement path_length / radius angular_measure angular_measure
rotation (empty) dimensionless none

special_speed and phase angle take their equation over from the parent, and rotational displacement restates its parent’s (isq::arc_length is isq::path_length), so none of the three defines one. Angular acceleration has depth 3 because its equation reaches angular velocity, whose equation reaches rotational displacement, and it carries angular measure through that chain.

The character of a quantity is checked before these rules (see Checks that come first).

20.11.2 Outcomes

A conversion gets one of four ranks, ordered from worst to best:

Rank
Meaning
none no conversion, not even with quantity_cast
cast same kind, different branches (quantity_cast is required)
explicit the target is more specific than the source, or a declared kind is lost or gained
implicit every source quantity is a target quantity, or the source is an uncommitted kind that the target specializes

implicitly-convertible() is true for implicit, explicitly-convertible() for implicit and explicit, and castable() for all but none.

A conversion is explicit for one of two reasons: the target is more specific than the source (a downcast), or the conversion drops or gains a declared kind. The two reasons lead to the same rank with one exception, a source that is a kind, such as the kind_of<isq::length> that 42 * m carries. A kind has not committed to any quantity of its tree yet, so a downcast from it takes nothing away and is implicit: kind_of<inverse(isq::time)> converts to isq::frequency implicitly. Dropping a declared kind loses the kind whatever the source is, so kind_of<isq::angular_measure / isq::time> to dimensionless / isq::time stays explicit.

A conversion is decided by a sequence of operations, described below. Each operation has a rank, and the conversion gets the lowest of them: inverse(isq::time) to isq::frequency expands frequency with implicit and pairs time with period_duration, which ranks explicit, so the conversion is explicit. When the operations can be applied in more than one way, the conversion gets the best rank over all of them.

20.11.3 Checks that come first

Identical quantity specifications convert with implicit. Quantity specifications of different dimensions never convert, and quantity_cast will not force them either:

static_assert(!castable(isq::time, isq::length));

A quantity specification also carries the abstraction of a quantity and, for a point, its origin (see The affine space). The conversion of a quantity follows the conversion of its specification, so one set of rules decides both, and the following checks come before the hierarchy:

  1. A point never converts to a delta, nor the other way round, even with quantity_cast.
  2. point<QS, A> converts to point<QS, B> only if A and B share their absolute point origin, the root of their chains of origins. Two natural origins are the same origin when the quantity of one converts implicitly to the other: the natural origin of length is the one of height and the one of width, while those two differ, as the relation isn’t transitive.
  3. A point converts up or down one branch of the tree only. The natural origins of two siblings are the zeros of different scales, along axes that may even point in different directions, so point<isq::height> and point<isq::width> don’t convert to each other, even with quantity_cast, while isq::height and isq::width do, with a cast.

After these checks, a point specification converts to another one with the outcome of their scales:

static_assert(implicitly-convertible(point<isq::height>, point<isq::length>));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(point<isq::length>, point<isq::height>));
static_assert(!castable(point<isq::height>, point<isq::width>));
static_assert(!castable(point<isq::height>, isq::height));
static_assert(implicitly-convertible(point<isq::altitude, ground>, point<isq::altitude, mean_sea_level>));
static_assert(!castable(point<isq::altitude, other_zero>, point<isq::altitude, mean_sea_level>));

Here mean_sea_level and other_zero are two absolute_point_origins of altitude, and ground is a relative_point_origin defined from mean_sea_level. A height point h becomes a width only through a delta from its origin, as in quantity_cast<isq::width>(h.delta_from_zero()).

A quantity specification has a character as well (see Quantity character), and a quantity doesn’t convert to a quantity of another character, even with quantity_cast. This covers a vector or a tensor and a scalar, a vector and a tensor, and a complex and a real quantity. A quantity kind has no character of its own and passes this check. The magnitude of a vector is the scalar that converts (see Conversions between characters):

static_assert(!castable(isq::velocity, isq::speed));
static_assert(!castable(isq::speed, isq::velocity));
static_assert(!castable(isq::displacement / isq::duration, isq::speed));
static_assert(implicitly-convertible(magnitude(isq::velocity), isq::speed));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(isq::speed, magnitude(isq::velocity)));
static_assert(implicitly-convertible(kind_of<isq::length / isq::time>, isq::velocity));

Everything below assumes equal dimensions, two deltas, and characters that pass this check.

20.11.4 Kinds

A kind kind_of<K> names a quantity somewhere in the tree below the kind root K without saying where. Because K is a kind root, a sideways relation could only arise below K, where the kind has no position yet, so a conversion between a kind of a named quantity and a named quantity never ranks cast.

20.11.4.1 A kind as the source

When the source is a kind, the target is implicit if it lies in the tree below K, sub-kinds included, unless its equation lacks a declared kind that K carries, which makes it explicit. A vector child of angular velocity defined as inverse(duration) is reached only explicitly. If the target is above K, the kind has to leave its declared kind and the rank is explicit. Anything else is none:

static_assert(implicitly-convertible(kind_of<isq::length>, isq::width));
static_assert(implicitly-convertible(kind_of<dimensionless>, isq::angular_measure));
static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(kind_of<isq::angular_measure>, dimensionless));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(kind_of<isq::angular_measure>, dimensionless));
static_assert(!castable(kind_of<isq::frequency>, isq::activity));

This is why quantity<isq::height[m]> tower_height = 42 * m; compiles: the right-hand side is a quantity of kind length and height is a length. The second line holds for the same reason: a bare 3 * one is a kind_of<dimensionless> and may become any quantity of its tree, an angle included. The same rule is what lets quantity<isq::frequency[Hz]> f = 1. / (2 * s); compile: the source is the kind 1 / time.

20.11.4.2 A kind as the target

When the target is a kind, asking for “any quantity of kind K” is the same as asking for K itself. A source below K is implicit, or explicit if one of them carries a declared kind the other does not, as for the tree rule in Two named quantities. A source above K is explicit, like any other downcast. Any other source, from another branch of the same tree or from a different tree, is none:

static_assert(implicitly-convertible(isq::width, kind_of<isq::length>));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(isq::angular_measure, kind_of<dimensionless>));
static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(isq::angular_measure, kind_of<dimensionless>));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(dimensionless, kind_of<isq::angular_measure>));
static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(dimensionless, kind_of<isq::angular_measure>));

20.11.4.3 Kinds in equations

When a derived quantity is involved, the equation rules below run with K in place of the kind. A kind of a derived quantity can still rank cast where a factor meets the target sideways. Every operation that downcasts from a source kind ranks implicit, while dropping a declared kind stays explicit:

static_assert(implicitly-convertible(kind_of<inverse(isq::time)>, isq::frequency));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(inverse(isq::time), kind_of<isq::frequency>));
static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(inverse(isq::time), kind_of<isq::frequency>));

The first line and the last two show the asymmetry. 1. / (2 * s) is a kind and becomes a frequency implicitly. 1. / isq::time(2 * s) is a typed inverse(time), and frequency is defined over period duration, so this one needs isq::frequency(...). An earlier design promoted the target side as well, so that inverse(isq::time) converted to kind_of<isq::frequency> implicitly. The intent behind it, that a quantity is implicitly convertible from its own equation, is already delivered by expanding the target below, and the promotion made a typed 1 / time a frequency.

A kind that meets a typed quantity in one equation stays a kind factor of the result, spelled kind_of_<K> inside the derived quantity, and the typed factor stays typed. The rules above then apply to each factor on its own: a kind factor on the source side converts as a kind does, a kind factor on the target side pairs as K does, and a kind factor and a typed factor of one tree are different factors, like isq::width and isq::length:

inline constexpr struct rate_of_climb : named_quantity_spec<isq::speed, isq::height / isq::time> {} rate_of_climb;

static_assert(implicitly-convertible(kind_of<isq::length> / isq::time, rate_of_climb));
static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(isq::length / isq::time, rate_of_climb));
static_assert(implicitly-convertible(isq::height / kind_of<isq::time>, isq::height / isq::period_duration));
static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(isq::height / isq::time, isq::height / isq::period_duration));
static_assert(implicitly-convertible(kind_of<isq::length> / isq::length, dimensionless));
static_assert(implicitly-convertible(kind_of<isq::length> * isq::length, isq::height * isq::length));
static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(pow<2>(isq::length), isq::height * isq::length));

The first two lines are 42 * m / isq::time(2 * s) against isq::length(42 * m) / isq::time(2 * s): only the first may be a rate of climb because only the first has a kind for its length. The fifth line is the ratio of two lengths, and the last two keep the product apart against the merged pow<2>(isq::length). Only a result whose factors are all kinds is a kind itself, kind_of<isq::length / isq::time> for 42 * m / (2 * s).

20.11.4.4 The unit of a product

The unit of q1 * q2 is U1 * U2, and the product converts to it as to every unit whose kind converts implicitly to its specification. A unit’s kind is the product of its factors’ kinds, and only some named units carry a kind of their own, mainly the base units, the angle units, and the ones the SI brochure reserves for particular quantities, Hz, Bq, Gy, Sv and kat. Every other named unit has the kind of its definition: N is kg * m / s², J is N * m and W is J / s, so the kind of N * m * W is a product of base kinds, and it converts to torque * power the way kg * m² / s² converts to an energy. That the joule is not written for a moment of force is a convention ISO 80000-1:2009 states and the library leaves to the author. A unit the brochure keeps for one quantity stays tied to it, alone and inside a product:

static_assert(unit_of<decltype(J), isq::torque>);
static_assert(!unit_of<decltype(Hz), isq::activity>);
