static_assert(!unit_of<decltype(Bq / m), isq::frequency / isq::length>);

20.11.5 Two named quantities

Between two named quantities their positions in the hierarchy decide. Equations are consulted only for the declared kinds they carry. The rule of The kind boundary lowers the rank of every rule below where a declared kind is lost or gained.

  1. Different trees: none. Frequency and activity both have the dimension of inverse time but belong to different trees.
  2. The source is a descendant of the target: implicit, unless one carries a declared kind the other does not, which makes it explicit. A kind the source carries may lie on the way up, the source included and the target excluded, or come from the source’s equation: phase coefficient is defined as phase_angle / path_length, so it carries a phase angle that its parent propagation coefficient does not. The reverse happens too. A vector child defined as inverse(duration) under angular velocity lacks the angle its parent’s equation carries, so its upcast is explicit as well.
  3. The target is a descendant of the source: explicit.
  4. Neither: cast if both have the same kind root, otherwise none. Two such quantities that each carry a declared kind the other lacks are none as well.
static_assert(!castable(isq::frequency, isq::activity));                     // 1
static_assert(implicitly-convertible(isq::width, isq::length));              // 2
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(isq::angular_measure, dimensionless));  // 2, kind loss
static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(isq::angular_measure, dimensionless));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(isq::phase_coefficient, isq::propagation_coefficient));  // 2
static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(isq::phase_coefficient, isq::propagation_coefficient));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(isq::length, isq::width));              // 3
static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(isq::length, isq::width));
static_assert(castable(isq::height, isq::width));                            // 4
static_assert(!explicitly-convertible(isq::height, isq::width));
static_assert(!castable(isq::angular_measure, isq::solid_angular_measure));  // 4, different kinds

A hierarchy of named quantities behaves like a class hierarchy, with upcasts implicit unless they drop or gain a declared kind, downcasts explicit, and cross-casts between siblings requiring quantity_cast, or refused where the siblings each carry a declared kind the other lacks.

20.11.6 Derived quantities

As soon as one side is a derived quantity, the question becomes whether the source can be rewritten into the target. Both sides are treated as lists of factors with exponents, and the library remembers which side each factor came from. A named quantity is a one-factor list, dimensionless is the empty list.

20.11.6.1 The three operations

Pair a source factor with a target factor from the same tree, numerator with numerator or denominator with denominator. The common exponent is consumed and the pair ranks like the two named quantities would by their positions in the tree: an upcast implicit, or explicit when a declared kind is left on the way, a downcast explicit (implicit when the source is a kind), siblings cast. The direction is always source to target, so 1 / isq::width to 1 / isq::length is implicit. A pair ranking none ends the conversion with none.

Self-cancel a numerator and a denominator factor of the same dimension on the same side. A source-side self-cancel ranks implicit, because a ratio of two quantities of one dimension is a number: height / width, distance / wavelength, or two luminous intensities measured under different photometric conditions. A target-side self-cancel ranks explicit, or implicit when the source is a kind, because it asserts that a number is one particular ratio, which is a downcast. Whether a declared kind is lost on the way is left to The kind boundary below.

Expand a factor into the equation of its defining ancestor. Expanding a source factor ranks implicit: every quantity satisfies its own equation, inherited or not. Expanding a target factor ranks as the downcast from that ancestor to the factor, which is implicit when they are the same quantity or the source is a kind, and explicit otherwise. Converting isq::length / isq::duration to speed expands speed with implicit, and converting it to special_speed expands special_speed with explicit.

20.11.6.2 The kind boundary

The kinds carried by the source and the target are compared once their common factors have canceled, regardless of the operations taken. Each side is netted first, as Vocabulary describes for a derived quantity, so an angle in the numerator and one in the denominator of the same side cancel. The positive part and the negative part of the two sides’ counts are then compared separately, an absent kind counting as zero. If either part is larger on the source side, a kind would be lost, and if either part is larger on the target side, one would be gained. Either ranks the conversion at best explicit: 1 / isq::angular_measure to dimensionless loses a denominator angle. If a kind is lost and one gained, the conversion is none (explicit on a hierarchy edge, see case 11 of Special cases), as between two unrelated kinds. This includes the same kind lost in one part and gained in the other. A kind as the source (kind_of<K>, which has no position below K yet) is exempt from the cap on a gained kind, which is what lets an uncommitted kind enter a declared kind. For such a source, a kind that the equation of a target numerator factor takes away is kept apart from the kinds that the other target factors carry, and counts as a gained kind instead of canceling them.

[ Editor's note: The example of the last rule was the kind of kg m² rad/s converting to isq::angular_velocity * isq::moment_of_inertia. That product is ill-formed now, as both factors are vectors or tensors, and moment of inertia is defined with an operation of [P4487R0]. A new example is pending. ]

The comparison lowers the final rank, and the result does not depend on which operations are taken:

static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(isq::arc_length / isq::radius, isq::angular_measure));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(isq::arc_length / isq::radius, isq::angular_measure));
static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(isq::angular_measure * isq::radius, isq::arc_length));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(isq::angular_measure * isq::radius, isq::arc_length));
static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(isq::angular_displacement / isq::duration / isq::frequency, dimensionless));
static_assert(implicitly-convertible(isq::angular_displacement / isq::duration / isq::frequency, isq::angular_measure));
static_assert(implicitly-convertible(kind_of<dimensionless>, isq::angular_measure));

The last two lines: an angular displacement per duration divided by a frequency is 2π rad, an angle, and a bare 3 * one may become an angle, as Kinds explains.

The kind boundary compares the positive part and the negative part of each kind’s netted count separately. Comparing only the difference of the two sides’ counts would describe a lost denominator angle as a gained numerator one. It also compares the two sides themselves and does not rank the operation that expands a declared-kind factor. Ranking that operation makes the result depend on which operations the procedure takes and on how the factors are grouped. Any guard whose result is independent of grouping and operation order has to forbid implicit kind changes outright.

20.11.6.3 Which operation applies

The rules say which operation applies when more than one could:

  • Common factors cancel first. A factor present on both sides, in the same part, is canceled before any operation. The rest is then decided as if it were converted on its own: isq::phase_coefficient * isq::mass to isq::propagation_coefficient * isq::mass is explicit, like the bare pair.

  • Exact equation first. If one side is a single named quantity, possibly raised to a power, and the other side is exactly the equation of that quantity’s defining ancestor raised to the same power, that factor is expanded before any other operation. isq::instantaneous_power * isq::duration / isq::period_duration to isq::active_power is such a case: both are children of power, and without this rule they would pair as siblings.

  • A product of its own tree. A single named quantity whose equation is non-empty and consists only of quantities from its own tree is expanded before pairing. In the ISQ this happens in the dimensionless tree, where every pure number is a sibling of every other, and for isq::intrinsic_carrier_density, defined as sqrt(electron_density * hole_density) within the number density tree. With pixel_x and pixel_y children of pixel_count, and pixel_area a dimensionless quantity defined as pixel_x * pixel_y but not a kind, pixel_area to pixel_count * pixel_y is implicit and the reverse is explicit, instead of both being a cast between siblings.

  • Pairing. Otherwise, whenever a source factor and a target factor share a tree, they are paired. A pair of siblings waits while some other factor, on either side and outside their tree, still has an equation that mentions their tree, so that siblings are paired only once every factor of their tree is present. From a kind source, a pairing that would rank none waits as well, while a factor outside the tree mentions it anywhere down its equations, however deep. When a tree offers several ways to pair, the rank of the pairing is the best over all pairings of that tree’s factors. Every self-cancel on a side has the same rank, so the choice among several possible self-cancels does not change it.

  • Different roots stay apart. Two named quantities of the same sign and dimension from different trees, left over after pairing, end the conversion with none, unless the equation of either mentions the other’s tree, in which case the equations decide. This keeps roots of one dimension apart inside products: isq::frequency * isq::width to isq::activity * isq::length is none, because neither equation mentions the other’s tree. An equation that does mention the other tree still resolves: isq::radiant_intensity * isq::solid_angular_measure to isq::radiant_flux is implicit.

  • Self-cancel only against an empty side. A side may self-cancel only once the other side is empty. Otherwise isq::arc_length / isq::radius to isq::angular_measure would cancel the source into a number before the equation is used.

  • Reduce the deepest factor. When nothing else applies, a factor with the greatest depth is expanded. It is taken from the first of these lists that holds a factor of that depth: the source numerator, the source denominator, the target numerator, the target denominator. Within that list every factor of that depth is tried and the best rank is kept, so the names of the quantities never decide the result. Reducing the deepest factor first makes both sides meet at the most specific common equation.

    While siblings wait in a conversion from a kind, the factor of the target with the least depth that has an equation is expanded instead, numerator first. Expanding the shallowest factor first lets the factor that brings the tree in meet the waiting siblings before a deeper factor defined over it cancels it.

    [ Editor's note: The example of this rule was the angle of kg * m² * rad / s reaching the angular velocity in angular_velocity * moment_of_inertia * rotation. That product is ill-formed now, as two of its factors are vectors or tensors. A new example is pending. ]

The process stops when both lists are the same: both empty, or the same product right after an exact equation. Its rank is the lowest rank of the operations taken, or implicit if no operation was needed, lowered further by the kind boundary where it applies. It stops with none when a pair ranks none, or when factors remain and no operation applies. It always stops: every operation either removes a factor or replaces one by factors of strictly smaller depth.

20.11.6.4 Worked examples

Each diagram below follows one conversion through the procedure. A box shows what is left to convert, an arrow is one operation with its rank in bold, and the conversion gets the lowest rank of its arrows. When the kind boundary applies, it is the last arrow, and it can only lower the result.

isq::width * isq::height to isq::area: implicit.

 

static_assert(implicitly-convertible(isq::width * isq::height, isq::area));

isq::area to isq::width * isq::height: explicit.

 

static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(isq::area, isq::width * isq::height));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(isq::area, isq::width * isq::height));

inverse(isq::time) to isq::frequency: explicit. isq::time names isq::duration.

 

static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(inverse(isq::time), isq::frequency));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(inverse(isq::time), isq::frequency));

isq::frequency to inverse(isq::time): implicit.

 

static_assert(implicitly-convertible(isq::frequency, inverse(isq::time)));

isq::width / isq::duration to special_speed: explicit. An expansion on the target side is not always implicit. Speed defines isq::length / isq::duration, so every length per duration is a speed and converts to it implicitly. special_speed only inherits that equation, and not every speed is a special speed. The equation alone cannot make a special speed implicitly, so expanding special_speed on the target side ranks explicit, like the downcast from speed.

 

The same conversion to isq::speed is implicit, because speed defines its equation:

static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(isq::width / isq::duration, special_speed));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(isq::width / isq::duration, special_speed));
static_assert(implicitly-convertible(isq::width / isq::duration, isq::speed));

inverse(isq::repetency) to isq::height: cast. Repetency is defined as inverse(wavelength), and wavelength and height are different branches of the tree of length:

 

static_assert(castable(inverse(isq::repetency), isq::height));
static_assert(!explicitly-convertible(inverse(isq::repetency), isq::height));

Flattening both sides to length would have ranked this explicit and treated a wavelength as a height.

isq::angular_displacement / isq::duration * isq::radius / isq::speed to dimensionless: explicit. In the ISQ angular_displacement names rotational_displacement, which restates the equation path_length / radius of angular measure. Every operation is implicit, but the source carries angular measure and the target carries nothing, so the kind boundary makes the conversion explicit:

  

static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(isq::angular_displacement / isq::duration * isq::radius / isq::speed, dimensionless));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(isq::angular_displacement / isq::duration * isq::radius / isq::speed, dimensionless));
static_assert(!castable(isq::angular_velocity * isq::radius / isq::speed, dimensionless));

The last line is the same quotient with the vector angular velocity in place of the scalar angular_displacement / duration. Its magnitude converts only explicitly, as Conversions between characters explains.

The same divided by isq::angular_measure: implicit. The source carries the angle once in the numerator and once in the denominator, so the carried kinds balance. Here rotational_displacement self-cancels against angular_measure first, and the numerator and the denominator both leave the kind. speed is expanded as above, and radius self-cancels against length. Every step is implicit, and the kind boundary finds nothing lost:

  

static_assert(implicitly-convertible(isq::angular_displacement / isq::duration * isq::radius / isq::angular_measure /
                                       isq::speed, dimensionless));

20.11.7 The procedure in order

The process runs in up to three steps. Step 1 picks the rule that applies. Between two single named quantities, or a named quantity and a kind, the tree rule of Two named quantities or the kind rules of Kinds decide the rank on their own. When a derived quantity is involved, the factors common to both sides cancel first. If a single named quantity is left on each side, the same rules decide. Otherwise the equation rule of Derived quantities continues with steps 2 and 3, with K in place of a kind kind_of<K>:

 

Step 2 makes one operation at a time. After each operation it starts again from the top, until both sides are the same: both empty, or the same product right after an exact equation:

 

Step 3 takes the lowest rank of the operations made in step 2, and The kind boundary may lower it:

 

[ Editor's note: The three flowcharts are the ones in the user’s guide. A figure in the style of img/quantities_of_energy.svg could replace them here. ]

20.11.8 Consequences

A declared kind is a boundary in both directions. isq::angular_measure to isq::arc_length / isq::radius is explicit, and so is the reverse, however the equation is rearranged: quantity<isq::arc_length[m]>(angle * r), isq::angular_measure(s / r). The same holds for declared kinds with a dimension, such as the fluid head under height from Creating distinct quantity kinds with subkind: convert it with isq::height(h) before using it in a formula.

static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(isq::angular_measure, isq::arc_length / isq::radius));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(isq::angular_measure, isq::arc_length / isq::radius));

An earlier design let a declared kind be left and entered implicitly through its exact equation. It left a hole: isq::angular_measure[rad] converted implicitly to (isq::arc_length / isq::radius)[rad], which converted implicitly to dimensionless[rad], two implicit steps that leave a declared kind, which one step may not, and the symmetric boundary rules this out. For conversions, the library thereby treats an angle as if it had a dimension of its own that only an explicit conversion may strip, while keeping the dimension the ISQ assigns to it. That is the position of [Brownstein 1997] and [Mohr & Phillips 2015], and [Quincey & Brown 2016] works out what adopting it in the SI would cost. The library already refuses to add an angle to a plain dimensionless quantity, and the kind boundary extends that refusal to products and quotients. The note in Angular quantities on making angle a base quantity refers to the same debate.

Distinct roots of one dimension stay apart inside products. isq::frequency * isq::width to isq::activity * isq::length is none, like isq::frequency to isq::activity, although both equations lead into the time tree. Without this rule the two would have been expanded to 1 / period_duration and 1 / duration and related through them.

A factor common to both sides does not change how they relate, and paired factors keep their relation. A * X to B * X is decided exactly as A to B as long as no factor of X cancels against A or B (isq::height / isq::width * isq::width is just isq::height), and pairing comes before the equation, so if isq::energy converts to isq::kinetic_energy only explicitly, so does isq::energy * isq::time / isq::period_duration to isq::kinetic_energy. With gravitational_potential_energy as defined in Hierarchies of derived quantities, isq::mass * magnitude(isq::acceleration_of_free_fall) * isq::width converts to it only with a cast, since width meets height sideways. The same holds for reciprocal ratios of plain quantities: isq::height / isq::width to isq::width / isq::height is cast. Reading height / width as a plain number first would have made it explicit. A declared kind is different: isq::angular_measure to inverse(isq::angular_measure) is none, for the reason given in case 8 of Special cases.

A kind converts implicitly into sub-kinds of its tree. quantity<isq::angular_measure[rad]> angle = 3. * m / (2 * m); compiles, since 3. * m / (2 * m) is a kind of dimensionless, as Kinds explains.

A named quantity is implicitly convertible from its own equation, but not from a more generic one. isq::length / isq::time converts implicitly to speed, and inverse(isq::period_duration) to frequency, while inverse(isq::time) converts to frequency only explicitly. There are two exceptions: a declared kind is gained implicitly only from a source kind, and a source kind kind_of<K> converts implicitly to anything below K that keeps the kinds K carries, so 1. / (2 * s), a kind of inverse(isq::time), converts to frequency implicitly.

Plain isq rotational mechanics needs an explicit conversion. The ISQ defines torque without an angle but angular velocity with one, so isq::torque * magnitude(isq::angular_velocity) to isq::power is explicit. Angular velocity is a vector, so isq::torque * isq::angular_velocity is a vector and doesn’t convert to power at all:

quantity power = quantity<isq::power[W]>(torque * omega.magnitude());

The conversion names a unit as well, because the call operator and quantity_cast accept only a unit of the target’s kind, and rad / s carries the angle.

20.11.9 Special cases

The cases below are not obvious from the rules above. Each case quotes the static test in [mp-units] that guards it, where one exists.

  1. An upcast between two named quantities consults the kind boundary. isq::phase_coefficient is a child of isq::propagation_coefficient, and its equation phase_angle / path_length carries a phase angle that the parent does not. The upcast is explicit. With the tree rule alone it would be implicit, and isq::propagation_coefficient * isq::path_length to dimensionless is implicit too, so two implicit steps would shed a declared kind that the single step isq::phase_coefficient * isq::path_length to dimensionless may shed only explicitly. The alternative, requiring every child whose equation carries a kind its parent lacks to be declared subkind, would be a check at definition time. The same rule makes the ISQ information quantities that carry storage capacity through transfer rate, such as isq::period_of_binary_digits, upcast to duration only explicitly, as an angle does. Guarded in isq_test.cpp:

    static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(isq::phase_coefficient, isq::propagation_coefficient));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(isq::phase_coefficient, isq::propagation_coefficient));
static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(isq::phase_coefficient * isq::path_length, dimensionless));
static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(isq::phase_coefficient * isq::mass, isq::propagation_coefficient * isq::mass));

  2. Names never decide a tie between equally deep factors. When several factors of the greatest depth sit in the list chosen by Which operation applies, each one is expanded in turn and the best rank is kept. Expanding only the first would make the verdict depend on the order of the names: with a user-defined climb rate height / time, isq::speed * climb_rate to isq::width * isq::height / pow<2>(isq::time) ranked explicit for one spelling of the name and cast for another. Deferring every pairing below implicit while another factor’s equation mentions the tree also removes the dependence, but it moves many other verdicts to a worse rank, because the sides then no longer meet at the most specific common equation. Guarded in isq_test.cpp by two test-local twins that differ only in their names, one sorting before mp_units::isq and one after it, and a test-local width_by_height_rate:

    static_assert(explicitly-convertible(isq::speed * ::aaa_isq_test_climb, width_by_height_rate));
static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(isq::speed * ::aaa_isq_test_climb, width_by_height_rate));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(isq::speed * ::zzz_isq_test_climb, width_by_height_rate));
static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(isq::speed * ::zzz_isq_test_climb, width_by_height_rate));

  3. dimensionless is a named quantity. Its equation is the empty product, so its depth is 1, not 0. Between a named quantity and dimensionless the tree rule decides before any factor cancels. Only when the equation rule runs is it the empty list of factors, because it is the identity of a product. Guarded in isq_test.cpp:

    static_assert(implicitly-convertible(isq::rotation, dimensionless));
static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(isq::angular_measure, dimensionless));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(isq::angular_measure, dimensionless));

  4. pow<N>(Q) is not a single named quantity. Only a named quantity with exponent 1 goes to the tree rule or the kind rules. pow<2>(A) to pow<2>(B) goes through the equation rule, so its verdict comes from the operations and the kind boundary, not from the tree rule. Guarded in isq_test.cpp, where the squared pair of phase coefficient and propagation coefficient stays explicit like the bare one:

    static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(pow<2>(isq::phase_coefficient), pow<2>(isq::propagation_coefficient)));

  5. A kind of a derived quantity runs the equation rule. kind_of<K> with a derived K runs the equation rule on K, with the source known to be a kind. A downcast from it ranks implicit, dropping a declared kind stays explicit, and a factor that meets the target sideways still ranks cast. Guarded in isq_test.cpp:

    static_assert(castable(kind_of<inverse(isq::repetency)>, isq::height));
static_assert(!explicitly-convertible(kind_of<inverse(isq::repetency)>, isq::height));

  6. Pairing may leave a source factor unpaired. A source factor may stay unpaired for a later self-cancel, as long as the remaining source factors of that tree still outweigh the target factors of that tree. The wording allows more choices than [mp-units] explores, and it takes the best rank over all of them.

  7. Siblings wait tree by tree. [mp-units] defers the pairing of a whole tree in two cases. It waits when the best pairing would be cast and a factor of another tree has an equation that mentions the tree. From a kind source, it also waits when the best pairing would be none and a factor of another tree mentions the tree anywhere down its equations. The wording decides pair by pair and doesn’t follow the equations of a factor transitively, so it doesn’t cover the second case yet.

    [ Editor's note: The wording is to be aligned with the implementation. ]

  8. none without “nothing in common”. isq::angular_measure to inverse(isq::angular_measure) and pow<2>(isq::angular_measure) to isq::solid_angular_measure are none by design. A declared kind behaves much like a dimension and does not convert to its inverse or to its square. Guarded in isq_test.cpp, and in quantity_spec_test.cpp with its test-local angular_measure:

    static_assert(!castable(isq::angular_measure, inverse(isq::angular_measure)));
static_assert(!castable(pow<2>(isq::angular_measure), isq::solid_angular_measure));
static_assert(convertible(inverse(angular_measure), angular_measure) == none);

  9. A kind passes the character check. A kind admits every character, so kind_of<isq::length / isq::time> converts implicitly to the vector isq::velocity, and kind_of<isq::acceleration * isq::time> to the scalar special_speed with a cast. The typed isq::acceleration * isq::duration is a vector and doesn’t convert to special_speed at all, while the magnitude of the acceleration times a duration is a speed and converts to it explicitly. Guarded in quantity_spec_test.cpp, with quantities local to that test:

    static_assert(convertible(kind_of<length / time>, velocity) == implicit);
static_assert(convertible(kind_of<acceleration * time>, special_speed) == cast);
static_assert(convertible(acceleration * time, special_speed) == none);
static_assert(convertible(magnitude(acceleration) * time, special_speed) == explicit_only);

  10. The kind boundary nets within a side first. Each kind’s numerator count is netted against its denominator count on the same side before the two sides are compared, so isq::angular_displacement / isq::duration * isq::radius / isq::angular_measure / isq::speed to dimensionless loses nothing and is implicit. Guarded in isq_test.cpp:

    static_assert(implicitly-convertible(isq::angular_displacement / isq::duration * isq::radius / isq::angular_measure /
                                       isq::speed, dimensionless));

  11. The kind boundary caps every verdict of the tree rule and of the kind rules. The tree rule does not look at equations. Without the boundary, a kind of angular velocity would reach a child defined without the angle implicitly, and two siblings that each carry a declared kind the other lacks would be cast while their squares, decided by the equation rule, are none. On a hierarchy edge the boundary lowers the tree rule’s rank to explicit and never to none. A declared-kind child defined as inverse(isq::duration) under angular velocity gains its own kind and lacks the angle, converts to its parent and from it only explicitly, and quantity_cast between them, in a unit both accept, keeps compiling. The squared pair of such a child and its parent still ranks none, because the equation rule applies the boundary without this exemption. Both children are declared vectors, as the scalar equation inverse(isq::duration) would make them scalars, which don’t convert to the vector angular velocity at all. Guarded in isq_test.cpp, with quantities local to that test:

    inline constexpr struct turn_rate :
  named_quantity_spec<isq::angular_velocity, inverse(isq::duration), quantity_tensor_order::vector> {} turn_rate;
inline constexpr struct turn_rate_kind :
  named_quantity_spec<isq::angular_velocity, inverse(isq::duration), subkind, quantity_tensor_order::vector> {} turn_rate_kind;
inline constexpr struct angled_ratio :
  named_quantity_spec<dimensionless, isq::angular_measure * isq::length / isq::width> {} angled_ratio;
inline constexpr struct solid_angled_ratio :
  named_quantity_spec<dimensionless, isq::solid_angular_measure * isq::length / isq::width> {} solid_angled_ratio;

static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(kind_of<isq::angular_velocity>, turn_rate));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(kind_of<isq::angular_velocity>, turn_rate));
static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(kind_of<isq::angular_velocity * isq::mass>, turn_rate * isq::mass));
static_assert(!castable(angled_ratio, solid_angled_ratio));
static_assert(!castable(pow<2>(angled_ratio), pow<2>(solid_angled_ratio)));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(turn_rate_kind, isq::angular_velocity));
static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(turn_rate_kind, isq::angular_velocity));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(isq::angular_velocity, turn_rate_kind));

20.11.10 The common quantity specification

When two quantities meet in one expression, the library has to decide which quantity specification the result has. width + height needs one that fits both a width and a height, the comparison a < b, std::common_type, fma, hypot, lerp, midpoint, and the difference of two quantity points ask the same question. get-common-quantity-spec(q1, q2) answers it with the conversion rules of this chapter: the result is the most specific quantity specification that both operands convert to implicitly, and the call is ill-formed when there is none. Apart from a unit’s own symbol, which only orders two members of one magnitude inside a common_unit, the result depends on how a quantity or a unit is defined and never on its name in C++. Over every pair of ISQ quantities and every pair of units of the SI, yard-pound, USC, imperial, IEC, CGS, HEP, IAU, astronomy and typographic systems the result was checked to be the same for both argument orders.

A specification Q reaches C when implicitly-convertible(Q, C) holds. Two specifications are interconvertible when each reaches the other. The candidates considered are the operands themselves, every ancestor of a named operand, the kind root of each operand as a committed specification (one that isn’t a kind_of<>), which is speed for special_speed and length / time for height / duration, and the join of two forms, at most one of them named, sharing a factor to an integer power: the shared factor is canceled, the common specification of the remainders is found, and the shared factor is multiplied back in. The result is the most specific candidate both operands reach.

With three or more operands the call is evaluated from the left, and every operand has to reach the result: isq::frequency and inverse(isq::time) meet at inverse(isq::time), whose common specification with isq::activity is isq::activity, which a frequency never reaches, so get-common-quantity-spec(isq::frequency, inverse(isq::time), isq::activity) is ill-formed.

static_assert(get-common-quantity-spec(isq::width, isq::height) == isq::length);
static_assert(get-common-quantity-spec(kind_of<isq::length>, isq::width) == isq::width);
static_assert(get-common-quantity-spec(isq::frequency, inverse(isq::time)) == inverse(isq::time));
static_assert(get-common-quantity-spec(isq::width / isq::period_duration, isq::height / isq::period_duration) ==
              isq::length / isq::period_duration);

isq::frequency is defined over isq::period_duration, a child of isq::time, so it reaches 1 / time but not the reverse, and the less specific form is the result. The two ratios share period_duration, and the join keeps it, while the kind roots alone would have given length / time.

When the most specific candidates are interconvertible, one of them has to be chosen, and the preference is, in this order:

  1. a committed specification over a kind (length over kind_of<length>),
  2. a named quantity over a derived form, also when the named one is not an operand (speed over length / time; special_speed with length / time gives speed), and a power of one named quantity next (pow<2>(speed) over length² / time²),
  3. two derived forms fold toward each other: whenever one side contains the equation of a named factor present on the other side (a factor that defines its own equation and is not a declared kind), that part is replaced by the factor, until nothing folds. When both sides end identical, that form is the result, and it can be more composed than either operand (area * length³ with length² * volume gives area * volume),
  4. when the packagings are incompatible, the more composed operand: the greater sum of factor depths, then the fewer factors (area * speed over volume / time),
  5. otherwise the expansion of either side.

isq::angular_measure and dimensionless have no common specification (see Consequences). Two quantities of different trees have none either, isq::energy and isq::torque. Quantities of different characters have none, isq::velocity and isq::speed, and neither have two vectors that meet only in a scalar ancestor, isq::displacement and isq::position_vector. Two point specifications have a common specification only when one of them converts implicitly to the other (see Checks that come first). It is the point of the common specification of their scales, measured from their origin when it is the same, and from the absolute point origin they share otherwise. get-common-quantity-spec(point<isq::height>, point<isq::length>) is point<isq::length>, while siblings, such as point<isq::height> and point<isq::width>, two points that share no absolute point origin, and a point and a delta have none.

20.12 Quantity references

Note: We know that probably the term “reference” will not survive too long in the Committee, but we couldn’t find a better name for it in the [mp-units] library (https://github.com/mpusz/mp-units/issues/486).

[ISO/IEC Guide 99] says:

quantity - property of a phenomenon, body, or substance, where the property has a magnitude that can be expressed as a number and a reference. … A reference can be a measurement unit, a measurement procedure, a reference material, or a combination of such.

In the library a quantity reference represents all the domain-specific meta-data about the quantity besides its representation type and its value. A quantity_reference concept is satisfied by either of:

  • an associated unit (e.g., si::metre) other than an offset one,
  • a delta reference, the type of delta<QS>[U] or of QS[U] (the same reference, when U isn’t an offset unit), explicitly specifying the quantity type and its unit, or of delta<U>, the delta of a unit,
  • a point reference, the type of point<QS, PO>[U], point<QS>[U], point<U, PO>, or point<U> (see The affine space).

A delta reference is implicitly created as a result of the following expression:

constexpr quantity_reference auto distance = isq::distance[m];

The above example defines a delta reference that binds isq::distance with si::metre. A specification bound to a unit of which it is the associated kind gives the unit itself: kind_of<isq::length>[m] and delta<kind_of<isq::length>>[m] are si::metre.

A delta reference also exposes an arithmetic interface similar to the one that we have already discussed in case of units and quantity types. It forwards the operation to its quantity type and unit and normalizes the result: when the quantity specification is the kind associated with the unit, the result is the unit alone (kind_of<isq::length>[m] * s is the unit m * s).

constexpr quantity_reference_of<isq::speed> auto speed = distance / si::second;

As a result we get a delta reference binding derived_quantity_spec<distance, per<kind_of_<duration>>> with derived_unit<metre, per<second>>.

Similarly to the unit, such a reference can be used to construct a quantity, and it is also the construction helper of a delta in it:

quantity_of<isq::speed> auto s1 = 60 * speed;
quantity_of<isq::speed> auto s2 = speed(60);

A unit that is the scale of a point (si::kelvin, si::degree_Celsius, usc::degree_Fahrenheit, and their scaled versions) is not a reference on its own: a value in such a unit does not say whether a difference of temperatures or a temperature measured from the origin of its scale is meant. delta<U> and point<U> are its two references (see delta and point creation helpers). For the same reason QS[U] is ill-formed for such a unit, and the unit is bound to delta<QS> or to a point specification instead, giving a delta reference, delta<isq::thermodynamic_temperature>[deg_C], or a point reference, point<isq::thermodynamic_temperature, si::ice_point>[deg_C]. The multiply syntax is disabled for all of them. A unit derived from such a unit (pow<2>(deg_C), K / s) is a plain delta reference, as a point has no algebra and every factor of a derived unit is a delta. Every reference that an equation produces is a delta reference: where the unit algebra yields the scale of a point, the result is the delta of it (delta<K>(6.5) / (1000 * m) * (500 * m) is a quantity<delta<K>>).

delta<U> is the reference of the delta of U for every unit, so delta<m>(42) creates a delta the way point<m>(42) creates a point. For a unit other than an offset one the wrapper is kept only where the user spells it as a type (quantity<delta<m>>): delta<m>(42) is a quantity<m, int>, and delta<m> * m is pow<2>(m).

20.13 Quantities

The quantity class template is a workhorse of the library. It can be considered a generalization of std::chrono::duration, but is not directly compatible with it.

Based on the ISO definition provided in the Quantity references chapter, the quantity class template has the following signature:

template<quantity_reference auto R, representation_of<get_quantity_spec(R)> Rep = double>
class quantity;

It stores only one data member of Rep type. Unfortunately, this data member has to be publicly exposed to satisfy the C++ language requirements for structural types. Hopefully, the language rules for structural types will improve with time before this library gets standardized.

20.13.1 Multiply syntax commutativity

As of today, the multiply syntax that creates quantities is not commutative:

quantity q1 = 1 * m;  // OK
quantity q2 = m * 1;  // Compile-time error

We decided to go this way to increase the readability of the code and limit possible confusion with this syntax. After a while, we extended it to support also the following:

quantity q3 = 1 * m / s;    // OK
quantity q4 = 1 * m * m;    // OK
quantity q5 = 1 / s * m;    // OK
quantity q6 = s / 2;        // Compile-time error
quantity q7 = m * (1 / s);  // Compile-time error
quantity q8 = m * (1 * m);  // Compile-time error

However, [mp-units] users requested the following use case:

if(num < Unit / 1'000'000'000'000) {
  quantity<si::femto<Unit>, double> n{num};
  out << n;
} else if(num < Unit / 1'000'000'000) {
  quantity<si::pico<Unit>, double> n{num};
  out << n;
} else // ...

Today, this does not compile. Should we extend the multiply syntax to support such use cases and with this have entire commutative property?

20.13.2 Why don’t we use UDLs to create quantities?

Quantity construction chapter describes and explains why we introduced the multiply syntax as a construction helper for quantities. Many people ask why we chose this approach over battle-proven User Defined Literals (UDLs) that work well for the std::chrono library.

It turns out that many reasons make UDLs a poor choice for a physical units library:

  1. UDLs work only with literals (compile-time known values). Our observation is that besides the unit tests, only a few compile-time known quantity values are used in the production code. Please note that for Physical constants, we recommend using units rather than compile-time constants.

  2. Typical implementations of UDLs tend to always use the widest representation type available. In the case of std::chrono::duration in libstdc++, the following is true:

    using namespace std::chrono_literals;
auto d1 = 42s;
auto d2 = 42.s;
static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(d1)::rep, std::int64_t>);
static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(d2)::rep, long double>);

    When such UDL is intermixed in arithmetics with any quantity type of a shorter representation type, it will always expand it to the longest one. In other words, such long type spreads until all types use it everywhere.

  3. While increasing the coverage for the [mp-units] library, we learned that many unit symbols conflict with built-in types or numeric extensions. A few of those are: F (farad), J (joule), W (watt), K (kelvin), d (day), l or L (litre), erg, ergps. Using the '_' prefix would make it work for [mp-units], but if the library is standardized, those naming collisions would be a big issue. This is why we came up with the _q_ prefix that would become q_ after standardization (e.g., 42q_s), which is not that nice anymore.

  4. UDLs with the same identifiers defined in different namespace can’t be disambiguated in the literal syntax. If both SI and CGS systems define q_s UDL for a second unit, then it would not be possible to specify which one to use in case both namespaces are “imported” with using directives.

  5. Another bad property of UDLs is that they do not compose. A coherent unit of angular momentum would have a UDL specified as q_kg_m2_per_s. Now imagine that we want to make every possible user happy. How many variations of that unit would we predefine for differently scaled versions of all unit ingredients?

  6. UDLs are also really expensive to define and specify. Typically, for each unit, we need two definitions. One for integral and another one for floating-point representation. In version 0.8.0 of the [mp-units] library, the coherent unit of angular momentum was defined as:

    constexpr auto operator"" _q_kg_m2_per_s(unsigned long long l)
{
  gsl_ExpectsAudit(std::in_range<std::int64_t>(l));
  return angular_momentum<kilogram_metre_sq_per_second, std::int64_t>(static_cast<std::int64_t>(l));
}

constexpr auto operator"" _q_kg_m2_per_s(long double l)
{
  return angular_momentum<kilogram_metre_sq_per_second, long double>(l);
}

The multiply syntax that we chose for this library does not have issues 1, 2, 5, and 6, and its unit symbols can always be qualified (e.g., si::unit_symbols::min) when names clash.

20.13.3 Special values of a quantity

quantity class template, similarly to std::chrono::duration, exposes some special values as static member functions:

  • min(),
  • max(),
  • zero().

Also, similarly to std::chrono::duration those functions are implemented in terms of a type trait:

template<typename Rep>
struct representation_values : chrono::duration_values<Rep> {
  static constexpr Rep one() noexcept
    requires constructible_from<Rep, int>
 {
    return Rep(1);
 }
};

An additional one() function in representation_values is provided for use with the multiply syntax when constructing quantities. Users can create a quantity with numerical value of one using: representation_values<double>::one() * si::metre. This function is not exposed as a static member of quantity because one() is not a true multiplicative identity for dimensional quantities. For example, pow<2>(quantity<si::metre>::one()) would change the dimension from length to area.

Please also note that in C++26, std::chrono::duration_values is not a part of the freestanding library.

20.13.4 Quantity arithmetics

20.13.4.1 quantity is a numeric wrapper

If we think about it, the quantity class template is just a “smart” numeric wrapper. It exposes properly constrained set of arithmetic operations on one or two operands.

Every single arithmetic operator is exposed by the quantity class template only if the underlying representation type provides it as well and its implementation has proper semantics (e.g., returns a reasonable type).

For example, in the following code, -a will compile only if MyInt exposes such an operation as well:

quantity a = MyInt{42} * m;
quantity b = -a;

Assuming that:

  • q is our quantity,
  • qq is a quantity implicitly convertible to q,
  • q2 is any other quantity,
  • kind is a quantity of the same kind as q,
  • one is a quantity of dimension_one with the unit one,
  • number is a value of a type “compatible” with q’s representation type,

here is the list of all the supported operators:

Unary
Compound assignment
Binary
Ordering & comparison
+q
-q
++q
q++
--q
q--		 q += qq
q -= qq
q %= qq
q *= number
q *= one
q /= number
q /= one		 q + kind
q - kind
q % kind
q * q2
q * number
number * q
q / q2
q / number
number / q		 q == kind
q <=> kind

As we can see, there are plenty of operations one can do on a value of a quantity type. As most of them are obvious, in the following chapters, we will discuss only the most important or non-trivial aspects of quantity arithmetics.

20.13.4.2 Addition and subtraction

Quantities can easily be added or subtracted from each other:

static_assert(1 * m + 1 * m == 2 * m);
static_assert(2 * m - 1 * m == 1 * m);
static_assert(isq::height(1 * m) + isq::height(1 * m) == isq::height(2 * m));
static_assert(isq::height(2 * m) - isq::height(1 * m) == isq::height(1 * m));

The above uses the same types for LHS, RHS, and the result, but in general, we can add, subtract, or compare the values of any quantity type as long as both quantities are of the same kind. The result of addition and subtraction will be the common type of the arguments:

static_assert(1 * km + 1.5 * m == 1001.5 * m);
static_assert(isq::height(1 * m) + isq::width(1 * m) == isq::length(2 * m));
static_assert(isq::height(2 * m) - isq::distance(0.5 * m) == 1.5 * m);
static_assert(isq::radius(1 * m) - 0.5 * m == isq::radius(0.5 * m));

Please note that for the compound assignment operators, we always need to end up with the left-hand-side argument type:

quantity q1 = 1 * m;
q1 += 1 * km;                   // 1001 m
quantity q2 = isq::length(1 * m);
q2 += isq::height(1 * m);       // isq::length(2 * m)
quantity q3 = isq::height(1.5 * m);
q3 -= 1 * m;                    // isq::height(0.5 * m)

If we break those rules, the code will not compile:

quantity q1 = 1 * m;
q1 -= 0.5 * m;                    // Compile-time error (1)
quantity q2 = 1 * km;
q2 += 1 * m;                      // Compile-time error (2)
quantity q3 = isq::height(1 * m);
q3 += isq::length(1 * m);         // Compile-time error (3)

(1) Conversions of the floating-point to integral representation type is considered narrowing.

(2) Conversion of quantity with integral representation type from a unit of a higher resolution to the one with a lower resolution is considered narrowing.

(3) Conversion from a more generic quantity type to a more specific one is considered unsafe.

Please note that all the above operations either preserved the input representation types or returned a common type if those were different for both arguments. This is not the case for irrational conversion factors. In such cases, the library will force the user to use at least one floating-point representation type to prevent truncation:

template<typename... Ts>
consteval bool invalid_arithmetic(Ts... ts)
{
  return !requires { (... + ts); } && !requires { (... - ts); };
}

static_assert(invalid_arithmetic(1 * rad, 1 * deg));
static_assert(is_of_type<1. * rad + 1 * deg, quantity<common_unit<deg, rad>{}, double>>);
static_assert(is_of_type<1 * rad + 1. * deg, quantity<common_unit<deg, rad>{}, double>>);
static_assert(is_of_type<1. * rad + 1. * deg, quantity<common_unit<deg, rad>{}, double>>);

20.13.4.3 Multiplication and division

Multiplying or dividing a quantity by a number does not change its quantity type or unit. However, its representation type may change. For example:

static_assert(isq::height(3 * m) * 0.5 == isq::height(1.5 * m));

Unless we use a compound assignment operator, in which case we always have to result with the type of the left-hand-side argument. This, together with the fact that this library tries to prevent truncation of a quantity value means, that the following does not compile:

quantity q = isq::height(3 * m);
q *= 0.5;  // Compile-time error

However, suppose we multiply or divide quantities of the same or different types, or we divide a raw number by a quantity. In that case, we most probably will end up in a quantity of yet another type:

static_assert(120 * km / (2 * h) == 60 * km / h);
static_assert(isq::width(2 * m) * isq::length(2 * m) == isq::area(4 * m2));
static_assert(50 / isq::time(1 * s) == isq::frequency(50 * Hz));

An exception from the above rule happens when one of the arguments is a dimensionless quantity. If we multiply or divide by such a quantity, the quantity type will not change. If such a quantity has a unit one, also the unit of a quantity will not change:

static_assert(120 * m / (2 * one) == 60 * m);

An interesting special case happens when we divide the same quantity kinds or multiply a quantity by its inverted type. In such a case, we end up with a dimensionless quantity.

static_assert(isq::height(4 * m) / isq::width(2 * m) == 2 * one); // (1)
static_assert(5 * h / (120 * min) == 0 * one);                    // (2)
static_assert(5. * h / (120 * min) == 2.5 * one);

(1) The resulting quantity type of the LHS is isq::height / isq::width, which is a quantity of the dimensionless kind.

(2) The resulting quantity of the LHS is 0 * dimensionless[h / min]. To be consistent with the division of different quantity types, we do not convert quantity values to a common unit before the division.

20.13.4.3.1 Beware of integral division

The physical units library can’t do any runtime branching logic for the division operator. All logic has to be done at compile-time when the actual values are not known, and the quantity types can’t change at runtime.

If we expect 120 * km / (2 * h) to return 60 km/h, we have to agree with the fact that 5 * km / (24 * h) returns 0 km/h. We can’t do a range check at runtime to dynamically adjust scales and types based on the values of provided function arguments.

This is why we often prefer floating-point representation types when dealing with units. Some popular physical units libraries even forbid integer division of quantities whose units differ.

20.13.4.4 Modulo

Now that we know how addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division work, it is time to talk about modulo. What would we expect to be returned from the following quantity equation?

auto q = 5 * h % (120 * min);

Most of us would probably expect to see 1 h or 60 min as a result. And this is where the problems start.

The C++ language defines its / and % operators with the quotient-remainder theorem:

q = a / b;
r = a % b;
q * b + r == a;

The important property of the modulo operator is that it only works for integral representation types (the built-in % is ill-formed for floating-point operands, and fmod() and remainder() cover them). However, as we saw in the previous chapter, integral types are tricky because they often truncate the value.

From the quotient-remainder theorem, the result of modulo operation is r = a - q * b. Let’s see what we get from such a quantity equation on integral representation types:

quantity a = 5 * h;
quantity b = 120 * min;
quantity q = a / b;
quantity r = a - q * b;

std::cout << "reminder: " << r << "\n";

The above code outputs:

reminder: 5 h

And now, a tough question needs an answer. Do we really want modulo operator on physical units to be consistent with the quotient-remainder theorem and return 5 h for 5 * h % (120 * min)?

This is exactly why we decided not to follow this hugely surprising path in this library. The selected approach was also consistent with the feedback from C++ experts. For example, this is what Richard Smith said about this issue:

I think the quotient-remainder property is a less important motivation here than other factors – the constraints on % and / are quite different, so they lack the inherent connection they have for integers. In particular, I would expect that A / B works for all quantities A and B, whereas A % B is only meaningful when A and B have the same dimension. It seems like a nice-to-have for the property to apply in the case where both / and % are defined, but internal consistency of / across all cases seems much more important to me.

I would expect 61 min % 1 h to be 1 min, and 1 h % 59 min to also be 1 min, so my intuition tells me that the result type of A % B, where A and B have the same dimension, should have the smaller unit of A and B (and if the smaller one doesn’t divide the larger one, we should either use the gcd / std::common_type of the units of A and B or perhaps just produce an error). I think any other behavior for % is hard to defend.

On the other hand, for division it seems to me that the choice of unit should probably not affect the result, and so if we want that 5 mm / 120 min = 0 mm/min, then 5 h / 120 min == 0 hc (where hc is a dimensionless “hexaconta”, or 60x, unit). I don’t like the idea of taking SI base units into account; that seems arbitrary and like it would do the wrong thing as often as it does the right thing, especially when the units have a multiplier that is very large or small. We could special-case the situation of a dimensionless quantity, but that could lead to problematic overflow pretty easily: a calculation such as 10 s * 5 GHz * 2 uW would overflow an int if it produces a dimensionless quantity for 10 s * 5 GHz, but it could equally produce 50 G * 2 uW = 100 kW without any overflow, and presumably would if the terms were merely reordered.

If people want to use integer-valued quantities, I think it’s fundamental that you need to know what the units of the result of an operation will be, and take that into account in how you express computations; the simplest rule for heterogeneous operators like * or / seems to be that the units of the result are determined by applying the operator to the units of the operands – and for homogeneous operators like + or %, it seems like the only reasonable option is that you get the std::common_type of the units of the operands.

To summarize, the modulo operator on physical units has more in common with addition and division operators than with the quotient-remainder theorem. To avoid surprising results, the operation uses a common unit to do the calculation and provide its result:

static_assert(5 * h / (120 * min) == 0 * one);
static_assert(5 * h % (120 * min) == 60 * min);
static_assert(61 * min % (1 * h) == 1 * min);
static_assert(1 * h % (59 * min) == 1 * min);

20.13.4.5 Comparison against zero

Zero is special. It is the only number that unambiguously defines the value of a delta of any kind, regardless of its units: zero inches and zero meters and zero miles are all identical. For this reason, it’s very common to compare the value of a quantity against zero. For example, when checking the sign of a quantity, or when making sure that it’s nonzero.

We could implement such checks in the following way:

if(q1 / q2 != 0 * m / s)
  // ...

The above would work (assuming we are dealing with the quantity of speed), but it’s not ideal. If the result of q1 / q2 is not expressed in m / s, we’ll incur an extra unit conversion. Even if it is in m / s, it’s cumbersome to repeat the unit in a context where it makes no difference.

We could avoid repeating the unit, and guarantee there won’t be an extra conversion, by writing:

if(auto q = q1 / q2; q != q.zero())
  // ...

But that is a bit inconvenient, and inexperienced users could be unaware of this technique and its rationale.

For the above reasons, the library provides zero, a named constant of an empty tag type. Only this one value doesn’t have to state the unit, as the numerical value zero is common to all scaled units of any kind. Our check becomes:

if (q1 / q2 != zero)
  // ...

The comparison against zero works for any representation type rep for which representation_values<rep>::zero() is provided: == and != when rep is equality comparable, and all six comparison operators when it is also three-way comparable. zero also initializes or assigns a quantity of any unit:

quantity<si::metre> total = zero;

zero doesn’t convert to a representation type. It compares against representation types and against quantity-like types such as std::chrono::duration as well, which lets a generic algorithm check the sign of a double, a std::chrono::duration, and a quantity in the same way. The value of zero is carried by its type, and it keeps working when it is passed to a function, as in std::ranges::find(v, zero). The std::ranges algorithms need zero to convert to the element type, so they accept it for quantities and quantity-like types, but not for a double. A point can’t be compared against zero, because its numerical value depends on the origin. [P4406R0] compares this design with the alternatives, among them a comparison against a literal 0.

20.13.4.6 Other maths

This chapter scoped only on the quantity type’s operators. However, there are many named math functions provided in the [mp-units] library. Among others, we can find there the following:

  • pow(), sqrt(), cbrt(),
  • exp(),
  • abs(),
  • epsilon(),
  • fma(), fmod(), remainder(),
  • isfinite(), isinf(), isnan(),
  • floor(), ceil(), round(),
  • inverse(),
  • hypot(),
  • sin(), cos(), tan(),
  • asin(), acos(), atan(), atan2().

In the library, we can also find the <mp-units/utility/random.h> header file with quantity versions of all the random number distributions.

We plan to provide a separate paper on those in the future.

20.13.5 Dimensionless quantities

The quantities we discussed so far always had some specific type and physical dimension. However, this is not always the case. While performing various computations, we sometimes end up with so-called “dimensionless” quantities, which [ISO/IEC Guide 99] correctly defines as quantities of dimension one:

  • Quantity for which all the exponents of the factors corresponding to the base quantities in its quantity dimension are zero.
  • The measurement units and values of quantities of dimension one are numbers, but such quantities convey more information than a number.
  • Some quantities of dimension one are defined as the ratios of two quantities of the same kind.
  • Numbers of entities are quantities of dimension one.

20.13.5.1 Dividing two quantities of the same kind

Dividing two quantities of the same kind always results in a quantity of dimension one. However, depending on what type of quantities we divide or what their units are, we may end up with slightly different types.

Dividing two quantities of the same dimension always results in a quantity with the dimension being dimension_one. This is often different for other physical units libraries, which may return a raw representation type for such cases. A raw value is also always returned from the division of two std::chrono::duration values.

In the initial design of the [mp-units] library, the resulting type of division of two quantities was their common representation type (just like std::chrono::duration):

static_assert(std::is_same_v<decltype(10 * km / (5 * km)), int>);

The reasoning behind it was not providing a false impression of a strong quantity type for something that looks and feels like a regular number. Also, all of the mathematic and trigonometric functions were working fine out of the box with such representation types, so we did not have to rewrite sin(), cos(), exp(), and others.

However, the feedback we got from the production usage was that such an approach is really bad for generic programming. It is hard to handle the result of the two quantities’ division (or multiplication) as it might be either a quantity or a fundamental type. If we want to raise such a result to some power, we must use units::pow or std::pow depending on the resulting type (units::pow takes the power as template arguments). Those are only a few issues related to such an approach.

Moreover, suppose we divide quantities of the same dimension, but with units of significantly different magnitudes. In such case, we may end up with a really small or a huge floating-point value, which may result in losing lots of precision. Returning a dimensionless quantity from such cases allows us to benefit from all the properties of scaled units and is consistent with the rest of the library.

20.13.5.1.1 Dividing quantities of the same type

First, let’s analyze what happens if we divide two quantities of the same type:

constexpr quantity_of<dimensionless> auto q = isq::height(200 * m) / isq::height(50 * m);

In such a case, we end up with a dimensionless quantity that has the following properties:

static_assert(q.quantity_spec == dimensionless);
static_assert(q.dimension == dimension_one);
static_assert(q.unit == one);

In case we would like to print its value, we would see a raw value of 4 in the output with no unit being printed.

20.13.5.1.2 Dividing quantities of different types

We can divide quantities of the same dimension and unit but of different quantity types:

constexpr quantity_of<dimensionless> auto q = isq::mechanical_work(200 * J) / isq::heat(50 * J);

Again we end up with dimension_one and one, but this time:

static_assert(q.quantity_spec == isq::mechanical_work / isq::heat);

As shown above, the result is not of a dimensionless type anymore. Instead, we get a quantity type derived from the performed quantity equation. According to the [ISO/IEC 80000], work divided by heat is the recipe for the thermodynamic efficiency quantity, thus:

static_assert(implicitly-convertible(q.quantity_spec, isq::thermodynamic_efficiency));

Please note that the quantity of isq::thermodynamic_efficiency is of a kind dimensionless, so it is implicitly convertible to dimensionless and satisfies the quantity_of<dimensionless> concept.

20.13.5.1.3 Dividing quantities of different units

Now, let’s see what happens when we divide two quantities of the same type but different units:

constexpr quantity_of<dimensionless> auto q = isq::height(4 * km) / isq::height(2 * m);

This time we get a quantity of dimensionless type with a dimension_one as its dimension. However, the resulting unit is not one anymore:

static_assert(equivalent(q.unit, mag_power<10, 3> * one));

In case we would print the text output of this quantity, we would not see a raw value of 2000, but 2 km/m.

First, it may look surprising, but this is actually consistent with the division of quantities of different dimensions. For example, if we divide 4 * km / (2 * s), we do not expect km to be “expanded” to m before the division, right? We would expect the result of 2 * (km / s), which is exactly what we get when we divide quantities of the same kind.

This is a compelling feature that allows us to express huge or tiny ratios without the need for big and expensive representation types. With this, we can easily define things like a Hubble’s constant that uses a unit that is proportional to the ratio of kilometers per megaparsecs, which are both units of length:

inline constexpr struct hubble_constant :
    named_constant<{u8"H₀", "H_0"}, mag_ratio<701, 10> * si::kilo<si::metre> / si::second / si::mega<parsec>> {
} hubble_constant;

20.13.5.2 Counts of things

Another important use case for dimensionless quantities is to provide strong types for counts of things. For example:

  • [ISO/IEC 80000] (part 3) provides a rotation quantity defined as the number of revolutions,
  • [ISO/IEC 80000] (part 6) provides a number of turns in a winding quantity,
  • [ISO/IEC 80000] (part 13) provides a Hamming distance quantity defined as the number of digit positions in which the corresponding digits of two words of the same length are different.

Thanks to assigning strong names to such quantities, they can be used in the quantity equation of other quantities. For example, rotational frequency is defined by rotation / duration.

20.13.5.3 Predefined units of the dimensionless quantity

As we observed above, the most common unit for dimensionless quantities is one. It has the ratio of 1 and does not output any textual symbol.

A unit one is special in the entire type system of units as it is considered to be an identity operand in the unit symbolic expressions. This means that, for example:

static_assert(one * one == one);
static_assert(one * si::metre == si::metre);
static_assert(si::metre / si::metre == one);

The same is also true for dimension_one and dimensionless in the domains of dimensions and quantity specifications, respectively.

Besides the unit one, there are a few other scaled units predefined in the library for usage with dimensionless quantities:

inline constexpr struct percent : named_unit<"%", mag_ratio<1, 100> * one> {} percent;
inline constexpr struct per_mille : named_unit<{u8"‰", "%o"}, mag_ratio<1, 1000> * one> {} per_mille;
inline constexpr struct parts_per_million : named_unit<"ppm", mag_ratio<1, 1'000'000> * one> {} parts_per_million;
inline constexpr auto ppm = parts_per_million;

inline constexpr struct pi : named_constant<symbol_text{u8"π" /* U+03C0 GREEK SMALL LETTER PI */, "pi"}, mag<pi-c> * one> {} pi;
inline constexpr auto π /* U+03C0 GREEK SMALL LETTER PI */ = pi;
20.13.5.3.1 Superpowers of the unit one

Quantities implicitly convertible to dimensionless with the unit equivalent to one are the only ones that are:

  • implicitly constructible from the raw value,
  • explicitly convertible to a raw value,
  • comparable to any raw value (every delta compares against zero, see Comparison against zero).
quantity<one> inc(quantity<one> q) { return q + 1; }
void legacy(double) { /* ... */ }

if (auto q = inc(42); q != 0)
  legacy(static_cast<int>(q));

This property also expands to usual arithmetic operators.

Please note that those rules do not apply to all the dimensionless quantities. It would be unsafe and misleading to allow such operations on units with a magnitude different than 1 (e.g., percent) or for quantities that are not implicitly convertible to dimensionless (e.g., angular_measure).

20.13.5.4 Angular quantities

Special, often controversial, examples of dimensionless quantities are the angular measure and solid angular measure quantities that are defined in [ISO/IEC 80000] (part 3) to be the result of a division of arc_length / radius and area / pow<2>(radius) respectively. Moreover, [ISO/IEC 80000] also explicitly states that both can be expressed in the unit one. This means that both isq::angular_measure and isq::solid_angular_measure should be of a kind of dimensionless.

On the other hand, [ISO/IEC 80000] also specifies that the unit radian can be used for angular measure, and the unit steradian can be used for solid angular measure. Those should not be mixed or used to express other types of dimensionless quantities. We should not be able to measure:

  • basic dimensionless quantity in radians or steradians,
  • angular measure in steradians,
  • solid angular measure in radians.

This means that both isq::angular_measure and isq::solid_angular_measure should also be quantity kinds by themselves.

Note: [SI] defines an angle as the ratio of an arc length to a radius, which makes it a quantity of dimension one. Several authors argue that an angle should be a base quantity and rad a base unit [Brownstein 1997],[Mohr & Phillips 2015]. The library supports the current definition and keeps angles a distinct kind, so arc_length / radius converts to an angle explicitly.

20.13.5.4.1 Radians and degrees support

Thanks to the usage of magnitudes the library provides efficient strong types for all angular types. This means that with the built-in support for magnitudes of π\pi we can provide accurate conversions between radians and degrees. The library also provides common trigonometric functions for angular quantities:

quantity speed = 110 * km / h;
quantity rate_of_climb = -0.63657 * m / s;
quantity glide_ratio = speed / -rate_of_climb;
quantity glide_angle = angular::asin(1 / glide_ratio);

std::println("Glide ratio: {::N[.1f]}", glide_ratio.in(one));
std::println("Glide angle:");
std::println(" - {::N[.4f]}", glide_angle);
std::println(" - {::N[.2f]}", glide_angle.in(angular::degree));
std::println(" - {::N[.2f]}", glide_angle.in(angular::gradian));

The above program prints:

Glide ratio: 48.0
Glide angle:
 - 0.0208 rad
 - 1.19°
 - 1.33ᵍ

20.13.5.5 Nested quantity kinds

Angular quantities are not the only ones with such a “strange” behavior. A similar case is the storage capacity quantity specified in [ISO/IEC 80000] (part 13) that again allows expressing it in both one and bit units.

Those cases make dimensionless quantities an exceptional tree in the library. This quantity hierarchy contains more than one quantity kind and more than one unit in its tree:

Dotted lines denote subkind relationships, where a child quantity forms a distinct kind incompatible with quantities of the same parent.

To provide such support in the library, we provided a subkind specifier that can be appended to the quantity specification:

inline constexpr struct angular_measure : named_quantity_spec<dimensionless, arc_length / radius, subkind> {} angular_measure;
inline constexpr struct solid_angular_measure :
  named_quantity_spec<dimensionless, area / pow<2>(radius), subkind> {} solid_angular_measure;
inline constexpr struct storage_capacity : named_quantity_spec<dimensionless, subkind> {} storage_capacity;

With the above, we can constrain radian, steradian, and bit to be allowed for usage with specific quantity kinds only:

inline constexpr struct radian : named_unit<"rad", metre / metre, kind_of<isq::angular_measure>> {} radian;
inline constexpr struct steradian : named_unit<"sr", square(metre) / square(metre), kind_of<isq::solid_angular_measure>> {} steradian;
inline constexpr struct bit : named_unit<"bit", one, kind_of<isq::storage_capacity>> {} bit;

This still allows the usage of one (possibly scaled) for such quantities which is exactly what we wanted to achieve.

It is worth mentioning here that converting up the hierarchy beyond a subkind requires an explicit conversion. For example:

static_assert(implicitly-convertible(isq::rotation, dimensionless));
static_assert(!implicitly-convertible(isq::angular_measure, dimensionless));
static_assert(explicitly-convertible(isq::angular_measure, dimensionless));

This increases type safety and prevents accidental quantities with invalid units. For example, a result of a conversion from isq::angular_measure[rad] to dimensionless would be a reference of dimensionless[rad], which contains an incorrect unit for a dimensionless quantity. Such a conversion must be explicit and be preceded by an explicit unit conversion:

quantity q1 = isq::angular_measure(42. * rad);
quantity<dimensionless[one]> q2 = dimensionless(q1.in(one));

20.13.6 Value conversions

Truncation prevention and Unit safety chapters describe the motivation, usage, and safety benefits of the value_cast and in value conversion functions.

20.13.6.1 template disambiguation concerns

Initially mp-units library allowed changing of the quantity representation type only via the value_cast non-member function. Introducing such a functionality to the in member function would mandate the usage of the template disambiguator in generic contexts that we encourage with Generic interfaces.

After bringing those concerns to LEWGI in St. Louis, the room agreed that we should provide this functionality for member functions as well. It is really useful and user-friendly in non-generic contexts and for the cases where we deal with a dependent name, we should leave value_cast even if it is an always conversion-forcing operation.

20.13.6.2 Value conversions summary

A conversion that the framework considers truncating takes a rounding policy as its last argument. The policy is what enables such a conversion, and it states which of the neighboring representable values the caller wants. In the table below, x is a quantity, either a delta or a point, and p is one of truncated, rounded, rounded_down, and rounded_up:

Truncating
Representation
Unit
Member function
Non-member function
No Same u x.in(u)
No T Same x.in<T>()
No T u x.in<T>(u)
Yes Same u x.in(u, p) value_cast<u>(x, p)
Yes T Same x.in<T>(p) value_cast<T>(x, p)
Yes T u x.in<T>(u, p) value_cast<u, T>(x, p) or value_cast<T, u>(x, p)

The non-member functions also accept no policy, in which case they keep static_cast-like truncating semantics.

20.13.6.3 Rounding policies

Before adopting the above, [mp-units] spelled a truncating conversion x.force_in(u), with x.force_numerical_value_in(u) for the numerical value. That name was never satisfying: force_in is ambiguous in a quantities and units library, as writing x.force_in(s) reads as being about force rather than a quantity of time, and the C++ standard does not use “force” to describe a conversion anywhere.

A long search for a better name (x.forced_into(u), x.unsafe_in(u), x.lossy_in(u), x.narrow_in(u), x.unchecked_in(u), x.coerce_in(u) as in [Au], x.cast_to(u)) kept stalling on the same two obstacles. First, whichever prefix wins has to compose with a family that keeps growing: in(u), in<T>(), in<T>(u), and numerical_value_in(u), on deltas and points alike. No prefix reads well across all of it, which is what the choice between cast_numerical_value_to and numerical_value_cast_to demonstrated. Second, and more importantly, a name cannot say which of the two neighboring representable values the result should be, and that is what a caller most often needs to state.

The override therefore moved from the name into an argument:

quantity q1 = (1234 * m).in(km, truncated);        // 1 km, towards zero
quantity q2 = (1567 * m).in(km, rounded);          // 2 km, nearest, ties to even
quantity q3 = (-1234 * m).in(km, rounded_down);    // -2 km, towards negative infinity
quantity q4 = (1.23 * s).in<int>(ms, rounded_up);  // 1230 ms

We chose an argument for the following reasons:

  • One policy slot serves in, numerical_value_in, value_cast, and scale_by_magnitude alike, on both deltas and points, which brings the member interface down from six spellings to three and gives every future accessor its truncating variant without inventing a new name.
  • The policy names the consequence the caller accepts and the value they get.
  • Tag dispatch keeps the decision at compile time, so a policy can be constrained on, branched on, and rejected with a dedicated diagnostic where the requested rounding cannot be delivered. It is also established standard-library vocabulary: std::nothrow, std::in_place, std::from_range, std::sorted_unique.
  • The argument position leaves room to grow. A future saturating or checked conversion can be added as another policy.

The four policies map onto the std::chrono conversion functions:

Policy
Rounds towards
std::chrono counterpart
truncated zero duration_cast
rounded nearest, to even in halfway cases round
rounded_down negative infinity floor
rounded_up positive infinity ceil

This also puts the difference between truncated and rounded_down for negative values at the call site instead of leaving it as a default to be surprised by, which is the trap that made std::chrono retrofit floor, ceil, and round after shipping the truncating duration_cast. The floor, ceil, and round function templates listed in Other maths keep their own, different meaning: they round to an integral multiple of the provided unit even when the representation holds the exact value, while a policy never adjusts a value that the destination type represents exactly. The two coincide for integral representations.

x.force_in(u) and x.force_numerical_value_in(u) are deprecated in [mp-units] and delegate to the new functions, with x.in(u, truncated) as their exact replacement.

[Au] arrived at the same mechanism independently. It now takes a policy argument, spelled q.as(u, ignore(TRUNCATION_RISK)), and is deprecating its coerce_as and coerce_in functions in favour of it. Two libraries converging on “keep one verb and pass the override as an argument” supports this choice.

The vocabularies differ for the following reason. [Au]’s compile-time overflow check is an aggressive heuristic that produces false positives by design, so the caller has to be able to name the risk being waived. The [mp-units] check fires only when the conversion is guaranteed to overflow every non-zero value, so there is no false positive to waive. What is left for the caller to state is the value loss they accept, which is what these policies describe.

20.13.6.4 Order of the template parameters of quantity

The class template is quantity<R, Rep>, while its constructor takes the number first: quantity{40, si::second}. We keep the reference first for three reasons:

  • Rep defaults to double, and a template parameter with a default has to come after those without one. quantity<si::second> is a complete type, and quantity<double, si::second> would need the representation spelled every time.
  • The reference is what varies between quantity types and what a reader looks for first. In a signature like quantity<isq::speed[km / h], int>, it says what the value means, and the representation says how it is stored.
  • Written as a type, quantity<si::second> reads like what it holds, a quantity in seconds. The constructor follows the order of a written value, number first.

std::chrono::duration<Rep, Period> puts the representation first and gives it no default. LEWG may prefer to follow that precedent, which would also mean dropping the default double.

20.13.6.5 Bikeshedding quantity::rep

[mp-units] initially tried to be compatible with std::chrono::duration. This is why we chose rep as the name for a public member type exposed from quantity to denote its representation type. This is consistent but may not be the best name.

First, we use q.numerical_value_in() to get the underlying value which is already inconsistent with std::chrono::duration::count(). Also, as we mentioned already, quantity is a numeric wrapper. To provide compatibility between different numeric types maybe we should set a policy that those should expose value_type or element_type? Both seem to be valid choices here as well.

20.13.7 Binary operators
