Binary operators for delta and point quantities should take both arguments as template parameters. Implementing them in terms of implicit convertibility leads to invalid resulting types. Let’s see the following example:

static_assert(std::convertible_to<quantity<isq::speed[m/s], int>,
                                  quantity<(isq::length / isq::time)[m/s], double>>);
static_assert(!std::convertible_to<quantity<(isq::length / isq::time)[m/s], double>,
                                   quantity<isq::speed[m/s], int>>);

As we see above, quantity<isq::speed[m/s], int> converts to quantity<(isq::length / isq::time)[m/s], double>, but this is not the case in the other direction. This is caused by the fact that conversion from double to int is considered truncating. If we would implement the operators in terms of the implicit conversion then we would end up with the quantity of isq::length / isq::time as a result, which is suboptimal. We prefer isq::speed in this case:

quantity q1 = isq::speed(1 * m/s);
quantity q2 = isq::length(1. * m) / isq::time(1. * s);
static_assert(is_of_type<q1 + q2, quantity<isq::speed[m/s], double>>);

In the following example, we consistently use floating-point representation types and both quantities are interconvertible:

static_assert(std::convertible_to<quantity<(isq::mass * pow<2>(isq::length / isq::time))[J], double>,
                                  quantity<isq::energy[kg*m2/s2], double>>);
static_assert(std::convertible_to<quantity<isq::energy[kg*m2/s2], double>,
                                  quantity<(isq::mass * pow<2>(isq::length / isq::time))[J], double>>);

We could think that the problem is gone, and we can use implicit conversions. However, depending on how we implement it, this might lead to an ambiguous overload resolution or lack of substitutability of addition. Even if we somehow solve those issues, none of the types would be perfect as a return type. While forming a resulting type isq::energy should have a priority over isq::mass * pow<2>(isq::length / isq::time) and J should have a priority over kg*m2/s2:

quantity q1 = (isq::mass(1 * kg) * pow<2>(isq::length(1 * m) / isq::time(1 * s))).in(J);
quantity q2 = isq::energy(1 * kg*m2/s2);
static_assert(is_of_type<q1 + q2, quantity<isq::energy[J], int>>);

It is also worth noting that this approach is compatible with binary operators for std::chrono::duration. As we can read in the Interoperability with the std::chrono abstractions chapter, std::chrono::duration is interconvertible with the quantity. Nevertheless, with the above, we always need to explicitly convert the argument to a proper entity before doing any arithmetic:

static_assert(1 * s + 1s == 2 * s); // does not compile
static_assert(1 * s + quantity{1s} == 2 * s); // OK

This prevents ambiguity with std::chrono::duration operators and works the same for any user-defined quantity-like type or any other type that is convertible to a quantity.

20.14 Quantity Points

20.14.1 delta and point creation helpers

The features described in this chapter directly solve an issue raised on std-proposals reflector. As it was reported, the code below may look correct, but it provides an invalid result:

quantity Volume = 1.0 * m3;
quantity Temperature = 28.0 * deg_C;
quantity n_ = 0.04401 * kg / mol;
quantity R_boltzman = 8.314 * N * m / (K * mol);
quantity mass = 40.0 * kg;
quantity Pressure = R_boltzman * Temperature.in(K) * mass / n_ / Volume;
std::cout << Pressure << "\n";

The problem is related to the accidental usage of a delta rather than a point for Temperature. This means that after conversion to kelvins, we will get 28 K instead of the expected 301.15 K, corrupting all further calculations.

A correct code should use a point:

quantity<point<deg_C>> Temperature = point<deg_C>(28.0);

This might be an obvious thing for domain experts, but new users of the library may not be aware of the affine space abstractions and how they influence temperature handling.

After a lengthy discussion on handling such scenarios, we decided to:

  • make the above code ill-formed,
  • provide an alternative way to create deltas and points with the delta and point construction helpers respectively.

Here are the main points of this new design:

  1. All references/units that specify point origin in their definition (i.e., si::kelvin, si::degree_Celsius, and usc::degree_Fahrenheit) are excluded from the multiply syntax.

  2. A new delta quantity construction helper is introduced:

    • delta<m>(42) results with a quantity<si::metre, int>,
    • delta<deg_C>(5) results with a quantity<delta<si::degree_Celsius>, int>, as a bare si::degree_Celsius is not a reference,
    • delta<isq::height>[m](42) results with a quantity<isq::height[m], int>, as delta<QS>[U] is the reference QS[U] for a unit that isn’t an offset one,
    • delta<isq::thermodynamic_temperature>[deg_C](5) results with a quantity<delta<isq::thermodynamic_temperature>[si::degree_Celsius], int>, as isq::thermodynamic_temperature[deg_C] is ill-formed.

  3. A new point construction helper is introduced:

    • point<m>(42) results with a quantity<point<si::metre>, int>, measured from natural_point_origin<kind_of<isq::length>>,
    • point<deg_C>(5) results with a quantity<point<si::degree_Celsius>, int>, measured from si::ice_point,
    • point<isq::height>[m](42) results with a quantity<point<isq::height>[m], int>, measured from natural_point_origin<isq::height>,
    • point<isq::altitude, msl>[m](42) results with a quantity<point<isq::altitude, msl>[m], int>, measured from the origin msl.

    delta<> and point<> take a unit or a plain quantity specification. They don’t take a reference, so delta<isq::height[m]> and point<isq::altitude[m], msl> are ill-formed.

Please note that si::kelvin is also excluded from the multiply syntax to prevent the following surprising issues:

Before
Now 
quantity q(300 * K);
quantity<point<K>> qp(300 * K);
static_assert(q.in(deg_C) != qp.in(deg_C).delta_from_zero());
 
constexpr quantity q = delta<K>(300.);
constexpr quantity qp = point<K>(300.);
static_assert(q.in(deg_C) != qp.in(deg_C).delta_from_zero());

Note: [P4185R3] lifts this exclusion for si::kelvin. The origin of the kelvin is a natural origin, so the kelvin is not an offset unit there, and 300 * K is an absolute temperature rather than a delta.

We believe that the code enforced with new utilities makes it much easier to understand what happens here.

With such changes to the interface design, the offending code will not compile as initially written. Users will be forced to think more about what they write. To enable the compilation, the users have to create explicitly:

  • a point (the intended abstraction in this example) with any of the below syntaxes:

    quantity Temperature = point<deg_C>(28.0);
auto Temperature = point<deg_C>(28.0);
quantity<point<deg_C>> Temperature(delta<deg_C>(28.0));

  • a delta (an incorrect abstraction in this example) with:

    quantity Temperature = delta<deg_C>(28.0);
auto Temperature = delta<deg_C>(28.0);

Thanks to the new design, we can immediately see what happens here and why the result might be incorrect in the second case.

20.14.2 default_point_origin(R), delta_from_zero(), and natural_point_origin<QuantitySpec>

default_point_origin(R), delta_from_zero(), and natural_point_origin<QuantitySpec> are introduced to simplify the usage of:

  • temperature (and quantities with similar units) points where each unit has its own origin,
  • quantity points for domains with one unquestionable “zero” origin and for which we do not have other predefined origins known at compile time.

In theory, those abstractions are not needed, and in this chapter, we will describe how the API and use cases would look like without it.

Let’s try to reimplement parts of our room AC temperature controller from the Temperature support chapter:

constexpr struct room_reference_temp : relative_point_origin<si::ice_point + delta<deg_C>(21)> {} room_reference_temp;
using room_temp = quantity<point<isq::thermodynamic_temperature, room_reference_temp>[deg_C]>;

room_temp room_ref{};

std::println("Room reference temperature: {} ({}, {::N[.2f]})\n",
             room_ref.delta_from(si::ice_point).in(deg_C),
             room_ref.delta_from(usc::fahrenheit_zero).in(deg_F),
             room_ref.delta_from(si::absolute_zero).in(K));
// prints: Room reference temperature: 21 °C (69.8 °F, 294.15 K)

Now let’s compare it to the implementation using the currently proposed design:

constexpr struct room_reference_temp : relative_point_origin<point<deg_C>(21)> {} room_reference_temp;
using room_temp = quantity<point<isq::thermodynamic_temperature, room_reference_temp>[deg_C]>;

room_temp room_ref{};

std::println("Room reference temperature: {} ({}, {::N[.2f]})\n",
             room_ref.delta_from(default_point_origin(deg_C)).in(deg_C),
             room_ref.delta_from(default_point_origin(deg_F)).in(deg_F),
             room_ref.delta_from(default_point_origin(K)).in(K));
// prints: Room reference temperature: 21 °C (69.8 °F, 294.15 K)

First, removing those features also renders point<deg_C>(21) impossible to implement. Second, default_point_origin(unit) always gives the correct standard origin for the current unit, so if someone changes the unit, no origin name needs updating.

For points already at their unit’s default origin (the common case for directly constructed temperature points), text output works directly and delta_from_zero() returns the delta from that origin:

quantity temp = point<deg_C>(21.);  // PO = default_point_origin(deg_C) = ice_point

std::println("{} ({}) ({::N[.2f]})", temp, temp.in(deg_F), temp.in(K));
// prints: 21 °C (69.8 °F) (294.15 K)

auto delta_C = temp.delta_from_zero();        // 21 °C — from ice_point
auto delta_K = temp.in(K).delta_from_zero();  // 294.15 K — from absolute_zero

.delta_from_zero() is constrained to PO == default_point_origin(R), matching zero(). For points at custom origins (such as room_ref above), use delta_from(default_point_origin(unit)) to obtain the delta from the standard origin.

To extract the raw number at a program boundary (serialization, hardware registers, a legacy API), a point provides numerical_value_in(unit), the exact inverse of point<unit>(value). It reads the point on the scale of the requested unit, re-anchoring across offset units so that the value always matches the one a point<unit>(value) constructor would round-trip:

double celsius = temp.numerical_value_in(deg_C);  // 21   — same number passed to point<deg_C>(21.)
double kelvin  = temp.numerical_value_in(K);      // 294.15 — re-anchored to absolute_zero

A policy-taking overload, numerical_value_in(unit, policy), is provided for conversions that numerical_value_in(unit) rejects as non-value-preserving (for example an integer representation scaled to a coarser unit), mirroring the same pair of overloads on a delta (see Rounding policies). Both are constrained to PO == default_point_origin(R) (the same condition as delta_from_zero() and text output), because a point at a custom origin has no unique numerical representation. For such points, request the value from an explicit origin instead:

double from_ice = room_ref.delta_from(default_point_origin(deg_C)).numerical_value_in(deg_C);  // 21

20.15 Interoperability with other libraries

It is easy to cooperate with similar entities of other libraries. No matter if we want to provide interoperability with a simple home-grown strongly typed wrapper type (e.g., Meter, Timestamp, …) or with a feature-rich quantities and units library, we have to provide a specialization of quantity_like_traits with:

  • a delta reference (e.g., a unit) for an external delta-like type,
  • a point reference, such as point<QS, PO>[U] or point<U, PO>, for an external point-like type.

The framework names a type adapted this way, other than a quantity itself, with the exposition-only concept QuantityLike.

20.15.1 Specifying a conversion kind

Before we delve into the template specialization details, let’s first decide if we want the conversions to happen implicitly or if explicit ones would be a better choice. Or maybe the conversion should be implicit in one direction only (e.g., into abstractions in this library) while the explicit conversions in the other direction should be preferred?

There is no one unified answer to the above questions. Everything depends on the use case.

Typically, in the C++ language, the implicit conversions are allowed in cases where:

  • both abstractions mean exactly the same, and interchanging them in the code should not change its logic,
  • there is no significant runtime overhead introduced by such a conversion (e.g., no need for dynamic allocation or copying of huge internal buffers),
  • the target type of the conversion provides the same or better safety to the users,
  • we prefer the simplicity of implicit conversions over safety during the (hopefully short) transition period of refactoring our code base from the usage of one library to the other.

In all other scenarios, we should probably enforce explicit conversions.

The kinds of inter-library conversions can be easily configured in specializations of conversion traits in the mp-units library. Conversion traits should provide a static constexpr bool data member. If the value is true, then the conversion is explicit. Otherwise, if the value is false, implicit conversions will be allowed. The names of the flags are as follows:

  • explicit_import to describe conversion from the external entity to the one in this library (import case),
  • explicit_export to describe conversion from the entity in this library to the external one (export case).

20.15.2 Quantities conversions

For example, let’s assume that some company has its own Meter strong-type wrapper:

struct Meter {
  int value;
};

As every usage of Meter is at least as good and safe as the usage of quantity<si::metre, int>, and as there is no significant runtime performance penalty, we would like to allow the conversion to std::quantity to happen implicitly.

On the other hand, the quantity type is much safer than the Meter, and that is why we would prefer to see the opposite conversions stated explicitly in our code.

To enable such interoperability, we must define a specialization of the quantity_like_traits<T> type trait. Such specialization should provide:

  • reference static data member that provides the quantity reference (e.g., unit),
  • rep type that specifies the underlying storage type and matches representation_of with the character of reference,
  • explicit_import static data member of type bool that specifies that the conversion from T to a quantity type should happen explicitly (if true),
  • explicit_export static data member of type bool that specifies that the conversion from a quantity type to T should happen explicitly (if true),
  • to_numerical_value(T) static member function returning a quantity’s raw value of rep type,
  • from_numerical_value(rep) static member function returning T.

For example, for our Meter type, we could provide the following:

template<>
struct std::quantity_like_traits<Meter> {
  static constexpr auto reference = si::metre;
  static constexpr bool explicit_import = false;
  static constexpr bool explicit_export = false;
  using rep = decltype(Meter::value);
  static constexpr rep to_numerical_value(Meter m) { return m.value; }
  static constexpr Meter from_numerical_value(rep v) { return Meter{v}; }
};

After that, we can check that a quantity is constructible from Meter, which is what the traits provide:

static_assert(std::constructible_from<quantity<si::metre>, Meter>);

and we can write the following:

void print(Meter m) { std::cout << m.value << " m\n"; }

int main()
{
  using namespace std::si::unit_symbols;

  Meter height{42};

  // implicit conversions
  std::quantity h1 = height;
  std::quantity<std::isq::height[m], int> h2 = height;

  std::cout << h1 << "\n";
  std::cout << h2 << "\n";

  // explicit conversions
  print(Meter(h1));
  print(Meter(h2));
}

No matter if we decide to use implicit or explicit conversions, the library’s framework will not allow unsafe operations to happen.

If we extend the above example with unsafe conversions, the code will not compile, and we will have to fix the issues first before the conversion may be performed:

Unsafe
Fixed 
quantity<isq::height[m]> h3 = height;
quantity<isq::height[mm], int> h4 = height;
quantity<isq::height[km], int> h5 = height;  // Error (1)

std::cout << h3 << "\n";
std::cout << h4 << "\n";
std::cout << h5 << "\n";

print(Meter(h3));                            // Error (2)
print(Meter(h4));                            // Error (3)
print(Meter(h5));
 
quantity<isq::height[m]> h3 = height;
quantity<isq::height[mm], int> h4 = height;
quantity<isq::height[km], int> h5 = quantity{height}.in(km, truncated);

std::cout << h3 << "\n";
std::cout << h4 << "\n";
std::cout << h5 << "\n";

print(Meter(value_cast<int>(h3)));
print(Meter(h4.in(m, truncated)));
print(Meter(h5));

(1) Truncation of value while converting from meters to kilometers.

(2) Conversion of double to int is not value-preserving.

(3) Truncation of value while converting from millimeters to meters.

20.15.3 Quantity points conversions

To play with quantity point conversions, let’s assume that we have a Timestamp strong type in our codebase, and we would like to start using this library to work with this abstraction.

struct Timestamp {
  int seconds;
};

As we described in The Affine Space chapter, timestamps should be modeled as quantity points rather than deltas.

To allow the conversion between our custom Timestamp type and a point quantity, we need to provide the following in the specialization of the same quantity_like_traits<T> type trait, this time with a point reference:

  • reference static data member that provides the point reference point<U, PO>, which names both the unit and the origin of our measurement scale,
  • rep type that specifies the underlying storage type,
  • explicit_import static data member of type bool that specifies that the conversion from T to a quantity type should happen explicitly (if true),
  • explicit_export static data member of type bool that specifies that the conversion from a quantity type to T should happen explicitly (if true),
  • to_numerical_value(T) static member function returning a raw value of the quantity being the offset of the point from the origin,
  • from_numerical_value(rep) static member function returning T.

For example, for our Timestamp type, we could provide the following:

template<>
struct std::quantity_like_traits<Timestamp> {
  static constexpr auto reference = point<si::second>;
  static constexpr bool explicit_import = false;
  static constexpr bool explicit_export = false;
  using rep = decltype(Timestamp::seconds);
  static constexpr rep to_numerical_value(Timestamp ts) { return ts.seconds; }
  static constexpr Timestamp from_numerical_value(rep v) { return Timestamp(v); }
};

After that, we can check that a point is constructible from Timestamp, which is what the traits provide:

static_assert(std::constructible_from<std::quantity<std::point<std::si::second>>, Timestamp>);

and we can write the following:

void print(Timestamp ts) { std::cout << ts.seconds << " s\n"; }

int main()
{
  Timestamp ts{42};

  // implicit conversion
  std::quantity qp = ts;

  std::cout << qp << "\n";

  // explicit conversion
  print(Timestamp(qp));
}

20.15.4 Interoperability with the std::chrono abstractions

In the C++ standard library, we have two types that handle quantities and model the affine space. Those are:

  • std::chrono::duration - specifies quantities of time,
  • std::chrono::time_point - specifies quantity points of time.

This library comes with built-in interoperability with those types thanks to:

  • specializations of quantity_like_traits (for deltas and for points) that provide support for implicit conversions between types in both directions,
  • chrono_point_origin<Clock> point origin for std clocks,
  • to_chrono_duration and to_chrono_time_point dedicated conversion functions that result in types exactly representing this library’s abstractions.

The specialization for std::chrono::duration provides a delta reference:

template<typename Rep, typename Period>
struct quantity_like_traits<chrono::duration<Rep, Period>> {
  static constexpr auto reference = time-unit-from-chrono-period<Period>();
  static constexpr bool explicit_import = false;
  static constexpr bool explicit_export = false;
  using rep = Rep;
  using T = chrono::duration<Rep, Period>;

  [[nodiscard]] static constexpr rep to_numerical_value(const T& q) noexcept(is_nothrow_copy_constructible_v<rep>)
  {
    return q.count();
  }

  [[nodiscard]] static constexpr T from_numerical_value(const rep& v) noexcept(is_nothrow_copy_constructible_v<rep>)
  {
    return T(v);
  }
};

quantity q = 42s;
std::chrono::seconds dur = 42 * s;

A std::chrono::time_point is a point, so its traits provide a point reference:

template<typename C, typename Rep, typename Period>
struct quantity_like_traits<chrono::time_point<C, chrono::duration<Rep, Period>>> {
  static constexpr auto reference = point<time-unit-from-chrono-period<Period>(), chrono_point_origin<C>>;
  static constexpr bool explicit_import = false;
  static constexpr bool explicit_export = false;
  using rep = Rep;
  using T = chrono::time_point<C, chrono::duration<Rep, Period>>;

  [[nodiscard]] static constexpr rep to_numerical_value(const T& tp) noexcept(is_nothrow_copy_constructible_v<rep>)
  {
    return tp.time_since_epoch().count();
  }

  [[nodiscard]] static constexpr T from_numerical_value(const rep& v) noexcept(is_nothrow_copy_constructible_v<rep>)
  {
    return T(chrono::duration<Rep, Period>(v));
  }
};

quantity qp = time_point_cast<std::chrono::seconds>(std::chrono::system_clock::now());
std::chrono::sys_seconds q = qp + 42 * s;

It is important to note here that only a point that uses chrono_point_origin<Clock> as its origin can be converted to the std::chrono abstractions:

inline constexpr struct ts_origin : relative_point_origin<chrono_point_origin<system_clock> + 1 * h> {} ts_origin;
inline constexpr struct my_origin : absolute_point_origin<isq::time> {} my_origin;

quantity qp1 = sys_seconds{1s};
auto tp1 = to_chrono_time_point(qp1);  // OK

quantity qp2 = chrono_point_origin<system_clock> + 1 * s;
auto tp2 = to_chrono_time_point(qp2);  // OK

quantity qp3 = ts_origin + 1 * s;
auto tp3 = to_chrono_time_point(qp3);  // OK

quantity qp4 = my_origin + 1 * s;
auto tp4 = to_chrono_time_point(qp4);  // Compile-time Error (1)

quantity qp5 = point<s>(1);
auto tp5 = to_chrono_time_point(qp5);  // Compile-time Error (2)

(1) my_origin is not defined in terms of chrono_point_origin<Clock>.

(2) natural_point_origin is not defined in terms of chrono_point_origin<Clock>.

Here is an example of how interoperability described in this chapter can be used in practice:

using namespace std::chrono;

sys_seconds ts_now = floor<seconds>(system_clock::now());

quantity start_time = ts_now;
quantity speed = 925. * km / h;
quantity distance = 8111. * km;
quantity flight_time = distance / speed;
quantity exp_end_time = start_time + flight_time;

sys_seconds ts_end = value_cast<sys_seconds::rep>(exp_end_time.in(s));

auto curr_time = zoned_time(current_zone(), ts_now);
auto mst_time = zoned_time("America/Denver", ts_end);

std::cout << "Takeoff: " << curr_time << "\n";
std::cout << "Landing: " << mst_time << "\n";

The above may print the following output:

Takeoff: 2023-11-18 13:20:54 UTC
Landing: 2023-11-18 15:07:01 MST

As mentioned above, conversions between entities in this and std::chrono libraries are implicit in both directions when the representation conversion preserves every value. This simplifies many scenarios. However, with such rules, common_type_t<chrono::seconds, quantity<si::second, chrono::seconds::rep>> and the ternary operator on such arguments don’t work. If this concerns LEWG, we may consider implicit conversion in only one direction. However, it is not easy to decide which one to choose.

21 Teachability

Through the last years [mp-units] library proved to be very intuitive to both novices in the domain and non-C++ experts. Thanks to the user-friendly multiply syntax, support for CTAD, excellent readability of generated types in compiler error messages, and simplicity of systems definitions, this library makes it easy to do the first steps in the dimensional analysis domain.

21.1 Target audiences

Following the practice suggested in [P1700R0], we identify four distinct user populations for this library, each with different needs and interactions:

Audience
Population
Roles and skills
Application Developers millions Write application code using pre-defined quantities, units, and systems. Perform arithmetic with automatic dimensional analysis and compile-time unit safety. Use quantity for deltas and points (temperature, GPS, timestamps). Write generic interfaces constrained with quantity_of. Interoperate with std::chrono. Modernise existing codebases by replacing raw numeric types with strongly-typed quantities.
Unit Authors tens of thousands Add named or scaled units to existing quantity types: standard-system extensions (imperial, binary prefixes) and derived combinations. Work entirely within the provided ISQ hierarchy; no new dimensions or quantity specifications required.
Domain Modelers thousands Properly model a new domain: define quantity systems (ISQ-like hierarchies), dimensions, quantity specifications, quantity kind hierarchies, and units. Design domain frameworks (physics engines, geodesy libraries, robotics toolkits) with correct ISQ-style structure. Require domain knowledge and familiarity with the quantity type system; deep C++ metaprogramming is not needed.
Deep Integrators hundreds Bridge custom or legacy types into the quantity system via quantity_like_traits. Implement custom representation types with specialised scaling behaviour. Require template metaprogramming expertise and understanding of library internals; domain-specific quantity modelling is not needed.

The vast majority of users (Application Developers) can be productive with minimal learning, and expert users can still extend the library.

The following table maps library features to their primary target audiences:

Application Developers need only the first eleven rows, the core usage features. Unit Authors additionally define named and scaled units within the existing ISQ hierarchy. Domain Modelers and Deep Integrators are largely disjoint audiences: Domain Modelers bring domain expertise to define quantity systems, dimensions, and specifications, while Deep Integrators bring C++ metaprogramming expertise to extend the library’s type machinery. Both groups build on Unit Author skills.

21.2 Prerequisites and target audience

Students should have basic familiarity with:

  • C++ fundamentals (variables, functions, basic templates)
  • Basic physics concepts (distance, time, speed) for motivation

The library is suitable for:

  • introductory programming courses, where it teaches type safety early with intuitive physical examples,
  • scientific computing courses, where it provides practical dimensional analysis tools,
  • software engineering courses, where it demonstrates modern C++ library design and compile-time safety,
  • physics and engineering courses, where it replaces error-prone raw numeric computations.

No prior knowledge of template metaprogramming or dimensional analysis is required for basic usage.

21.3 Motivation through real-world disasters

Real failures help students understand why strong typing matters:

  • [Mars Orbiter] - Lost in 1999 because ground software produced pound-force-seconds while the navigation system expected newton-seconds ($125M loss)
  • [Gimli Glider] - Air Canada Flight 143 ran out of fuel mid-flight in 1983 after the load was calculated in pounds instead of kilograms
  • [Columbus] - Mixed up the Arabic mile and the Roman mile while preparing his voyage, badly underestimating the size of the equator and his expected travel distance
  • [Ariane flight V88] - Ariane 5 rocket destroyed in 1996 by an overflow when converting a 64-bit floating-point value to a 16-bit signed integer ($370M loss)

See Safety concerns for more examples and a deeper discussion of why these errors happen.

These examples demonstrate that unit and conversion errors are costly and can slip through code review and testing. A short comparison of untyped and typed code:

// Unsafe - compiles but crashes spacecraft
double orbital_velocity(double radius, double period)
{
  return 2 * 3.14159 * radius / period;
}
auto v = orbital_velocity(6'771'000, 5'561);  // What units? Which one is length? Compiler can't tell!

// Safe - units enforced at compile time
quantity<si::metre / si::second> orbital_velocity(quantity<si::metre> radius, quantity<si::second> period)
{
  return 2 * pi * radius / period;
}
quantity v = orbital_velocity(6'771 * km, 92.68 * min);  // OK: 7651 m/s

21.4 Learning path for beginners

21.4.1 Step 1: Basic quantities

If someone is new to the domain, a concise introduction of Systems of units, the [SI], and the US Customary System (and how it relates to SI) might be needed.

After that, every new user, even a C++ newbie, should have no problems with understanding the topics of the Quantity construction chapter and should be able to start using the library successfully. At least as long as they keep operating in the safety zone using floating-point representation types.

Start with the multiply syntax for creating quantities:

import std;

int main()
{
  using namespace std::si::unit_symbols;

  std::quantity distance = 100.0 * m;
  std::quantity time = 9.58 * s;
  std::quantity speed = distance / time;

  std::println("Usain Bolt's speed: {::N[.2f]}", speed);  // 10.44 m/s
}

Key teaching points:

  • Natural syntax: 100.0 * m reads like physics notation
  • Automatic unit propagation: m / s derived from division
  • Type safety: Cannot accidentally add distance + time
  • CTAD eliminates verbose type spelling

21.4.2 Step 2: Unit conversions and safety

Eventually, the library will stand in the way, disallowing “unsafe” conversions. This would be a perfect place to mention the importance of providing safe interfaces at compile-time and describe why narrowing conversions are unwelcome and what the side effects of those might be. After that, the rounding policies that enable lossy conversions should be presented.

Demonstrate safe conversions:

quantity<m> race_distance = 100. * m;
quantity<km> trip_distance = race_distance.in(km);  // Safe: 0.1 km

quantity<m, int> d1 = 5 * m;          // OK
quantity<m, int> d2 = 5.5 * m;        // Error: narrowing conversion
quantity<m, int> d3 = (5.5 * m).in<int>(truncated);  // Explicit truncation

quantity<km, int> d4 = 1500 * m;      // Error: truncation in conversion
quantity<km, int> d5 = (1500 * m).in(km, truncated);  // Explicit: d5 == 1 km

This introduces:

  • The .in(unit) member function for safe conversions
  • Why the library prevents narrowing (data loss, bugs)
  • An explicit rounding policy (.in(unit, truncated)) for intentional lossy conversions
  • Difference between representation narrowing and unit conversion narrowing

21.4.3 Step 3: Interacting with legacy code

In case a target audience needs to interact with legacy interfaces that take raw numeric values, Safe quantity numerical value getters chapter should be introduced. In such a case, it is important to warn students of why this operation is unsafe and what are the potential maintainability issues.

// Legacy API
void legacy_api(double distance_in_meters);

// Modern code
quantity dist = 5 * km;
legacy_api(dist.numerical_value_in(m));  // Explicit: I know this is in meters

Emphasize the dangers: the compiler cannot verify that distance_in_meters actually expects meters rather than feet or kilometers. You must manually ensure the unit in .numerical_value_in() matches the legacy API’s expectations, which may be undocumented or ambiguous.

21.4.4 Step 4: Custom units and extensions

Next, we could show how easy extending the library with custom units is. A simple and funny example like the below could be a great exercise here:

import std;

inline constexpr struct smoot : std::named_unit<"smoot", std::mag<67> * std::usc::inch> {} smoot;

int main()
{
  constexpr std::quantity dist = 364.4 * smoot;
  std::println("Harvard Bridge length = {::N[.5]} ({::N[.5]}, {::N[.5]}) ± 1 εar",
               dist, dist.in(std::usc::foot), dist.in(std::si::metre));
}

This demonstrates that the library is extensible and students can define domain-specific units (e.g., furlongs per fortnight, pixels for graphics).

21.4.5 Step 5: Temperature and affine spaces

After a while, we can also introduce students to The affine space abstractions and discuss the Temperature support.

This introduces the distinction between deltas (delta<deg_C>) and points (point<deg_C>), both modeled with quantity, using temperature as the most intuitive example:

quantity temp_diff = delta<deg_C>(20);      // Temperature difference
quantity temp = point<deg_C>(20);           // Absolute temperature

quantity diff = temp - point<deg_C>(0);     // OK: difference between points
// auto sum = temp + point<deg_C>(10);      // Error: can't add points

With the above, we have learned enough for most users’ needs and do not need to delve into more details. The library is intuitive and turns most unit and affine-space mistakes into compile-time errors.

21.5 Advanced topics

For more advanced classes, groups, or use cases, we can introduce Generic Interfaces and Systems of quantities but we don’t have to describe every detail and corner cases of quantity types design and their convertibility. It is good to start here with Why do we need typed quantities?, followed by Quantities of the same kind and System of quantities is not only about kinds.

21.5.1 Type system and quantity hierarchies

According to our experience, the most common pitfall in using quantity types might be related to the names chosen for them by the [ISO/IEC 80000] (e.g., length). It might be good to describe what length means when we say “every height is a length” and what it means when we describe a box of length, width, and height dimensions. In the latter case, length will not restrict us to the horizontal dimension only. This is how the ISQ is defined, and we should accept this. However, we should present a way to define horizontal length as presented in the Comparing, adding, and subtracting quantities of the same kind and describe its rationale.

Advanced students can explore:

  • Generic programming with quantity concepts (quantity_of<isq::length>)
  • Defining custom quantity types (e.g., horizontal_length, gravitational_potential_energy)
  • Interoperability with std::chrono::duration and other libraries
  • Vector and tensor quantities for mechanics and graphics

21.6 Compiler diagnostics and debugging

When students make mistakes, the library gives them readable compiler errors:

quantity d = 100. * m;
quantity t = 50. * s;
quantity wrong = d + t;  // Error

Type names in errors remain close to the source code: quantity<si::metre, double> rather than expanded template instantiations.

A debugger shows the unit as part of the type next to the value. Print formatting with std::print produces human-readable output without custom formatters.

21.7 Exercises and assessment

Suggested exercises for different skill levels:

Beginner:

  1. Convert recipe measurements between metric and imperial units
  2. Calculate speed from distance and time (e.g., average speed for a road trip)
  3. Compute area and volume (rectangle, box) with mixed units

Intermediate:

  1. Implement projectile motion calculator (initial velocity, angle, range, max height)
  2. Energy and power calculations (kinetic energy, potential energy, power consumption over time)
  3. Pressure, volume, and temperature conversions (ideal gas law scenarios)

Advanced:

  1. Implement generic numeric algorithms (linear interpolation, integration) that work with quantities
  2. Design a domain-specific unit system (e.g., astronomical units, parsecs, light-years)
  3. Integrate existing strongly-typed wrappers with the library using quantity_like_traits

21.8 Common mistakes and misconceptions

Based on teaching experience with [mp-units]:

  1. Using integer representation types: Leads to narrowing and overflow errors
    • Example: quantity d = 1500 * m; quantity km_val = d.in(km); fails (truncation)
    • Example: quantity<nm, int> small = 5 * m; compiles but overflows at run time (the compile-time overflow check rejects only a conversion that overflows every non-zero value)
    • Solution: Use floating-point for most cases, an explicit rounding policy (e.g., .in(km, truncated)) when integer truncation is intentional
  2. Operator precedence with unit literals: Forgetting parentheses in expressions
    • Example: quantity frequency = 1. / 2 * s; gives 0.5 s, not 0.5 1/s
    • Correct: quantity frequency = 1. / (2 * s); or quantity period = 2. * s; auto frequency = 1 / period;
    • Solution: Use parentheses or intermediate variables for clarity
  3. Confusing deltas and points: Attempting invalid affine space operations
    • Example: auto result = point<deg_C>(20) + point<deg_C>(30); fails (two points can’t be added)
    • Solution: Understand the difference between deltas (delta<deg_C>) and points (point<deg_C>)
  4. Forgetting namespace qualification: Writing 42 * m without importing unit symbols
    • Solution: Add using namespace std::si::unit_symbols; or use qualified names
  5. Overusing .numerical_value_in(): Extracting raw values unnecessarily
    • Problem: Defeats type safety, makes refactoring harder
    • Solution: Keep quantities typed as long as possible, extract only at boundaries

21.9 Integration with curricula

This library can be used in existing courses:

In CS1/CS2 (introductory programming):

  • Introduce alongside basic types as motivation for type safety
  • Use in physics-based programming exercises (projectile motion, etc.)
  • Teaches good habits early: explicit units, compile-time verification

In numerical methods and scientific computing:

  • Replace raw double arrays with typed quantities
  • Demonstrate that abstraction doesn’t hurt performance
  • Real-world applications: simulation, data analysis

In software engineering:

  • Case study in modern C++ library design
  • Example of zero-overhead abstractions
  • Unit testing with dimensional analysis

In physics and engineering computation:

  • Drop-in replacement for manual unit tracking
  • Lets students focus on the problem
  • Prevents unit-mismatch bugs

21.10 Teaching impact beyond C++

The previous sections focus on teaching the library itself. A standardized quantities and units library can also be used to teach units and quantities in general, beyond computer science: in physics and engineering courses and in primary education.

21.10.1 Enabling interdisciplinary education

Physics teachers can build hands-on computational exercises where students implement real physics equations (projectile motion, circuit analysis, thermodynamics) with compile-time verification that their dimensional analysis is correct. Engineering instructors can create laboratory exercises where sensor data is processed with proper unit handling from the start, mirroring professional practice. Chemistry educators can teach stoichiometry and gas laws with students writing code that keeps moles, grams, litres, and atmospheres apart.

A student learning physics implements the formulas, and the compiler checks the dimensional relationships in them.

21.10.2 Supporting faculty with limited programming experience

Many science and engineering faculty have computational needs but limited software engineering expertise. The library’s intuitive multiply syntax (distance = 50 * km) requires minimal C++ knowledge while providing significant safety benefits. Faculty can create course materials using straightforward code that reads like mathematical notation, lowering the barrier to incorporating computation into their curriculum. The library’s compile-time errors also point at dimensional analysis mistakes that indicate conceptual misunderstandings.

21.10.3 Enriching K-12 and informal education

Computing education increasingly begins in primary and secondary schools. Robotics programs provide rich opportunities to introduce quantities and units naturally. A middle school robotics team programming their robot to navigate a course benefits from using speed = 30 * cm / s instead of raw numbers. The units in the code tell young programmers what each number means.

When students can write if (distance < 50 * cm) { stop(); } the connection between their physical robot and their code becomes clearer. The compiler stops them from comparing a distance with a time.

Similarly, informal education settings (science museums, summer camps, maker spaces) can use the library in interactive exhibits and workshops.

21.10.4 Preparing students for professional practice

With a standard library, what students learn about units handling in C++ transfers directly to professional software development. Students who learn to write quantity area = width * height; where width and height are quantities develop habits that prevent real-world errors in safety-critical systems.

This is particularly important for students entering industries where C++ dominates: aerospace, automotive, embedded systems, robotics, quantitative finance, and game development. A graduate who has used quantities and units throughout their coursework arrives at their first job already familiar with dimensional analysis in code.

Without a standard, each company uses incompatible internal libraries or ad-hoc approaches, and new graduates relearn concepts they should already know.

22 Synopsis

This chapter lists the declarations of the proposed framework so that its scope and exact interfaces can be reviewed in one place. It does not specify any semantics. It also does not cover systems of quantities and units, math utilities, or any other part of [mp-units] that this paper does not propose. Where a declaration says see below, the definition is not given here.

The declarations are taken from the headers of the version-3 branch of [mp-units], ahead of its 3.0.0 release. The following adjustments apply:

  • Everything is shown in namespace std, as proposed in Library namespace. Names are kept as in [mp-units], including those that Names that need a decision leaves open, except that the customization point objects are shown in the nested namespace std::math and per and power are exposition-only.
  • The types of the wrapper variable templates (delta, point, kind_of, and the unit prefixes) are exposition-only: users write the variable templates, never the types, so the types need no public name and stay out of the interface. Recommended practice: implementations should name these types as shown here, so that diagnostics read the same across vendors.
  • Workarounds for current compiler limitations are replaced with the form intended for standardization (e.g., a single pow with a defaulted Den template parameter, and named_quantity_spec defined without CRTP using an explicit object parameter). Disjuncts that exist in constraints only to improve diagnostics are removed.
  • Features of [mp-units] that this paper does not propose are omitted: uncertainty of measured constants, bounds and overflow policies of point origins and constraint violation handlers ([P4412R0]), frame projections, non-negative quantity specifications ([P4411R0]), component access for vector quantities and their construction from components ([P4407R0]), the unit_for, reference_for, and rep_for traits, and the observers of unit magnitudes (e.g., get_value) used internally by the scaling engine.
  • Names that the implementation does not expose, most of them kept in a detail namespace, appear in italics as exposition-only names, and their definitions are not given. The exceptions are the types whose members or base classes are part of the interface: quantity-spec-interface provides the subscript and call operators of every quantity specification, delta-spec-t is the type of delta<QS>, delta-t is the type of delta<QS>[U], QS[U], and delta<U> (the reference of a delta), point-t is the type of point (a quantity specification for point<QS> and point<QS, PO>, and a reference for point<QS, PO>[U] and point<U, PO>), reference-interface provides the call operator and the observers shared by the two references, quantity-point-members provides the members that only a point has, the base classes listed below provide the hidden friends, and natural-point-origin-t and kind-of-t are the types of natural_point_origin and kind_of. The definitions of the exposition-only concepts QuantityLike and RoundingPolicy are given, as they say which types the framework accepts. QuantityLikeTraits<T> checks that quantity_like_traits<T> provides the members listed in Interoperability with other libraries. Public data members that exist only to make a type structural are shown as exposition-only too.
  • The static data members of dimensions, quantity specifications, units, magnitude constants, point origins, and point references are implementation details and are not shown.
  • Hidden friends are shown as friend declarations in the class that defines them, so they are found by argument-dependent lookup only. Those of delta-t and point-t take the class itself and are shown in it. The others don’t depend on the template arguments of the classes they serve, so a definition in a class template would be repeated by every specialization. They are shown in exposition-only non-template base classes, where each one is defined only once: dimension-interface, quantity-spec-interface, unit-magnitude-interface, unit-interface, reference-interface, point-origin-interface, symbol-text-interface, and quantity-interface.
  • Inside quantity and quantity-point-members, the concepts quantity_spec, dimension, and unit are qualified with std::, as members of the same names would hide them.
  • Facilities marked as // hosted (stream insertion operators and std::formatter specializations) are provided only by hosted implementations.

22.1 Symbol text

namespace std {

enum class character_set {
  unicode,  // µs; m³;  L²MT⁻³
  basic     // us; m^3; L^2MT^-3
};

template<size_t N, size_t M>
class symbol_text;

struct symbol-text-interface {  // exposition only
  // concatenation
  template<size_t N1, size_t M1, size_t N2, size_t M2>
  friend constexpr symbol_text<N1 + N2, M1 + M2> operator+(const symbol_text<N1, M1>& lhs, const symbol_text<N2, M2>& rhs);

  // comparison
  template<size_t N1, size_t M1, size_t N2, size_t M2>
  friend constexpr auto operator<=>(const symbol_text<N1, M1>& lhs, const symbol_text<N2, M2>& rhs) noexcept;

  template<size_t N1, size_t M1, size_t N2, size_t M2>
  friend constexpr bool operator==(const symbol_text<N1, M1>& lhs, const symbol_text<N2, M2>& rhs) noexcept;

  template<size_t N1, size_t M1>
  friend constexpr bool operator==(const symbol_text<N1, M1>& lhs, char rhs) noexcept
    requires requires { symbol_text<N1, M1>(rhs); };

  template<size_t N1, size_t M1>
  friend constexpr auto operator<=>(const symbol_text<N1, M1>& lhs, char rhs) noexcept
    requires requires { symbol_text<N1, M1>(rhs); };

  template<size_t N1, size_t M1, size_t N2>
  friend consteval bool operator==(const symbol_text<N1, M1>& lhs, const char (&rhs)[N2])
    requires requires { symbol_text<N1, M1>(rhs); };

  template<size_t N1, size_t M1, size_t N2>
  friend consteval auto operator<=>(const symbol_text<N1, M1>& lhs, const char (&rhs)[N2])
    requires requires { symbol_text<N1, M1>(rhs); };
};

template<size_t N, size_t M>
class symbol_text : public symbol-text-interface {
public:
  fixed_u8string<N> utf8-symbol;     // exposition only
  fixed_string<M> portable-symbol;   // exposition only

  // constructors
  constexpr explicit(false) symbol_text(char ch);
  consteval explicit(false) symbol_text(const char (&txt)[N + 1]);
  constexpr explicit(false) symbol_text(const fixed_string<N>& txt);
  consteval symbol_text(const char8_t (&u)[N + 1], const char (&a)[M + 1]);
  constexpr symbol_text(const fixed_u8string<N>& utf8, const fixed_string<M>& portable);

  // observers
  constexpr const auto& utf8() const;
  constexpr const auto& portable() const;
  constexpr bool empty() const;
};

symbol_text(char) -> symbol_text<1, 1>;

template<size_t N>
symbol_text(const char (&)[N]) -> symbol_text<N - 1, N - 1>;

template<size_t N>
symbol_text(const fixed_string<N>&) -> symbol_text<N, N>;

template<size_t N, size_t M>
symbol_text(const char8_t (&)[N], const char (&)[M]) -> symbol_text<N - 1, M - 1>;

template<size_t N, size_t M>
symbol_text(const fixed_u8string<N>&, const fixed_string<M>&) -> symbol_text<N, M>;

}

22.2 Symbolic expressions

namespace std {

template<SymbolicArg T, SymbolicArg... Ts>
struct per final {};  // exposition only

template<SymbolicArg F, int Num, int... Den>
  requires(valid-ratio<Num, Den...> && positive-ratio<Num, Den...> && !ratio-one<Num, Den...>)
struct power final {};  // exposition only

}

Note: Users never name per and power. These types come from *, /, inverse, pow, sqrt, cbrt, square, and cubic, so the standard does not reserve their names. An implementation chooses reserved spellings, for example __per and __power, and the resulting types keep the structure specified here.

22.3 Dimensions

namespace std {

struct dimension-interface;  // exposition only

template<symbol_text Symbol>
struct base_dimension;

// concepts
template<typename T>
concept dimension = derived_from<T, dimension-interface> && SymbolicConstant<T> &&
                    !is-specialization-of<remove_const_t<T>, base_dimension>;

struct dimension-interface {  // exposition only
  template<dimension Lhs, dimension Rhs>
  friend consteval dimension auto operator*(Lhs, Rhs);

  template<dimension Lhs, dimension Rhs>
  friend consteval dimension auto operator/(Lhs, Rhs);

  template<dimension Lhs, dimension Rhs>
  friend consteval bool operator==(Lhs, Rhs);

  friend consteval dimension auto inverse(dimension auto d);

  template<intmax_t Num, intmax_t Den = 1, dimension D>
    requires(Den != 0)
  friend consteval dimension auto pow(D d);

  friend consteval dimension auto sqrt(dimension auto d);

  friend consteval dimension auto cbrt(dimension auto d);
};

// dimensions
template<symbol_text Symbol>
struct base_dimension : dimension-interface {};

template<SymbolicTerm... Expr>
struct derived_dimension final : dimension-interface {};

inline constexpr struct dimension_one final : dimension-interface {
} dimension_one;

// symbol text
struct dimension_symbol_formatting {
  character_set char_set = character_set::unicode;
};

template<typename CharT = char, output_iterator<CharT> Out, dimension D>
constexpr Out dimension_symbol_to(Out out, D d, const dimension_symbol_formatting& fmt = dimension_symbol_formatting{});

template<dimension_symbol_formatting fmt = dimension_symbol_formatting{}, typename CharT = char, dimension D>
consteval basic_string_view<CharT> dimension_symbol(D);

}
// hosted
namespace std {

template<typename CharT, typename Traits, dimension D>
basic_ostream<CharT, Traits>& operator<<(basic_ostream<CharT, Traits>& os, D d);

template<typename D, typename Char>
  requires dimension<D>
class formatter<D, Char> {
public:
  constexpr auto parse(basic_format_parse_context<Char>& ctx) -> decltype(ctx.begin());

  template<typename FormatContext>
  constexpr auto format(const D& d, FormatContext& ctx) const -> decltype(ctx.out());
};

}

22.4 Quantity specifications

namespace std {

template<auto...>
struct named_quantity_spec;

struct quantity-spec-interface;  // exposition only

// concepts
template<typename T>
concept quantity_spec = derived_from<T, quantity-spec-interface> && SymbolicConstant<T> &&
                        !is-specialization-of<remove_const_t<T>, named_quantity_spec>;

template<typename T, auto V>
concept quantity_spec_of =
  quantity_spec<T> &&
  ((quantity_spec<decltype(V)> && implicitly-convertible(T{}, V)) ||
   (CharacterValue<V> &&
    overlaps(admitted-character(T{}).order, character-constraint<V>().order) &&
    overlaps(admitted-character(T{}).field, character-constraint<V>().field)));

// quantity character
enum class quantity_tensor_order { scalar, vector, tensor };
enum class quantity_field { real, complex };

struct quantity_character {
  quantity_tensor_order order = quantity_tensor_order::scalar;
  quantity_field field = quantity_field::real;

  consteval quantity_character() = default;
  consteval quantity_character(quantity_tensor_order tensor_order, quantity_field numeric_field);
  consteval quantity_character(quantity_tensor_order tensor_order);
  consteval quantity_character(quantity_field numeric_field);
};

// quantity specification properties
inline constexpr struct subkind {
} subkind;

// quantity specification interface
struct quantity-spec-interface {  // exposition only
  // the reference of a delta, or of a point for a point specification; for a QS that isn't a point
  // specification, QS[U] is ill-formed for an offset unit U, where delta<QS>[U] is the reference of
  // a delta, and QS[U] is the same reference as delta<QS>[U] for any other unit; point<QS>[U] is
  // ill-formed when the origin of U is not the natural origin of QS
  template<typename Self, unit_of<Self{}> U>
  consteval quantity_reference auto operator[](this Self, U);

  template<typename Self, typename FwdQ, delta_quantity Q = remove_cvref_t<FwdQ>>
    requires(explicitly-convertible(Q::quantity_spec, Self{})) &&
            requires { typename quantity<make-reference(Self{}, Q::unit), typename Q::rep>; }
  constexpr delta_quantity auto operator()(this Self, FwdQ&& q);

  // point-target(QS, PO) is QS for a point specification, and for any other QS it is
  // point<QS, PO> when PO is an origin for QS, and point<QS> otherwise;
  // make-point-reference(QS, U, PO) is the reference of a point of the point specification QS in
  // the unit U, measured from PO when PO is an origin for the scale of QS, and from the origin of
  // QS otherwise; delta<QS>(qp) is ill-formed, and the origin of the result is computed: the origin
  // of qp is kept, rebased onto the origin of the target, or the call is ill-formed
  template<typename Self, typename FwdQP, point_quantity QP = remove_cvref_t<FwdQP>>
    requires(explicitly-convertible(QP::quantity_spec, point-target(Self{}, QP::point_origin))) && requires {
      typename quantity<make-point-reference(point-target(Self{}, QP::point_origin), QP::unit, QP::point_origin),
                        typename QP::rep>;
    }
  constexpr point_quantity auto operator()(this Self, FwdQP&& qp);

  template<typename Self, typename FwdValue, representation_of<Self{}> Value = remove_cvref_t<FwdValue>>
    requires(explicitly-convertible-to-dimensionless(Self{}))
  constexpr delta_quantity auto operator()(this Self, FwdValue&& val);

  // operations; ScalarOperand<Q> holds when Q admits the scalar order (a scalar or a quantity
  // kind), and NonScalarOperand<Q> when Q admits the vector or the tensor order
  template<quantity_spec Lhs, quantity_spec Rhs>
    requires(!PointQuantitySpec<Lhs>) && (!PointQuantitySpec<Rhs>) &&
            (ScalarOperand<Lhs> || ScalarOperand<Rhs>)
  friend consteval quantity_spec auto operator*(Lhs lhs, Rhs rhs);

  template<quantity_spec Lhs, quantity_spec Rhs>
    requires(!PointQuantitySpec<Lhs>) && (!PointQuantitySpec<Rhs>) && ScalarOperand<Rhs>
  friend consteval quantity_spec auto operator/(Lhs lhs, Rhs rhs);

  template<quantity_spec Lhs, quantity_spec Rhs>
  friend consteval bool operator==(Lhs, Rhs);

  template<quantity_spec Q>
    requires(!PointQuantitySpec<Q>) && ScalarOperand<Q>
  friend consteval quantity_spec auto inverse(Q q);

  template<intmax_t Num, intmax_t Den = 1, quantity_spec Q>
    requires(Den != 0) && (!PointQuantitySpec<Q>) && (ScalarOperand<Q> || Num == Den)
  friend consteval quantity_spec auto pow(Q q);

  template<quantity_spec Q>
    requires(!PointQuantitySpec<Q>) && ScalarOperand<Q>
  friend consteval quantity_spec auto sqrt(Q q);

  template<quantity_spec Q>
    requires(!PointQuantitySpec<Q>) && ScalarOperand<Q>
  friend consteval quantity_spec auto cbrt(Q q);

  // a real scalar of the dimension of Q, magnitude-t<Q> for a Q that isn't a quantity kind,
  // and Q itself for a quantity kind
  template<quantity_spec Q>
    requires(!PointQuantitySpec<Q>) && NonScalarOperand<Q>
  friend consteval quantity_spec auto magnitude(Q q);

  // observers
  template<quantity_spec QS>
  friend consteval dimension auto get_dimension(QS qs);
};

// quantity specifications
template<BaseDimension auto Dim, QSProperty auto... Args>
struct named_quantity_spec<Dim, Args...> : quantity-spec-interface {};

// EquationSpec<T> holds for a derived quantity specification and for magnitude-t<V>
template<EquationSpec auto Eq, QSProperty auto... Args>
struct named_quantity_spec<Eq, Args...> : quantity-spec-interface {};

template<NamedQuantitySpec auto QS, QSProperty auto... Args>
struct named_quantity_spec<QS, Args...> : quantity-spec-interface {};

// defining-equation-fits(Eq, QS) is explicitly-convertible(Eq, QS) with the character of the two
// left out, so that a vector can be defined below a scalar
template<NamedQuantitySpec auto QS, EquationSpec auto Eq, QSProperty auto... Args>
  requires(defining-equation-fits(Eq, QS))
struct named_quantity_spec<QS, Eq, Args...> : quantity-spec-interface {};

template<SymbolicTerm... Expr>
struct derived_quantity_spec : quantity-spec-interface {};

// the magnitude of a vector or tensor quantity specification V that isn't a quantity kind
template<quantity_spec V>
struct magnitude-t : quantity-spec-interface {};  // exposition only

inline constexpr struct dimensionless : named_quantity_spec<derived_quantity_spec<>{}> {
} dimensionless;

template<typename Q>
struct kind-of-t;

template<quantity_spec Q>
  requires SymbolicArg<Q> && (!QuantityKindSpec<Q>) && (!PointQuantitySpec<Q>) && (!DeltaQuantitySpec<Q>) &&
           (get-kind-tree-root(Q{}) == Q{})
struct kind-of-t<Q> : see below {};

template<quantity_spec auto Q>
  requires(!PointQuantitySpec<decltype(Q)>) && (!DeltaQuantitySpec<decltype(Q)>) &&
           requires { typename kind-of-t<decltype(Q)>; }
constexpr kind-of-t<decltype(Q)> kind_of;

// quantity specification of a delta: delta<QS> stands for QS wherever a quantity specification is
// expected, and its subscript operator also accepts an offset unit
template<quantity_spec Q>
  requires SymbolicArg<Q> && (!PointQuantitySpec<Q>) && (!DeltaQuantitySpec<Q>)
struct delta-spec-t : quantity-spec-interface {};  // exposition only

// quantity specifications of points
template<typename...>
struct point-t;

// point<QS>, measured from natural_point_origin<QS>
template<quantity_spec Q>
  requires SymbolicArg<Q> && (!PointQuantitySpec<Q>) && (!DeltaQuantitySpec<Q>)
struct point-t<Q> : quantity-spec-interface {};

// point<QS, PO>, measured from PO
template<quantity_spec Q, PointOrigin PO>
  requires SymbolicArg<Q> && (!PointQuantitySpec<Q>) && (!DeltaQuantitySpec<Q>) && point_origin_for<PO, Q{}>
struct point-t<Q, PO> : quantity-spec-interface {};

// observers

template<quantity_spec Q>
consteval quantity_spec auto get_kind(Q);

}

22.5 Unit magnitudes

namespace std {

template<auto... Ms>
struct unit-magnitude;  // exposition only

// concepts
template<typename T>
concept unit_magnitude = is-specialization-of<remove_const_t<T>, unit-magnitude>;

struct unit-magnitude-interface {  // exposition only
  template<unit_magnitude M>
  friend consteval unit_magnitude auto operator-(M m);

  template<unit_magnitude Lhs, unit_magnitude Rhs>
  friend consteval unit_magnitude auto operator*(Lhs lhs, Rhs rhs);

  template<unit_magnitude Lhs, unit_magnitude Rhs>
  friend consteval auto operator/(Lhs lhs, Rhs rhs);

  template<unit_magnitude Lhs, unit_magnitude Rhs>
  friend consteval bool operator==(Lhs, Rhs);

  template<int Num, int Den = 1, unit_magnitude M>
  friend consteval auto pow(M m);
};

template<auto... Ms>
struct unit-magnitude : unit-magnitude-interface {};  // exposition only

// magnitude constants
template<symbol_text Symbol, long double Value>
  requires(Value > 0)
struct mag_constant {};

inline constexpr struct pi-c final :  // exposition only
    mag_constant<symbol_text{u8"π", "pi"}, numbers::pi_v<long double>> {} pi-c;

// magnitude factories
template<MagArg auto V>
  requires is-nonzero-mag-arg<V>
constexpr unit_magnitude auto mag = see below;

template<intmax_t N, intmax_t D>
  requires(N != 0)
constexpr unit_magnitude auto mag_ratio = see below;

template<MagArg auto Base, int Num, int Den = 1>
  requires is-positive-mag-arg<Base>
constexpr unit_magnitude auto mag_power = pow<Num, Den>(mag<Base>);

}

22.6 Units

22.6.1 Concepts

namespace std {

struct unit-interface;  // exposition only

template<symbol_text Symbol, auto...>
struct named_unit;

template<typename T>
concept unit = derived_from<T, unit-interface> && SymbolicConstant<T> &&
               !is-specialization-of<remove_const_t<T>, named_unit> &&
               !is-specialization-of-prefixed-unit<remove_const_t<T>>;

template<typename T>
concept prefixable_unit = unit<T> && is-derived-from-specialization-of<T, named_unit>;

template<typename U, auto QS>
concept unit_of = unit<U> && quantity_spec<decltype(QS)> && implicitly-convertible(get_quantity_spec(U{}), remove-point(QS));

}

22.6.2 Unit types

namespace std {

struct unit-interface {  // exposition only
  // operations
  template<unit_magnitude M, unit U>
  friend consteval unit auto operator*(M, U u);
  friend consteval unit auto operator*(unit auto, unit_magnitude auto) = delete;

  template<unit_magnitude M, unit U>
  friend consteval unit auto operator/(M m, U u);

  template<unit Lhs, unit Rhs>
  friend consteval unit auto operator*(Lhs lhs, Rhs rhs);

  template<unit Lhs, unit Rhs>
  friend consteval unit auto operator/(Lhs lhs, Rhs rhs);

  template<unit Lhs, unit Rhs>
  friend consteval bool operator==(Lhs, Rhs);

  template<unit Lhs, unit Rhs>
  friend consteval bool equivalent(Lhs lhs, Rhs rhs);  // exposition only

  template<intmax_t Num, intmax_t Den = 1, unit U>
    requires(Den != 0)
  friend consteval unit auto pow(U u);

  friend consteval unit auto sqrt(unit auto u);
  friend consteval unit auto cbrt(unit auto u);
  friend consteval unit auto square(unit auto u);
  friend consteval unit auto cubic(unit auto u);
  friend consteval unit auto inverse(unit auto u);

  // observers
  template<unit Self>
  friend consteval Self get_unit(Self self);

  template<unit U>
  friend consteval quantity_spec auto get_quantity_spec(U);
};

// scaled_unit
template<unit_magnitude auto M, unit U>
  requires(M != mag<1>) && SymbolicArg<U>
struct scaled_unit final : unit-interface {};

// named_unit
template<symbol_text Symbol, auto...>
struct named_unit;

template<symbol_text Symbol, QuantityKindSpec auto QS>
  requires(!Symbol.empty()) && (BaseDimension<decltype(get_dimension(QS))> || remove-kind(QS) == dimensionless)
struct named_unit<Symbol, QS> : unit-interface {};

template<symbol_text Symbol, QuantityKindSpec auto QS, PointOrigin auto PO>
  requires(!Symbol.empty()) && (BaseDimension<decltype(get_dimension(QS))> || remove-kind(QS) == dimensionless)
struct named_unit<Symbol, QS, PO> : unit-interface {};

template<symbol_text Symbol, unit auto U>
  requires(!Symbol.empty()) && is-positive-canonical-unit-mag<U>
struct named_unit<Symbol, U> : unit-interface {};

template<symbol_text Symbol, unit auto U, PointOrigin auto PO>
  requires(!Symbol.empty()) && is-positive-canonical-unit-mag<U>
struct named_unit<Symbol, U, PO> : unit-interface {};

template<symbol_text Symbol, unit auto U, QuantityKindSpec auto QS>
  requires(!Symbol.empty()) &&
          (get_dimension(QS) == get_dimension(get-associated-quantity(U))) &&
          is-positive-canonical-unit-mag<U>
struct named_unit<Symbol, U, QS> : unit-interface {};

template<symbol_text Symbol, unit auto U, QuantityKindSpec auto QS, PointOrigin auto PO>
  requires(!Symbol.empty()) &&
          (get_dimension(QS) == get_dimension(get-associated-quantity(U))) &&
          is-positive-canonical-unit-mag<U>
struct named_unit<Symbol, U, QS, PO> : unit-interface {};

// named_constant
template<symbol_text Symbol, unit auto U>
  requires(!Symbol.empty())
struct named_constant : unit-interface {};

// prefixed_unit
template<symbol_text Symbol, unit_magnitude auto M, prefixable_unit auto U>
  requires(!Symbol.empty() && M != mag<1>)
struct prefixed_unit : unit-interface {};

// common_unit
template<unit U1, unit U2, unit... Rest>
  requires SymbolicArg<U1> && SymbolicArg<U2> && (... && SymbolicArg<Rest>)
struct common_unit final : unit-interface {};

// derived_unit
template<SymbolicTerm... Expr>
struct derived_unit final : unit-interface {};

// one
inline constexpr struct one final : unit-interface {} one;

}

22.6.3 Dimensionless units and constants

namespace std {

inline constexpr struct percent final :
    named_unit<"%", mag_ratio<1, 100> * one> {} percent;

inline constexpr struct per_mille final :
    named_unit<symbol_text{u8"‰", "%o"}, mag_ratio<1, 1000> * one> {} per_mille;

inline constexpr struct parts_per_million final :
    named_unit<"ppm", mag_ratio<1, 1'000'000> * one> {} parts_per_million;

inline constexpr auto ppm = parts_per_million;

inline constexpr struct pi final :
    named_constant<symbol_text{u8"π", "pi"}, mag<pi-c> * one> {} pi;

inline constexpr auto π = pi;

}

22.7 Unit symbols

namespace std {

enum class unit_symbol_solidus {
  one_denominator,  // m/s;   kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹
  always,           // m/s;   kg/(m s)
  never             // m s⁻¹; kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹
};

enum class unit_symbol_separator {
  space,         // kg m²/s²
  half_high_dot  // kg⋅m²/s²  (valid only for the `unicode` character set)
};

struct unit_symbol_formatting {
  character_set char_set = character_set::unicode;
  unit_symbol_solidus solidus = unit_symbol_solidus::one_denominator;
  unit_symbol_separator separator = unit_symbol_separator::space;
};

template<unit auto U>
constexpr bool space_before_unit_symbol = true;

template<>
inline constexpr bool space_before_unit_symbol<one> = false;

template<typename CharT = char, output_iterator<CharT> Out, unit U>
constexpr Out unit_symbol_to(Out out, U u, const unit_symbol_formatting& fmt = unit_symbol_formatting{});

template<unit_symbol_formatting fmt = unit_symbol_formatting{}, typename CharT = char, unit U>
consteval basic_string_view<CharT> unit_symbol(U);

}
// hosted
namespace std {

template<typename CharT, typename Traits, unit U>
basic_ostream<CharT, Traits>& operator<<(basic_ostream<CharT, Traits>& os, U u);

template<typename U, typename Char>
  requires unit<U>
class formatter<U, Char> {
public:
  constexpr auto parse(basic_format_parse_context<Char>& ctx) -> decltype(ctx.begin());

  template<typename FormatContext>
  constexpr auto format(const U& u, FormatContext& ctx) const -> decltype(ctx.out());
};

}

22.8 References

namespace std {

// concepts
template<typename T>
concept quantity_reference = LinearReference<remove_const_t<T>> || PointReference<T>;

template<typename T, auto QS>
concept quantity_reference_of = quantity_reference<T> && quantity_spec_of<decltype(get_quantity_spec(T{})), QS>;

// the interface shared by the references of a delta and of a point
struct reference-interface {  // exposition only
  template<typename Self, typename FwdRep, representation_of<get_quantity_spec(Self{})> Rep = remove_cvref_t<FwdRep>>
  constexpr quantity<see below, Rep> operator()(this Self, FwdRep&& value);

  // observers
  template<WrappingReference R>
  friend consteval quantity_spec auto get_quantity_spec(R);

  template<WrappingReference R>
  friend consteval unit auto get_unit(R);
};

// class template delta-t, the reference of a delta
template<typename...>
struct delta-t;

// delta-t<U> for a unit, delta-t<QS, U> for a plain quantity specification QS and a unit; the
// quantity specification of both is a plain one, never delta-spec-t
template<typename... Args>
  requires delta-arguments<Args...>
struct delta-t<Args...> : reference-interface {
  template<typename... Args2>
  friend consteval bool operator==(delta-t, delta-t<Args2...>);

  template<unit U2>
  friend consteval bool operator==(delta-t, U2 u2);

  // the operations of references follow those of their quantity specifications (QS is the
  // quantity specification of this reference, and QS2 the one of delta-t<Args2...>)
  template<typename... Args2>
    requires(ScalarOperand<QS> || ScalarOperand<QS2>)
  friend consteval quantity_reference auto operator*(delta-t, delta-t<Args2...>);

  template<unit U2>
  friend consteval quantity_reference auto operator*(delta-t, U2);

  template<unit U1>
  friend consteval quantity_reference auto operator*(U1, delta-t);

  template<typename... Args2>
    requires ScalarOperand<QS2>
  friend consteval quantity_reference auto operator/(delta-t, delta-t<Args2...>);

  template<unit U2>
  friend consteval quantity_reference auto operator/(delta-t, U2);

  template<unit U1>
    requires ScalarOperand<QS>
  friend consteval quantity_reference auto operator/(U1, delta-t);

  friend consteval quantity_reference auto inverse(delta-t)
    requires ScalarOperand<QS>;

  template<intmax_t Num, intmax_t Den = 1>
    requires(Den != 0) && (ScalarOperand<QS> || Num == Den)
  friend consteval quantity_reference auto pow(delta-t);

  friend consteval quantity_reference auto sqrt(delta-t)
    requires ScalarOperand<QS>;
  friend consteval quantity_reference auto cbrt(delta-t)
    requires ScalarOperand<QS>;
};

// delta<U> of a unit U is the reference delta-t<decltype(U)>, and delta<QS> of a plain quantity
// specification QS is the quantity specification delta-spec-t<decltype(QS)>
template<auto Arg>
  requires unit<decltype(Arg)> ||
           (quantity_spec<decltype(Arg)> && !PointQuantitySpec<decltype(Arg)> && !DeltaQuantitySpec<decltype(Arg)>)
constexpr auto delta = see below;

// creating quantities
template<typename FwdRep, LinearReference R, representation_of<get_quantity_spec(R{})> Rep = remove_cvref_t<FwdRep>>
  requires(!OffsetUnit<decltype(get_unit(R{}))>)
constexpr quantity<R{}, Rep> operator*(FwdRep&& lhs, R r);

template<typename FwdRep, LinearReference R, representation_of<get_quantity_spec(R{})> Rep = remove_cvref_t<FwdRep>>
  requires(!OffsetUnit<decltype(get_unit(R{}))>)
constexpr delta_quantity auto operator/(FwdRep&& lhs, R);

template<LinearReference R, typename Rep>
  requires representation_of<remove_cvref_t<Rep>, get_quantity_spec(R{})>
constexpr auto operator*(R, Rep&&) = delete;

template<LinearReference R, typename Rep>
  requires representation_of<remove_cvref_t<Rep>, get_quantity_spec(R{})>
constexpr auto operator/(R, Rep&&) = delete;

// changing the reference of a quantity
template<typename FwdQ, LinearReference R, delta_quantity Q = remove_cvref_t<FwdQ>>
constexpr delta_quantity auto operator*(FwdQ&& q, R);

template<typename FwdQ, LinearReference R, delta_quantity Q = remove_cvref_t<FwdQ>>
constexpr delta_quantity auto operator/(FwdQ&& q, R);

template<LinearReference R, typename Q>
  requires delta_quantity<remove_cvref_t<Q>>
constexpr auto operator*(R, Q&& q) = delete;

template<LinearReference R, typename Q>
  requires delta_quantity<remove_cvref_t<Q>>
constexpr auto operator/(R, Q&& q) = delete;

}

22.9 Point origins

namespace std {

struct point-origin-interface;  // exposition only

// concepts
template<typename T>
concept PointOrigin =  // exposition only
  derived_from<T, point-origin-interface> && SymbolicConstant<T> &&
  !is-specialization-of-absolute-point-origin<remove_const_t<T>> &&
  !is-specialization-of-relative-point-origin<remove_const_t<T>>;

template<typename T, auto QS>
concept point_origin_for = PointOrigin<T> && quantity_spec_of<decltype(remove-point(QS)), remove-point(T::quantity-spec)>;

// point origins
template<quantity_spec auto QS>
struct absolute_point_origin;

template<point_quantity auto QP>
struct relative_point_origin;

struct point-origin-interface {  // exposition only
  template<PointOrigin PO>
  friend consteval quantity_spec auto get_quantity_spec(PO po);

  template<PointOrigin PO1, SameAbsolutePointOriginAs<PO1{}> PO2>
    requires(point_origin_for<PO2, get_quantity_spec(PO1{})> ||
             point_origin_for<PO1, get_quantity_spec(PO2{})>) &&
            (is-derived-from-specialization-of<PO1, relative_point_origin> ||
             is-derived-from-specialization-of<PO2, relative_point_origin>)
  friend constexpr delta_quantity auto operator-(PO1, PO2);

  // affine space operators with a point origin operand
  template<PointOrigin PO, typename FwdQ, delta_quantity Q = remove_cvref_t<FwdQ>>
    requires point_origin_for<PO, Q::quantity_spec>
  friend constexpr point_quantity auto operator+(PO po, FwdQ&& q);

  template<typename FwdQ, PointOrigin PO, delta_quantity Q = remove_cvref_t<FwdQ>>
    requires point_origin_for<PO, Q::quantity_spec>
  friend constexpr point_quantity auto operator+(FwdQ&& q, PO po);

  template<PointOrigin PO, delta_quantity Q>
    requires point_origin_for<PO, Q::quantity_spec> && requires(const Q& q) { -q; }
  friend constexpr point_quantity auto operator-(PO po, const Q& q);

  template<point_quantity QP, PointOrigin PO>
    requires quantity_of<QP, PO{}> && quantity_reference_of<decltype(QP::reference), get_quantity_spec(PO{})>
  friend constexpr delta_quantity auto operator-(const QP& qp, PO po);

  template<PointOrigin PO, point_quantity QP>
    requires quantity_of<QP, PO{}> && quantity_reference_of<decltype(QP::reference), get_quantity_spec(PO{})>
  friend constexpr delta_quantity auto operator-(PO po, const QP& qp);

  template<PointOrigin PO1, PointOrigin PO2>
  friend consteval bool operator==(PO1 po1, PO2 po2);
};

template<quantity_spec auto QS>
struct absolute_point_origin : point-origin-interface {};

template<point_quantity auto QP>
struct relative_point_origin : point-origin-interface {};

// a class derived from it, such as si::absolute_zero, is the same natural origin under a name of its own
template<quantity_spec auto QS>
  requires(!PointQuantitySpec<decltype(QS)>)
struct natural-point-origin-t : absolute_point_origin<QS> {};

template<quantity_spec auto QS>
constexpr natural-point-origin-t<remove-point(QS)> natural_point_origin;

}

22.10 Point references

namespace std {

// a unit, optionally preceded by the quantity specification of the scale and followed by the
// origin the point is measured from: point-t<U>, point-t<QS, U>, point-t<U, PO>, point-t<QS, U, PO>
template<typename... Args>
  requires point-reference-arguments<Args...>
struct point-t<Args...> : reference-interface {
  template<typename... Args2>
    requires PointReference<point-t<Args2...>>
  friend consteval bool operator==(point-t, point-t<Args2...>);

  template<LinearReference R2>
  friend consteval bool operator==(point-t, R2);
};

// the origin of the unit of R (si::ice_point for si::degree_Celsius), or the natural point
// origin of its quantity specification
template<typename R>
  requires unit<R> || LinearReference<R>
consteval point_origin_for<get_quantity_spec(R{})> auto default_point_origin(R);

// for a quantity specification QS that is not a point, point<QS> and point<QS, PO> are the quantity
// specifications point-t<decltype(QS)> and point-t<decltype(QS), decltype(PO)>, and their
// subscript operator gives the reference of a point; for a unit U, point<U> and point<U, PO> are the
// references point<K, default_point_origin(U)>[U] and point<K, PO>[U], where K is the quantity kind
// of U; a point reference is the type point-t spelled with its unit, preceded by its quantity
// specification when it is not the kind associated with the unit, and followed by its origin when
// it is not the default one of the unit
template<auto Arg, auto... Rest>
  requires PointArguments<Arg, Rest...>
constexpr auto point = see below;

}

22.11 Representation types

22.11.1 Traits

namespace std {

// representation_underlying_type
template<typename T>
struct representation_underlying_type {};

template<typename T>
struct representation_underlying_type<const T> : representation_underlying_type<T> {};

template<typename T>
  requires is_scoped_enum_v<T>
struct representation_underlying_type<T> {
  using type = underlying_type_t<T>;
};

template<has-value-type-member T>
struct representation_underlying_type<T> : cond-underlying-type<typename T::value_type> {};

template<has-element-type-member T>
struct representation_underlying_type<T> : cond-underlying-type<typename T::element_type> {};

template<has-value-type-member T>
  requires has-element-type-member<T>
struct representation_underlying_type<T> {};

template<has-value-type-member T>
  requires has-element-type-member<T> && same_as<remove_cv_t<typename T::value_type>, remove_cv_t<typename T::element_type>>
struct representation_underlying_type<T> : cond-underlying-type<typename T::value_type> {};

template<typename T>
  requires requires { typename representation_underlying_type<T>::type; }
using representation_underlying_type_t = typename representation_underlying_type<T>::type;

// representation_canonical_type
template<typename T>
struct representation_canonical_type {
  using type = T;
};

template<typename T>
struct representation_canonical_type<const T> : representation_canonical_type<T> {};

template<typename T>
struct representation_canonical_type<T&> : representation_canonical_type<T> {};

template<typename T>
struct representation_canonical_type<T&&> : representation_canonical_type<T> {};

template<typename T>
using representation_canonical_type_t = typename representation_canonical_type<T>::type;

// tensor_order
template<typename T>
constexpr unspecified-t tensor_order;

template<typename T>
  requires(!has-ambiguous-order<T>)
constexpr size_t tensor_order<T> = see below;

// numeric_field
template<typename T>
constexpr unspecified-t numeric_field;

template<typename T>
  requires field-consistent<T>
constexpr quantity_field numeric_field<T> = see below;

// disable_representation
template<typename T>
constexpr bool disable_representation = see below;

template<>
inline constexpr bool disable_representation<bool> = true;

template<>
inline constexpr bool disable_representation<char> = true;

template<>
inline constexpr bool disable_representation<wchar_t> = true;

template<>
inline constexpr bool disable_representation<char8_t> = true;

template<>
inline constexpr bool disable_representation<char16_t> = true;

template<>
inline constexpr bool disable_representation<char32_t> = true;

template<SymbolicConstant T>
inline constexpr bool disable_representation<T> = true;

// treat_as_floating_point
template<typename Rep>
constexpr bool treat_as_floating_point = see below;

// representation_values
template<typename Rep>
struct representation_values : chrono::duration_values<Rep> {
  // freestanding: not derived from chrono::duration_values<Rep>; instead declares
  //   static constexpr Rep zero() noexcept
  //     requires constructible_from<Rep, int>;
  //   static constexpr Rep min() noexcept
  //     requires numeric_limits<Rep>::is_specialized && requires {
  //       { numeric_limits<Rep>::lowest() } -> same_as<Rep>;
  //     };
  //   static constexpr Rep max() noexcept
  //     requires numeric_limits<Rep>::is_specialized && requires {
